1764649: My student and I were performing TOLs [Take Off and Landings] at Coolidge on the morning of Month, date, when the pattern was relatively light. At that time, there were two other aircraft in the pattern executing touch and goes for Runway 23. At some point, Aircraft Y flew in on what may have been the GPS approach. I am not sure Aircraft Y made any calls on his way in. There were a few planes lining up on that approach and their call may have been lost with the others. I was watching my ADS-B and noticed this aircraft had gone 'missed' on 23 and began a 45 degree turn toward downwind. My initial thought was that they were probably offsetting. However, their course did not change. This was extremely unsettling because we were on downwind. By the time I put this all together (a few seconds), I realized that I could not get a visual fix on the aircraft. Why? Because they were on a direct collision course with us as they climbed up through my student's download leg (which was perfect, according to her). I noticed Aircraft X's altitude, which I believe was -200 from us, looked out again and saw them coming right at us. 'My controls', power out and dive. I dropped us 400ft out of our pattern altitude. I believe this was the safest thing to do. I do not think I would have been able to safely out climb them and it was clear that they were oblivious to our presence. The aircraft passed over us at 2600 (right where we would have been). I cannot place myself in the mindset of the pilot, but what would possess a pilot or an instructor to fly into an established downwind pattern going the wrong way?ADS-B may have played a direct role in preventing a potentially fatal accident. Without ADS-B, the probability of making visual contact with Aircraft Y when the aircraft was angled at us and climbing was low. Knowing this makes me cringe a little when I think about the number of aircraft out there without this technology installed. Collision avoidance is not just about the skill level of the 'other guy'. There needs to be a moment of self reflection about what we do out there. Understanding that fact has given me pause about going back to P08 until I am able to justify the risks of being in an airspace with consistently unpredictable traffic. I am currently not able to convince myself that the risks are worth it. I can safely practice TOLs at Gateway, Chandler, or even (if one is cautious) Eloy. After about two more landings, my student and I decided to leave the pattern as more planes were joining from opposite directions on approaches. We came home to ZZZ where it was a busy, but safe environment. If I eventually decide to go back to that zoo for VFR flying I will do so with extra vigilance.
1764975: At approximately XA00 local time, at ZZZ at an uncontrolled field, I taxied out to the threshold of RWY XXL in biplane single place open cockpit with no Radio. Seeing [no] aircraft in the pattern or on final, I proceeded to take off. Unknown and unseen by myself, a Beech aircraft lowing four-place mono airplane was approaching to land on Rwy XXL. The Beech pilot initiated a go-around to an uneventful landing, announcing that a runway incursion had occurred. Aircraft separation was estimated as several hundred yards, and no damage was incurred by either Aircraft. Difficulty in seeing a blue and white aircraft with blue sky background, and the Aircraft was not flying the designated traffic Encourage all traffic to fly a designated flight pattern and maintain visual awareness and alert to all traffic.
1765143: Long Beach Harbor has a long history of sea plane operations that reach back to the dawn of Aviation. One of the first commercial aviation operations was passenger service to Catalina Island from Long Beach and the iconic Spruce goose flew it's only Flight there.Late on a hazy but otherwise benign weather weekend afternoon, I departed the Long Beach Airport for a short flight to the Harbor. From a vantage point at the foot of the LA River, I could see conditions were conducive to seaplane operations. I contacted the tower to inform them of my intentions to conduct multiple seaplane operations within the southern boundary of their Class D airspace and received the usual acknowledgment with the catchphrase 'At your own risk.'The area chosen for those operations lay parallel to the shoreline and 150 feet south of the swimming buoys. (I have conducted many seaplane operations in this same area over the last XX years, as have other seaplane pilots.)My first pass remained airborne at 50 feet above the surface to insure there were no hazards in the water. The next three passes involved multiple touch and goes from the surface. I saw no swimmers south of the buoys.I departed the area southbound, climbing to pattern altitude plus 500 feet before turning 180deg back to the airport.While taxing to parking, the tower informed me there had been a complaint that my operations were too close to swimmers.
1765261: We went around at 900 AGL due to improper configuration on an autoland. We were doing an Autoland approach and the system did not arm at GS intercept on the practice CAT III. PM was watching outside for traffic on a parallel approach. As the flying pilot I got totally sucked into my display and did [not] configure in time for a stabilized approach and decided at 900 AGL to initiate [a] go-around. Go-around was uneventful.Having not flown a lot in the last couple months I allowed myself to get distracted with the display and lost overall situational awareness in regards to proper aircraft configuration.
1765676: I was the pilot flying. I had never been to ZZZ. Captain was pilot monitoring. During descent, ZZZ Approach advised that the tower would be closing soon and to advise ZZZ in sight for a visual to XX. We had reviewed all applicable Jeppesen pages including Tower closed procedures. ZZZ confused us initially with the statement Tower would be closing soon, as it was a little after XA00L [local time], so we didn't know if that meant we would be getting in before they officially closed. We got the field in sight and Approach cleared us for the visual and said to contact them on the ground to close our flight plan. Focusing on flying, I don't remember them saying to switch to CTAF or XYZ.X for advisories, but I knew that was the plan and didn't see that when the Captain switched frequencies and began making call outs that he had switched to UNICOM instead of CTAF. While I haven't done a lot of flying into airports with a closed Tower, when I have, it wasn't uncommon for transmissions in the blind to go unanswered so it didn't concern me when no one responded to our calls. I followed the guidance to align with [Runway] XX and started descent on glide path. It was right around 1,000 when I called stable that I noticed yellow flashing lights in the center of the touchdown zone. I mentioned to the Captain and said I thought there might be a vehicle on the runway. We continued and just after he called out the 500 foot call I noticed the light moving down the runway and then could make out brake lights illuminate on the vehicle. I called out I was going around for a vehicle on the runway and the Captain acknowledged. I executed the go-around and we went back to approach frequency and advised them what had happened. He cleared us for another visual and we again made all the appropriate calls, although on the wrong frequency, and landed uneventfully.Although it was clear in the company pages, we had some initial confusion as to exactly when the Tower would close. NOTAM had said XA00L, but it was after that, approximately XA05L when approach said Tower would be closing shortly. We were only 5 minutes out so I think we both had some impression that Tower may still be open when we landed. On the Jeppesen pages UNICOM is listed right next to Tower/CTAF and I think as things were happening quickly when Tower cleared us and we realized Tower was now closed we were configuring and I believe the Captain just looked and grabbed the wrong frequency.A more thorough discussion between both pilots to make sure we are both seeing the same information and are on the same page as to what the exact procedures we will follow in unusual operations such as a closed Tower. Flying with ZZZ Approach vectoring for final to Runway XX when Approach warned of the Tower closing. First Officer flying and proceeded to the outer marker and called the field in sight. ZZZ Approach advised to switch frequency, but to call back and cancel IFR after we land. I looked at the airport diagram and saw UNICOM and used that frequency to announce our position. After we were fully configured and on short final we saw a vehicle on the runway. We continued until about 300 feet then did a go-around called ZZZ Approach to advise of our situation. He offered vectors, but we had the field in sight went back to UNICOM and landed canceled IFR clearance and taxied to the gate. First day back flying after taking extended time off. Leg 3 at night and not expecting the Tower closure. After reading the FOM the next day I realized CTAF is the correct frequency to use. Also looked at 10-9 pages and found the note about Tower closure procedures. Having been to an uncontrolled airport once in my career and the First Officer running the radio I was unaware of the procedures. Why would UNICOM frequency be listed?
1765992: While enroute to GTF, the CA (Captain) who was PM (Pilot Monitoring) requested direct DATSA with Center in order to set up for RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 21. As we neared DATSA, Approach Control gave us a vector towards the northeast for sequence. After a few minutes we were given a vector towards the southeast and the controller asked if we still wanted the RNAV Z Approach. We said yes. He gave us a clearance direct to 'DRIFT'. I pushed DTO (Direct To) and used the FMS to fly direct to the fix DRFTR (I thought the controller was simply using a different pronunciation of the same fix). Shortly after, the CA realized that there was another fix on the approach: DRYFT, which was not in our flight plan in the FMS since we had used DATSA as our IAF. He queried the controller who confirmed that he had cleared us to DRYFT. At this point I had the airport in sight and we requested a visual approach. We were cleared for the Visual to RWY 21 and performed a stable visual approach.The lesson I learned is to listen more carefully to the spelling of the fix the controller is giving us and not just assume it's the fix that sounds close to what he said. I recommend that one of these two fixes DRFTR and DRYFT be changed to something different. These two fixes are close to each other on the approach and the spelling and pronunciations are similar enough to cause confusion.
1766003: TCAS RA while flying inbound on ILS XXR ZZZ. Exceptionally busy local ZZZ Tower Controller with multiple VFR in pattern and adjacent Class D airspace including helicopter operations. Listening to [the] Controller manage multiple, busy aircraft in [the] pattern including one helicopter, [I] slowed [the] aircraft to 180 kt., downwind pattern entry. Numerous call outs additionally for traffic just outside control zone led to heavy workload for crew entering pattern. Called out airport in sight and given visual clearance on 8-mile left base XXR. Joined localizer inbound. [A] low level helicopter in pattern was consuming [the] majority of [the] Tower Controller instructions either due to training occurring in [the] helicopter, or [an] inability to comply with Tower instructions and widening their pattern out for [the] landing jet - us. Continuing inbound at the marker, I elected to stay one dot above glide slope due to [the] continuing inability of [the] helicopter to comply with Tower instructions to turn away from final approach course for us. Inside the marker one dot high, [I] received [a] TCAS RA from [the] helicopter turning base early towards us. PNF (Pilot not Flying) had helicopter in sight [the] entire time. Immediately started to arrest descent when TCAS RA abated. Continued [the] approach, reestablishing glide slope intercept without unusual maneuvering required, to an uneventful landing. ZZZ during VMC weather is always an exceptionally busy airport with mix of high and low speed traffic in addition to multiple flight schools based there. Slowing the aircraft significantly assisted us and likely ATC Tower with sequencing for landing XXR and smaller aircraft, XXL. Estimate [there was] one dozen aircraft in pattern, with more nearby. Additionally, staying high on glide slope using situational awareness VFR likely provided further altitude separation for this eventual encounter. Non-complying VFR pattern helicopter to Tower instructions for whatever reason, highlights perils at this airport and necessitates good crew situational awareness and CRM. I did not follow up with ZZZ Tower with non-complying instruction helicopter, deeming [the] encounter a good learning lesson for all of us.
1766489: I was Captain and the flying pilot for arrival into IAH. We were descending in VMC conditions on the LINKK1 Arrival for the assigned Runway 27. We had completed our Approach to Landing above the line and as we were approaching 10000' we were running our Approach to Landing checklist Below the Line when we were cleared by the Approach Controller for the ILS 27 Approach and to maintain 240 knots.I put on the appropriate lights and we finished our checklist. However I did not - in hindsight - set the lower 1500' at which we were to cross the FAF at REDOC. Between RDFSH and GEYGR we were queried as to whether we were going to make our crossing restriction of 4000 at GEYGR. We realized the error and started to descend on the approach. Shortly after not complying with the crossing restriction at GEYGR, we were broken off the approach and vectored back around-slowed to 210 and descended to rejoin the approach. We were given a phone number to call HOUSTON TRACON. We then completed the approach and landing. The error started when I did not select the lower altitude for the FAF of 1500. The timing of our clearance was a contributing factor but the error was in the failure to set lower FAF altitude. Typically we are double checking each other and we missed it. Greater vigilance would have eliminated this error. We were also discussing the fact we were at 240 as assigned still inside of RDFSH was also a factor. We debriefed this all on the ground in detail. I later spoke with TRACON about this. They informed me that there were no separation issues and he did note the timing of the clearance when they reviewed the tape. We were flying the LINKK 1 Arrival, runway 27 to IAH. We confirmed all points in the MCDU and set the altitude down to 6000 we both confirmed the altitude we were then given a speed of 240kts with a clearance of descend via the STAR. I believe we were between RDFSH and GEYGR and the controller asked if we were going to make the crossing restriction at GEYGR which was supposed to be 4000, at this point I looked at the distance to GEYGR and it showed 4.2 miles and we had 2000ft to lose. We both looked at each other to confirm everything before we started to descend down immediately. There was not enough time to report that we were not going to make the crossing restrictions at 240kts and also the altitude. We both realized at this time that the altitude had not been changed for the lower altitude of 1500ft. at REDOC. The controller gave us a 360-degree turn back on course as we lost our altitude. At this point we realized our error. The controller called back with a number to call Houston for TRACON, we completed the approach and landed. Timing of the clearance was a factor, as well as not selecting lower altitude for the FAF of 1500 or double checking each other. Also should have discussed that we were inside of RDFSH and still at 240. We talked when on the ground in detail.
1766491: During the landing rollout, after all three wheels were firmly on the ground and brakes were being applied, the airplane began to yaw to the right. At the same time, the right suspension settled down and the left wing rose significantly. I could not steer the airplane back towards the center line. I then brought the airplane to a stop via braking. Upon coming to a stop, I applied power to attempt to move and steer the airplane with neither being successful. The entire event was felt the same as a blown tire would. I then told the tower we had blown a tire and requested to shut down engines. After gaining permission, we shut down the engines and awaited city employees. After a city car arrived and circled the airplane to inspect the damage, I alone exited the airplane to speak with him and inspect the airplane myself. He informed me there appeared to be no damage, and I verified this with my own inspection of the tires and landing gear struts. I then decided to start the engines and attempt to move the airplane. Upon advising the tower, I started engines and applied power. The airplane moved normally. We then taxied to the gate with no further incident. It is my opinion, after observing no bald spots on the tires, that a gust of wind from the left lifted the left wing significantly and at the same time the right brake locked up or would not release from an applied position. After letting the airplane rest for a few minutes, the sticky brake may have released itself allowing movement as normal.
1766568: As part of my job as a CFI for a local flight school, I was looking to add tailwheel instruction to my list of instruction services I provide. I have about 15 total tailwheel hours, but very little recent experience. In order to improve proficiency, I went up with an instructor the day before the ground loop to get tailwheel current and get some additional training. We flew for an hour and did four full stop landings on the airfield's grass runway, and all were straight, and no issues came up during any of these landings that would suggest I needed additional training. On the day of the ground loop, the winds had shifted to be about 8 knots directly down the asphalt runway so I chose to use that one rather than the grass which would have had a 90-degree crosswind. During my first approach, I made a low pass to verify the sight picture in my mind and double check any wind correction that may need to be done. I executed a go around and came around for another uneventful approach to a planned 3-point landing. After a smooth touchdown with the airplane rolling down the runway, a gust lifted the right wing and a yaw to the left. My corrective actions did not prevent the airplane from ground looping. Upon reflection, there was a moment where I should have applied power to try to stop the yaw and execute a go-around. However, I believe my ego got in the way since I've been flying more than I ever have that I could 'save' the landing despite teaching my students to default to a go-around when things aren't looking right. My overconfidence in my skills, combined with ego resulted in me trying to save the rollout rather than going around. I also believe more than an hour of recurrent training prior to flying a tailwheel airplane is required, even though I have been flying a lot lately.
1766874: Day 1, leg 1 of a 4 day trip from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the pilot monitoring on this leg. Had not flown much in the last few weeks. Captain was PF. We flew to ZZZ1 at a pretty low altitude, I believe it was 14,000 feet cruise altitude. After starting the descent, we did not realize we had passed 10,000 feet so quickly, and noticed our speed was beyond 250 knots. The Captain immediately slowed the descent rate and airspeed, in order to return to 250 knots.We were distracted. We were on the first leg of the trip, had woken up pretty early, and the fact that we cruised at such a low altitude were possibly all factors. We did not pay enough attention in the descent.I should have kept better monitoring skills during the descent and avoided distractions.
1767231: We were just outside the MNARK waypoint descending via the TBARR1 into Denver when I requested an unrestricted descent in order to expedite down through some turbulence. ATC granted my request and cleared us to descend and maintain 14,000 FT. I took the aircraft out of the managed descent mode and used open descent to descend to 14,000 FT. ATC subsequently amended our clearance as follows, cross BDIVN at or above 14,000 FT then descend via the TBARR1. The next waypoint after BDIVN is KUSHH which has an altitude restriction of 14,000 FT. The Pilot Monitoring (PM) put 13,000 in the FCU as the bottom of the TBARR1 is 13,000 FT at LDORA which is the next waypoint after KUSHH. I acknowledged the change to the altitude in the FCU but failed to put the aircraft back into a managed descent. We were between BDIVN and KUSHH when Denver Center switched us over to approach. As the PM checked in with approach I was expecting the aircraft to level off at 14,000 FT in order to meet the restriction by KUSHH. Just as the aircraft approached 14,000 FT two things happened simultaneously. One, I realized the aircraft wasn't leveling off as I expected, and two, approach cleared us to descend to 10,000 FT and turn left to a heading of 040. I don't believe there was an altitude deviation but I was certainly very fortunate that approach gave us a lower altitude when they did. On TBARR1 arrival asked for expedited decent to 14,000 feet to get out of moderate turbulence. I put 14,000 feet in altitude window, captain started open descent. Next ATC transmission was a decent via following BDIVN intersection. I put 13,000 in altitude window. Approaching KUSHH intersection captain realized plane was not going to capture altitude to cross KUSHH at 14,000 feet. Managed descent was not selected. At same time got ATC frequency change and new instructions heading 020 descent to 10,000. I don't think we went below 14,000 feet, but would have if not given new ATC instructions while in an open descent Mode.
1767261: Upon being cleared for the visual approach to XXR ZZZ, Pilot Flying set FAF altitude and continued descent from 4000 ft. to 2400 ft. PM (Pilot Monitoring) contacted tower to inform them of their flight path: turning base [runway] XXR. The crew turned base inside of the FAF, and therefore continued descent to an intermediary altitude appropriate for the glide path intercept inside FAF. In the base turn, the aircraft aurally alerted to a group of antennas in the vicinity of our flight path. As we were already in the base, we continued in the base without interruption and continued the approach to land XXR. The cause was an EGPWS aural alert to man-made group of obstacles, antennas, in the vicinity of flight path. Crew suggest [increased] distance in the turn from proximity of antennas to prevent future aural alerts from EGPWS. Flying the visual backed up by the ILS XXR, we were cleared for the approach, turning right base for the XXR runway during VMC, crew was aware of the set of antennas in the vicinity, however the GWPS was trigger issuing a 'Caution Obstacle' alert. Pilot Flying increased rate of turn as a preventive course of action to stay south of the obstacle. The crew safely remained out of the path of the manmade obstacle and landed without any interruption. EGPWS ALERT of the antennas in the proximity of the field Increase lateral distance from obstacles to prevent alerts from anything around or in the EGPWS to avoid situations like this.
1767754: Aircraft Y was cleared for an approach and was cleared to land. Aircraft X called Ground to taxi and was given taxi instructions. This instruction should have resulted in Aircraft X coming out of the Ramp and making a right turn on to the taxiway. Aircraft X instead crossed the taxiway and made a right turn onto the runway. When Aircraft X entered the runway, Aircraft Y immediately stated, 'There's something on the runway;' and I initiated a go around. Aircraft Y went around and conducted another ILS approach to successfully land. Aircraft X exited the runway and continued down the taxiway to Runway 07, where they then departed.Aircraft Y was at 300 ft. at a ½-mile final when the go around was initiated. I asked the pilots of both aircraft to contact the Tower and notified them that I would file a report on the event. I did not say the words 'possible pilot deviation' to Aircraft X, as required to issue a proper brasher warning. I also did not get the pilots' names, phone numbers, and certificate numbers, as I did not know that these items were required until I began filling out the report. I did note on the report that the aircraft were both air carriers, and the information was able to be obtained by referencing the callsigns.I believe the weather was a contributing factor to Aircraft X making an incorrect turn, as it was raining moderately with periodic gusting wind. A ground based radar system or a taller Control Tower would have been incredibly helpful in this circumstance, as the taxiway and runway are pretty much indistinguishable from each other at night. The lights of the two blend together and you cannot tell which is which.
1767941: During the transition to landing in a C-172 at approximately five feet above the runway surface, two helicopters flying in loose formation, were also preparing to land in the grass field just south of the runway at West Point/Middle Peninsula Regional Airport. As the helicopters were making a descending right turn, the rotor vortices apparently were directed into the flight path of the landing runway (Runway 10). The wake vortex caused the C-172 to immediately bank left and climb without any input from the student pilot. At this moment, the instructor took control and executed go-around procedures to avoid going off the runway and impacting the terrain at a high rate of descent just north of the runway. Pilots in all three aircraft were in visual contact with one another. However, it does not appear any of the pilots in any of the aircraft involved were aware of the effects the rotor wash would have on the runway of intended landing. The effects of rotor wash from two helicopters flying in loose formation may have also contributed to the incident.It is my objective that pilots in all aircraft conducting approaches to landing understand the importance of maintaining proper separation from rotorcraft. There is a high volume of rotorcraft traffic in Virginia's Tidewater region. They frequently practice traffic pattern operations at uncontrolled airfields where many students are learning to fly. This incident could have easily resulted in an accident causing serious injury or death under slightly different circumstances. If a student pilot was flying solo, I don't think the outcome would have been the same.
1768208: ILS approach into ZZZ. I briefed the approach with course and frequency and confirmed the points in the FMS. Vectors to final were activated and I missed the course was not set on the inbound and I think when I briefed the frequency I was reading the frequency from NAV 2. We turned inbound and not seeing the errors I told the PNF that he had control, but this time we were well above the GS. We notified ATC that we were going to go missed and were given new instructions. After the missed, I reset the inbound course and reset the frequency. I then told the PNF that I had control and the next approach was done to a safe landing.I haven't flown in several months and the other pilot was his second flight in this type aircraft. I believe was a contributing factor on this approach. While being vectored to the ILS for Runway XX, the crew noticed that the localizer failed to auto-tune when the approach was armed. When it was determined that the course was not going to be captured the pilot transferred the auto pilot to the pilot monitoring side where the localizer did tune correctly. However, by this time the aircraft had flown through the course. The autopilot attempted to capture the course, but completed one or two 'S' turns. The crew agreed that the approach was not stabilized and we indicated to ATC that we intended to go-around and try the approach again. We were given vectors and an altitude and were cleared for the approach again. The following approach to landing was completed without issue. Crew should have been more vigilant to ensure that the correct NAV frequency was tuned and the decision to transfer the coupled side autopilot could have been made earlier.
1768267: Upon arrival in NEW airspace. ATC cleared [us] for approach via SAFES IAF to RNAV runway 36L. Clearance was then modified and was told to stay at 3,000 ft. until further advised for departing traffic. Aircraft flew past initial approach descent point. FMS dropped vertical navigation guidance at that point. A manual descent was initiated just prior to that. I hurriedly reloaded the FMS to re-establish vertical guidance. While reloading, I received a low altitude alert from ATC with my call sign. I appeared to be in the vertical path of the approach just inside TOYBO at 2,400 ft. I had the runway insight and asked for and was cleared for visual approach.I am unsure if descent rate or altitude tripped the low altitude warning issued by ATC as I appeared to be in parameters while trying to re-establish the approach in the aircraft FMS.Flight continued to runway on glide path with nothing unusual other than the low altitude warning from ATC near TOYBO intersection.
1768389: I was working Local 2 and Ground Control combined during slow traffic and the airport was in a North flow deice configuration. The aircraft were landing XXL with med-good braking action reports from pilots. Aircraft X was given a clearance to land with a med-good braking action report. Aircraft X rolled quickly pass to high speeds so I figured he was trying to roll to the end quickly. I instructed Aircraft X to turn left at the end. At that point he was approaching the end at a good rate of speed. I sent the next aircraft around as I watched Aircraft X go slightly passed the end of the runway, make a hard left turn back onto taxiway M from M10 taxiway. Aircraft X verified that he was off of runway XXL so L let the next aircraft continue and land without any issues. Aircraft X asked to have airport vehicle to check his aircraft in case he had hit any taxiway lights. The airport closed runway XXL. I later observed Aircraft X taxi back to the gate on his own power.Other aircraft seemed to be able to make the high speed taxiways without any issue. Maybe if the pilot came in with a slower approach speed it could have helped him not to roll long and slide. Completed all briefings prior to approach. We were expecting a VFR approach but briefed like full IFR approach and were prepared for the weather to change. We were preparing for a normal approach and landing to Runway XXL. ATIS Bravo showed three miles and overcast 4100 feet. ATIS BRAVO also advised RCC CODE 5-5-5 for Runways XXR, XXL, XYL. Planned a flap 15 landing. We used conservative number of CODE 4 RCC giving us Autobrakes 2, 1530 stopping margin. In essence 3000 feet, touchdown zone being the most restrictive of the 12,000 foot runway. On final approach, Tower stated Braking Action Good to RJ in front of us.We landing uneventfully. I believe we landed within 3,000 TDZE, however, I do remember floating a little with 10 knots ice additive. We did not have any markings visible outside center line do to white snow. Decelerated to 60 knots, F/O called 60 knots. I stowed the thrust reversers and pressed brakes to disconnect autobrakes. Nothing seemed unusual at that point. Deceleration rate seemed normal up to that point. Tower stated: 'Roll to end, aircraft behind you two-mile final.'I depressed brakes to further decelerate and realized there was zero braking available. I stated 'No brakes' to F/O a couple of times. F/O immediately told Tower and aircraft behind us went around. I extended full reverse thrust again to try and get aircraft stopped. We drifted about 45 degrees toward intended exit. We never left hard surface of runway/taxiway. I briefed F/O to contact Ground immediately and notify 'NILL BRAKING LAST THIRD OF RUNWAY XXL.'I also had F/O ask for inspection of runway/taxiway lights to make sure aircraft had no damage before we taxied any further. He also notified Company Ops what had just occurred. I briefed what had happened to Passengers on PA. ZZZ Ground Ops notified there were no runway/taxiway lights damaged. We taxied aircraft to gate without any further issues. Maintenance was waiting for us at gate and we described what had occurred. They inspected aircraft and found an actual blue taxiway light laying on top of wheel carriage on right main. There was no aircraft damage noted by the Maintenance inspection. I put a note in logbook and we deadheaded to ZZZ1.I take briefings very seriously. This was not the type of flight that either Pilot was out of loop or just not having a bad day. We were configured at the marker and on speed the whole time on approach. I may have floated a little do to 10 knot increase of VREF. The ATIS reports from ZZZ were RCC 5-5-5. The two previous aircraft reports BRAG. The only difference was, the two previous aircraft exited 2nd high speed. We rolled past the second high speed for passenger comfort. We never expected NIL braking under light snow covered runway in front of us. The airport needs to actually test the runway, if they're going to advertise 5-GOOD. It was one of the worst feelings a Pilot can have realizing he/she has lost effective control of an aircraft. Had I not redeployed the thrust reversers, I believe we would have encountered aircraft damage and maybe even injuries even though aircraft would have been exiting hard surface at a slow speed. I am actually shocked the runway had not been prepared for arrivals with so much equipment and men available at that airport. Very disappointed.
1768901: ATC had given us a series of headings to avoid an active MOA. After the headings, they gave us direct CULAB then DIESL for the DRLLR5 arrival into IAH. I was writing the clearance while the captain put the change in the FMS. I copied the correct clearance (direct CULAB, DEISL then the DRILR5) and the captain input direct CULAB then DIESL for the MSCOT4, our originally assigned arrival. A proper cross check was not applied and the change was CONFIRMED. The MSCOT4 and DRLLR5 are very similar coming from that direction and both start at DIESL so upon looking at the first page of the FMS all seemed correct to me. It was not until later in the arrival were we/nor ATC aware we were on the wrong arrival into IAH until around the SUUNR intersection on the MSCOT4. Proper cross checking was not implemented on the arrival change. We did confirm the route change to CULAB then DIESL. A more thorough cross check of the arrival change would have caught the issue. Neither of us caught it and continued the flight to IAH on the MSCOT4, even fully briefing it. ATC said 'no worries' and left us on the MSCOT4 all the way into IAH.
1769092: Upon landing the student was going too fast to make a 90 degree turn on to the taxiway. The instructor did not have enough time to correct the rudder input. If the instructor had pushed on the rudder to correct the aircraft would have tipped. So the instructor kept the aircraft going straight once it was aimed off the runway. We went into the dirt and on to a taxiway. The aircraft did not hit any lights or signs. The aircraft did not appear to sustain any damage. The engine appeared to be fine. Taxi the aircraft everything seemed to be normal.
1769329: Was advised inflight by ZZZZZ controllers that they were unable to contact ZZZ Approach controllers. ZZZ had closed one hour early due to their reduced hours, however, there was no NOTAM in our flight plan that advised of the early closure. In addition to there being no NOTAM, ZZZ had also failed to 'release' the airspace over to the Center before going home. As a result, ZZZZZ could not clear us for an approach into the airspace. We were issued holding instructions until someone in ZZZ returned to the airport to release the airspace. Initially, ZZZZZ seemed unsure if ZZZ was even open or not. I told them that they had indeed closed based off of the remarks section of the AWOS. I knew that ZZZ closed at XA00 local based on recent flights. Plus, the airport itself (Runways and taxiways) would close later due to the construction that takes place at night. However, because there were no NOTAMs for either closure this time, I thought that they would be open. We had no alternate, as the weather was good, and as such had limited time to hold. Fortunately, we eventually got clearance to proceed into ZZZ.ZZZ ATC failed to release the airspace to ZZZZZ prior to signing off for the night. As a result, we were held until the airspace could be released. In addition, there were no NOTAMs noting the early closure of the ATC facilities at ZZZ.
1769806: We made a call to take off from the active runway after someone called 'base leg', assuming we had sufficient time without causing a traffic conflict, we also had a visual on them. As we were on our roll-out, they requested that the aircraft 'holding short' stop. We continue to take off, and they break off final and sidestep us. We never heard a 'final' radio call or saw them turn final before we made our take-off radio call and took the active runway.
1769836: While I was training on Local during the busiest session since returning to training aswell as it being my trainer's first time training on local in more than 6 months thetraffic volume was enough that required us to split Local and Ground. For most of theyear our airport had been on a straight runway configuration due to construction and we had only been back to 2 runway operations for about a week. We had Aircraft Zdoing full stop taxi backs and Aircraft A doing stop and go's with afternoon push ofarrivals and departures. I had cleared Aircraft Y to land on runway YY (IFR arrival) andAircraft X was ready to go on runway XX (VFR departure). I asked Aircraft X if heneeded time on the runway or if he was ready to go and the pilot replied that he wasready to go. When I cleared Aircraft X for takeoff the Aircraft Z was on 2.5 mile finaland traffic was exchanged. After takeoff clearance I went back and told Aircraft X toclear for immediate takeoff and the pilot read it back. After 30 seconds the departingaircraft had not began its takeoff roll yet and my instructor told them to start roll now.At this time the arrival was at 1 mile final runway YY. When the arrival was at thethreshold the departure had barely cleared the intersection due to the delay it madeon the runway.To prevent this situation I could have waited until the arrival had landed to clear thedeparture for takeoff. I relied on expectation bias that the departure was going tobegin their takeoff roll immediately and not take time on the runway. I could havealso told the Aircraft Y to reduce to final approach speed to create a bigger hole forthe departure. Knowing when to slow down during busy sessions is also somethingthat could have prevented this situation. (Training in progress on Local Control on one of the busier sessions seen by all inmonths. Trainer's first time training on LC in over 9 months)Ground had been split off a couple minutes before due to increased traffic andproposed traffic. In addition to multiple arrivals and departures, there was Aircraft Zdoing multiple take offs with full stop taxi backs, and Aircraft A doing stop & go's.Aircraft X taxied out for departure contacted tower holding short of Runway XX. Trafficwas within a mile final for Runway XX so they were waiting to depart. Because therewas another aircraft inbound to Runway YY that we were going to try to depart insideof, Local Trainee was instructed to ask Aircraft X if they would need time on therunway or if they would be ready to go-they said they would be ready. Once the Stopand Go traffic was rolling and we would have our separation, Aircraft X was cleared fortakeoff and told about traffic on final for crossing runway. No hustle from aircraft.Trainee then told Aircraft X cleared for immediate takeoff. He still sat on the runway.Trainer keyed up and told Aircraft X to start their roll.The runway separation was extremely close to call and in the moment the trainerdecided that it was safer to let the arrival land than issue a go around and potentiallycause an evasive maneuver at a critical stage of flight with another departure.We should have just waited to clear Aircraft X for takeoff due to their tendency to beslow and spend time on the runway. Once they did not move with an immediatetakeoff, take off clearance should have been canceled.I do believe that traffic volume and complexity added and distracted the tower-teamfrom checking every aspect of the situation (speeds, timing, rolling of aircraft), but Ido not believe we should refrain from training on busy sessions like these.
1770344: Normal approach, wind out of the south at 3 kts. Pilot with tail wheel endorsement flying his plane made nice 3 point landing, no bounce. On rollout, the plane suddenly veered to the left and the right side of the airplane dropped to the runway. Pilot and I exited airplane. The right main gear leg was lying beneath the airplane. I think there was a complete mechanical failure of the right main landing gear leg. I was receiving instruction, we were attempting our first touch and go, uneventful three point landing, upon which the plane turned unexpectantly and violently to the left, right main landing gear collapsed.
1770469: I was on an IFR direct flight plan. Since I was in 5/5 VMC conditions, and there was no other observed traffic in the vicinity of the airport, I cancelled IFR approximately 10-12 miles from the airport after having it in sight. I elected to enter the pattern on an extended left base for landing on Runway XX and made the appropriate radio call on the CTAF frequency. While on base, I began to descend below 1,032 feet MSL (the approximate normal pattern altitude) to approximately 700 feet MSL and initiated a left turn to final, approximately 2 miles from the XX runway threshold. As I made the turn to final, I allowed my altitude to fall to approximately 400 feet MSL (this was directly over the waterway, so it was also approximately 400 feet AGL). I made my final approach radio call and upon realizing I was somewhat low and below the desired glidepath on final. I initiated a correction and maintained that altitude until I was able to intercept the correct glidepath and had a red and white indication on the airport Runway XX PAPI. At that point I was perhaps a little over a mile from the airport threshold. From there I proceeded to a normal final approach and landing. My flight hours shown above are approximate, I am away from home as I file this report and thus do not have access to my logbook.
1770623: Cleared for the Visual Approach [Runway] 24 in UNV. We had briefed the high terrain that we would fly over prior to intercepting the final approach course in the initial arrival briefing. We were proceeding directly to WOREX descending from 4,100 ft. to 3,100 ft. At approximately 3,800 ft. we got a terrain warning over the mountain. The Captain was the PF (Pilot Flying) and he added power and climbed to 4,000 ft. and the warning went away. We advised ATC and circled back around and completed the approach visually. GPWS warning. High terrain you fly over prior to intercepting the final approach course. Responded to GPWS. Climbed to a safe altitude. Stay higher over the mountain or if in doubt request the ILS to [Runway] 24 instead of visual.
1770873: Flight into KTN at night. We were stable on the ILS, on glide slope and speed, inside the final approach fix with the runway in sight. We received an oral warning 'obstacle ahead'. Nothing appeared on the display and the Ground Proximity Warning did not command any evasive maneuvers. We continued the approach and landed without incident. Unsure of the oral warning. An approach, KTN ILS, on the localizer and glide slope receive an amber caution advisory 'OBSTACLE AHEAD'.
1771059: Weather - clear beautiful flying day low wind, great visibility unlimited ceiling. Traffic - heavy traffic converging on un-towered airport from multiple directions and altitudes. Flight situation - initial approach was cautious due to traffic, got in the pattern and extended downwind to space landing traffic. At this point an aircraft (experimental RV-7 I believe) cut in front of me from above with smoke trailing and landed. I offset to the right of the airport flew to mid field turned right and executed a 360 gained 500 [ft.] above pattern and crossed the airport to re-enter the pattern on the other side (for normal left traffic for Runway XX wind calm). I made CTAF announcements when I left final, when I did my 360 and when I crossed mid field stating my intentions to enter a downwind from a 45. As I crossed the runway no traffic was visible in the downwind. After crossing the airport I made a tight right 360 to lose 500 feet and enter the downwind at 2,400 [ft.]. Upon rollout I realized traffic had overtaken me from the left in the pattern during my maneuver. The traffic was directly in front of me and slightly higher. It was at a close but manageable distance. I immediately began slowing down to increase separation. The leading traffic reduced speed faster than I could reduce speed closing our gap to an unsafe distance. I then veered right and descended to avoid the traffic. The leading traffic also veered right and I lost visual tracking of the traffic, and could only see his shadow on the ground. The pilot asked where I was and I told him I had descended and veered right to gain separation. I then veered further right to provide additional separation. The leading traffic was later identified as a C150/152. There was an A36 Bonanza behind me in the downwind at this point. I believed the safest thing to do was to stay to the right of the leading traffic and extend downwind to allow the leading traffic to land. I made additional CTAF announcements to communicate my intentions to the traffic. Contributing factors - loss of traffic awareness due to traffic data loss on GNS530 in our aircraft. Human performance issues - Heavy Workload: Heavy traffic from multiple directions and altitudes, uncontrolled airspace, evading previous potential incident. Human performance issues - Hazardous Attitude: The leading traffic was a student with a CFI. They demonstrated anti-authority attitude and a lack of situational awareness as they cut us off in the pattern. They did not accept that their intention to pass on the left was unsafe.
1771218: Visual Approach with both autopilots on, (CAT III showing) at approximately 3,000 feet aircraft excessively pitched nose down approximately 7-10 degrees following a false glide slope. Pilot flying (First Officer) disconnected the autopilot and leveled off at 2,000 feet as Tower called a low altitude alert. The aircraft glide slope recovered and showed a correct indication from the final approach fix to touchdown. was written up and documented after shut down. Aircraft did not descend below 2000 feet prior to the final approach fix. Final Approach Fix altitude is 2,000 feet.
1771351: During vectors into OKC from the east, the Approach Controller assigned us Runway 17R differently from the one we had setup (17L). After re-configuring for the ILS 17R, I asked the Pilot Monitoring to brief the approach so I can concentrate on flying (Approximately 14,000 feet MSL and descending to 4,000 feet). During the brief a bright shining white light, like a spotlight shined at us, caught our attention and cause a distraction. We still conducted the briefing, including the highest elevation figure. As I kept flying I was paying attention if the light shined us again, in the event it was a laser that needed to be reported. I had the terrain page setup from the previous briefing and both pilots were aware of the obstacle northeast of the airport (Antenna 2758 feet MSL). After the briefing was complete, we were given a vector (a 90 degree angle) for the approach within a close proximity of the Final Approach Fix (minimum altitude at FAF 3,000 feet MSL). This vector would have flown us south of the obstacle depicted in the plan view section of the approach chart. Approximately 18NM from the airport the Approach Controller queried the visual contact of the airport. Pilot Monitoring told me he had contact with it and after I picked it up in sight I asked to call for it if he still had it. At that point the Approach Controller cleared us for the visual approach for [Runway] 17R. Slightly after, the Approach Controller notified us of traffic on the approach to the parallel runway. Both pilots were trying to ID the traffic since it was below our altitude and we had to cross his approach path. We seemed clear of the traffic, but a strong wind from the south was drifting us north which cause a concern for us due to the known obstacle. The aircraft was just approaching 4,000 feet of altitude and started to level off, when I set 3;000n in the Altitude Select box. The aircraft transitioned into a shallow descent instead of holding 4,000 since it wasn't fully captured. While having a discussion about the wind I adjusted my heading and kept the descent to 3,000 feet so we could be close to level and slow when we intercepted the course outside of the FAF. Around 3500 feet we both remembered the obstacles when we saw its lights ahead and below us. I already started a transition into a climb when the Pilot Monitoring verbally reminded me of the obstacles. During the climb we got a 'Caution Obstacle', due to the projected descent, which was removed shortly since we were already compensating. We were 500 to 700 feet above the highest obstacle. The obstacle represented on the MFD was not the highest elevation figure on the IAP chart. This depicted obstacle was part of another group of towers not depicted on the chart but they can be seen on the VFR chart in the Jeppesen app. Since it was a visual approach, I had focused on maintaining the airport inside, and started to descend and slow down so we could be on a good position for the stable approach. Following the event, we landed with no issues and had a discussion at the gate on how we could have mitigated our error. We were below the MSA and had loss awareness of the obstacles due to other distractions and the tight vector to the approach with the visual approach. Several factors played key roles for the loss of situational awareness that led us to be at a lower altitude for our location. Flags:-A night Visual approach into an airport were an obstacle is a threat.-A night Visual approach to an airport were the elevation of the airport is higher than we are normally used to.-An arrival consisting of an extended base into a visual approach rather than a downwind arrival.-The change of runway that led to a new setup and briefing.-The distractions caused by the wind-drift, traffic, and the bright light.-The tight vector given and accepted for the original approach. Our error was the premature descent to 3000 feet with the goal of not being high once we intercept the final course with short distance to the final fix. Although the setup for the approach included the awareness of terrain and using the terrain displayed as an aid, we should have use TEM to establish a plan to avoid the premature descent. A briefed plan of using the last assigned altitude of 4,000 feet until intercepting would have avoided this. During the approach brief, I should have asked my Pilot Monitoring to intervene in the event I set a lower altitude while maneuvering for the visual (mitigation plan in the vent of losing SA). I realized that our briefings cover informational items that could be threats but we should discuss mitigating plans for them. Other actions that could have been taken are: 1) denying the visual at night due to the obstacle, 2) requesting a vector for the visual, and 3) querying if a lower altitude was needed which would have led the Controller to keep us at 4,000 feet. I was Pilot Monitoring. Approximately 20min out we were giving the option to change our landings intentions from [Runway] 17L to 17R which we took. Captain asked me if I could brief the approach which I did and then we performed the runway change items from the checklist. During this briefing moment we both noticed a bright light from about a 12 o'clock position which caught our attention. Captain was aware of the obstacles to the northeast of the airport (antennas) and turned on the terrain. At approximately 18 miles out we were asked if we had the airport in sight. We both saw it and were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17R. Winds were out of the south at approximately 26kt pushing us to the north since we were coming from the east. We were at 4,000 ft. and began a gradual descent. ATC advised us of traffic at 11 o'clock landing on the parallel runway. Looking for the traffic we began to noticed the red lights of the obstacles (towers) on the northeast of the airport. I pointed them out as [did] the Captain. The altitude window was set for 3,000 ft. we were currently at 3,400 ft. Captain turned off the autopilot and began a climb. As we were climbing we received a Caution for the obstacle but it cleared quickly since the Captain had already began the climb. Once cleared we continue to intercept the final approach course and perform a normal landing. We both had a long discussion after the flight and both agreed that we should had mitigated this by simply staying at 4;000ft when cleared for the visual approach since we knew about the MSA which is 3,800 ft. Also the parallel traffic played a role on this since we started looking for it due to it being in our path for intercepting the final approach course of [Runway] 17R. As a Pilot Monitoring I should had advised the Captain that selecting 3,000 ft. and continuing the descent once cleared for the visual would had put us close to the highest obstacle stated in the approach plate. I will keep this in consideration for future flights to come ensuring we are not at a lower altitude than the MSA not established on a final approach course as well as keeping in mind obstacles around us at all times.
1771432: I was training in Aircraft X, doing pattern work, and while on final to [Runway] 7R, I was looking out to my left and saw an Aircraft Y starting his turn from downwind to final for 7L. We originally were offset to the right as a precaution for traffic on 7L. As I was getting closer to the runway, I looked back again and saw that the Aircraft Y overshot his base to final turn and was on path to hit us (noticed him about 200-300 feet away). I took evasive action and went full power and a sharp turn to the right to get out of his path. About 3 seconds later he intercepted our path and if not for evasive maneuver, we would've had a mid-air collision.
1771838: My instructor and I were on downwind approach for landing. Meanwhile a C-172 had just performed a go-around. We were told they came around at a faster velocity than us, but at nearly our same altitude/path. We later were told (I believe the C-172 instructor told my instructor) that the C-172 was only 100 feet away from us, I believe from above. We had no concrete idea about any of this at the time. We proceeded to land. Afterward, my instructor asked me if I was aware that we were almost in a mid air collision. He had just spoken with the other pilot near the fuel pump. We then looked at radar tracking website to see the activity but we only saw our airplane and not theirs. Pilot from C-172 came into the office to get water (Instructor I believe) and saw us looking at the radar map but didn't seem too concerned about the incident. That's all the information I have.
1771842: In non-tower airport PRB, when exiting Runway 31 to Taxiway B, announced on CTAF intentions to exit runway, taxi on (Taxiway) B, cross Runway 1-19, then turn to Taxiway A. To do so, I had to turn my right hindquarters to the approach path of Runway 19, not realizing that a small plane was actually landing on Runway 19. I was unable to see the landing traffic from behind the right wing, and I never heard this plane on radio or made a radio contact. 1773413: I'm writing to report the challenging nature/difficulty in making visual approaches in a jet to Runways 35L/R at Henderson Exec Airport (HND), where terrain is a prominent factor as close as a 3-mile final approach. Compliance with ATC spacing instructions can leave the pilot and airplane in a position where neither of the options for trying to land straight-in are particularly good options: Maneuver in proximity to high terrain, knowing in advance that you will be facing the prospect of repeated GPWS warnings as you try to visually get into a position to make the final approach as stable as possible, or, remain high until well clear of the foothills, but face the prospect of a 'chop and drop' close-in final approach, which is neither stable nor desirable.Our afternoon arrival was in excellent VMC conditions. HND was landing 35L and 35R. I have been into HND a few times, and from several years ago I remembered the terrain issues to the south, so I made it a special point of emphasis prior to top-of-descent to brief the SIC that I intended to maintain visual separation with the terrain and expected we would be dealing with the GPWS while maneuvering to get the airplane in a position to fly a stable final segment.We did not fully fly our filed STAR, but instead we were vectored SW of LAS and eventually turned inbound on an E-NE vector on what looked like a 10-15 mile left base leg. This initial vector looked promising, as I thought it might allow for a close-in base to final, which I considered preferable to having to navigate the mountains to the south of the airport. However, as we got inside of 10 miles, approach control instructed us that Tower wanted us to 'widen out more to the east, and square the base turn to final...cleared visual approach 35L.' This instruction basically put us in the position of having to navigate the mountainous terrain on our left base, with a turn to final at approximately 5-6 miles. I set the autopilot to descend for 5,000 MSL (approximately 2,500 AGL above touchdown elevation), but I knew that I would have to get the airplane down to a lower altitude before rolling out on final, or else be faced with either a 'chop and drop' situation or needing to ask for a circling approach over the airport in VMC.I opted to hand fly the airplane and visually maneuvered between the saddles of some higher peaks as I transitioned from left base to final. I was able to gradually descend another few hundred feet as I was flying this portion of the approach, but the GPWS had become active with constant terrain cautions, as expected. I was able to keep the terrain in sight at all times while maneuvering, maintaining a 500-700 foot margin on the radar altimeter over the path I was flying. Beyond dealing with the GPWS audio until we cleared the highest points, I did get the airplane into position to fly a stable final segment and land. Everything transpired pretty much how I thought it might, starting from the descent briefing all the way to touchdown. But I walked away from the airplane not feeling satisfied, thinking there has to be some better way to set up and coordinate visual approaches to 35L/R. Of course, the pilot always has full responsibility to maintain terrain avoidance on visual approaches, but where difficult topography exists, such as south of HND, some extra assistance from ATC in the form of additional vectoring and/or coordination with the local tower could go a long way in helping to better manage visual approaches to 35L/R at this airport.When we were instructed to contact the tower, the approach controller was appreciative of our cooperation in squaring the base as instructed, but I am left wondering if he realized that making me deal with the high terrain on extended final made flying the visual approach that much tougher.I've already decided that if I am put into a similar situation at this airport in the future, I am not going to consider either of the two aforementioned solutions to try and make it straight-in on a visual approach. Going forward I will opt to negotiate a circling approach in the traffic pattern with the controller(s) instead of battling issues with terrain or excessively steep final approach considerations. It may make things a bit more complicated for the controllers and traffic flow, but I think this course of action is really the safest alternative of the lot.

1774183: I was doing pattern work at ZZZ between XA:00 and XB:00. The airfield had a large amount of arriving traffic during the hours I was flying. After a touch & go on RWY XX, I was asked to extend the upwind before flying a right pattern. About mid-field on the downwind, tower requested a left-360. After my first 360, I was instructed to extend my downwind. A second plane [Aircraft Y] was approaching the airport from the northwest. Aircraft Y was asked to 'make a right 270, keep it tight and get ready to line up behind a [jet]'ATC then asked me to widen out my downwind and look for Aircraft Y making the right 270. At this point it was at my 11 o clock, 3 miles. About 5 seconds later I was able to identify the aircraft, let tower know that I had them in sight and was preparing to line up behind them. About 15 seconds later, tower called me up again, asking 'Aircraft X - extend it out a little bit, actually just follow behind and I'll call your base you will have to follow a jet behind on final'. I read back and confirmed.About 30 seconds later, tower called me up again, 'Aircraft X just so I don't get you too far from the field, make a left 360'. I read back the instruction and began my left 360. At this point, I was already thinking about Aircraft Y as I was planning on how I would get back on the downwind and line up behind them. I believe Aircraft Y was just about to finish its right 270 as I was about 90 degrees into my 360. I was able to spot and track the plane on Foreflight with Sentry, but since I had to make a 360 I lost visual when I initiated my turn. Tower, likely receiving a traffic alert called the other plane to make them aware of me: 'Aircraft X about a mile south making a left 360 - he has you in sight'. I do not think he asked them to confirm that they had me in sight and I can't tell from the live-ATC recording whether they read it back. The added statement 'he has you in sight' was extremely dangerous and could have been fatal. Yes, I had the traffic in sight when I was heading toward it and planning to get behind them, but once I started my left 360 there was no way of maintaining a visual with the other plane since I was now heading the opposite direction. I immediately recognized the potential conflict and started looking both outside the plane and on Foreflight trying to spot and track the other plane's relative position. The other plane did not make a 270 turn, but instead kept turning toward the airport/runway i.e. cutting into my path.As I was about 270 degrees into my 360 turn tower called 'Aircraft X - as you are coming out of that 360 turn do you still have Aircraft Y in sight?'At this point, I was already banking hard left in a steep turn trying to pull away from the converging traffic that I saw coming closer toward me. Turning right was not an option as it would have put me in the middle of final with jets arriving. I do not think the other plane confirmed whether or not they had me in sight. If they did, they flew way too close to me for my comfort and should have initiated an avoidance maneuver. In response to tower's question I responded 'Aircraft X unable' because I had to focus on flying the airplane away from the other traffic. We then passed by each other with much less separation than I feel comfortable. The other plane heading toward the runway, and me pulling hard left to the North-West, initiating a climb up to gain altitude. It is hard to tell exactly but horizontal distance could have been less than 500 feet Vertical distance was virtually the same. It happened very quickly. If I had not realized the potential conflict and mitigated by tracking on foreflight and pulling hard left this could have been a really really bad situation. The biggest mistake here, in my opinion, was ATC communicating to the other plane that I had them in sight AFTER I started my 360. There is no way one can maintain visual during such a maneuver while also flying safely and ATC shouldunder no circumstances make that statement. I also think that having two planes completing maneuvers in a way where their exit paths can conflict (right 270 and left 360) in close proximity should be prohibited.There were multiple safer options here. Aircraft Y could have flown a proper base rather than cutting it short onto final. I could have been asked to fly west, or I could have been asked to fly another 360 right after the first one. The fact that ATC changed its instructions relative to how I should fly behind/around the other traffic 3 times in a minute indicates to me that they were not planning ahead but rather responding to/running behind.In the future, I will call out if ATC tells other people that I have them in sight when I don't (i.e. after starting my left 360). I am also surprised nobody (tower/the other plane) complained about how close this was. I am glad to be back on the ground. I hope this helps keep other people safe in the future!

1775022: Day VMC. Conducted initial approach [Runway] XXR. PF (Pilot Flying) called missed approach into ZZZ [Runway] XXR due to windshear with airspeed loss below 500 ft. Maintained visual descent rate with visual cues and instrumentation of the ILS. During round out to flare automation set the aural 'sink rate' message. Such as automation latencies detecting the windshear event prior to the windshear caution, or sink rate alert while the pilot is initiating real time assertive maneuvers in turbulent conditions. Approach into ZZZ on our 1st attempt we conducted a missed approach due to wind shear. 1775147: Working a slow but steady local session with Supervisor working GC/CD combined. Very low staffing due to COVID. Steady traffic all day, I wouldn't call it too busy though. 1775853: While flying into Burbank at night PF (Pilot Flying) / PIC (Pilot-in-Command) elected to do visual to [Runway] 15. Clearance was granted around JANNY [and] PF took a course that meant we would intercept the final approach course from the left of centerline. PM (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were left of centerline and that there was terrain in the area. We crossed over the ridge line at the standard 5,500 ft. but thereafter while still left of centerline the PF started a descent. PM had terrain display up on MFD and was watching, there was never a yellow or red terrain ahead of the aircraft at anytime. Yet PM noticed that the radio altimeter was showing a reading while still left of centerline. The radio altimeter reading went below 1,000 ft. and got to around 800 ft. The PM called out the altitudes as soon as they were decreasing below 1,000 ft. and the PF took evasive action by disconnecting the auto pilot and stopping the descent. Almost immediately after the radio altimeter reading went away and we continued a normal descent to landing on [Runway] 15. Taking a visual to [Runway] 15 at night is unnecessarily risky. With margins very tight on the left side of the approach course, situational awareness is reduced at night. The benefits certainly do not outweigh the risks. We never received a GPWS yet we came within below 1,000 ft. of terrain on around an 8 mile final. It is easy to become complacent with your surroundings when you can not see them, so don't bother putting yourself in this situation... The company needs to put into writing that visuals to [Runway] 15 should not be allowed at night. As PM I should have called an immediate go-around the second I saw the radio altimeter go below 1,000 ft. High terrain in the form of a mountain ridge exists just north of BUR. The BUR airport is located at the east end of the San Fernando Valley. Additional mountains are present just to the east of BUR.Discontinue night visual approaches to BUR Runway 15.

1776386: Aircraft X entered a terrain area at 7,200 ft. with a Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) of 7,400 ft. Aircraft X was cleared for the RNAV [Runway] XX approach. 1776992: After doing 5 touch and goes on runway 28R, I received clearance to land. I did a wheel landing, let the tail come down, and when the aircraft was traveling slowly at about 15 kts or less, I started turning left to aim for the taxiway exit, and the aircraft kept turning to the left and did a complete 360 ground loop on the runway. The aircraft did not suffer any damage or touch any part of the aircraft to the runway, except the wheels of course, and I did not leave the runway. Due to this unexpected delay the aircraft landing behind me had to go around. I attribute this ground loop to unexpected strong crosswind, and the fact that we just put air in the tires and the aircraft was a lot more responsive to rudder control inputs that on my previous flight. She just got away from me for a moment.
1777837: After being cleared for the visual approach and landing into ZZZ on Runway XX, we continued to configure the aircraft for landing. We proceeded to descend below 3,000 just inside the ZZZZZ fix. As we turned final around 2,600 feet MSL around 1,300 AGL we received a 'Obstacle' GWPS warning which we were given an RA to pull up. I immediately complied with the command until it confirmed and we visually confirmed that we were clear and continued the approach to land without incident. During the incident we did not observe nor did Tower observe any obstacles that we were in close proximity to. We maintained proper clearance of at least 1,000 feet AGL from all of the published towers that were on the approach plate.Cause - There were no noted obstacles that were within 1,000 feet AGL clearance and can only come to the conclusion that it was an anomaly with the GWPS system. At 2,800 feet we had turned inside the Tower that was 1,740 feet and turned well before the Tower at 1,809 maintain safe and legal separation from structures.Suggestions - Continue to follow protocol and respect a Resolution Advisory.
1778147: We were descending via the ZZZZZX arrival with the Autopilot off - on profile and speed. FO decided to hand fly the remainder of the approach and landing and disconnected both the Autopilot and Autothrust near ZZZZZ1 intersection. A minute later I looked away and when I looked again, I noticed the FO was high on profile and I mentioned that we needed to cross ZZZZZ1 level at 6,000 feet. The FO increased the rate of descent and crossed ZZZZZ1 level at 6,000 but then continued to descend to approximately 5,900 feet and around 250 knots - with accelerating trend. I verbalized both altitude and speed, and the FO quickly recovered both. We were soon level at 6,000 feet - 240 knots...and soon to slow to 210 knots by ZZZZZ2. There was very light traffic in the terminal area and ATC made no mention of conflicts of any kind. We then proceeded to land uneventfully on Runway XX. The main contributing factor was the FO being new as well as not having flown much for the last several months. We fully debriefed everything, including what to improve on, once at the gate when duties permitted.
1778419: I was conducting a private flight in my aircraft. I had utilized VFR flight following and was handed off to Tower. I heard numerous bangs in quick succession. They were alarming and my wife whom was in the front passenger seat abruptly turned to me and exclaimed in a concerned tone, 'what was that'? I too was extremely concerned and began checking all aircraft systems. Fortunately, all systems were functioning and I continued the approach to an uneventful landing. Upon examination of the aircraft post-landing, I noted damage to the fairing protruding from the underwing of the right main landing gear. Although I did not see what caused the damage, I am certain the damage was not present before the return flight due to my preflight inspection. I surmise the aircraft was struck by an unmanned aerial system as there were no signs of blood or feathers consistent with a bird strike.
1778504: Great weather, normal fuel burn. Entering terminal area we were vectored around then low and slow which created more fuel burn in terminal area. Did go-around for XXL due to an animal on runway. Aircraft in front of us did same. Declared minimum fuel on go-around in order to expedite landing since fuel now was an issue with extra fuel burn and not much to play. Controller was going to extend us downwind behind an arriving aircraft which would have added more time and fuel so I elected to [request] an immediate turn to the FAF for XXC. I didn't want XXL because of animal issue and another possible go-around. Controller vectored preceding aircraft off their approach and cleared us for visual XXC. Landed uneventfully with 3.9 fuel.....2.10 left tank and 1.8 right tank. Reserve Fuel on Flight Plan was 3.78.Cause: Dispatched with normal arrival fuel with very good weather. Controller vectored us low and slow which increased fuel burn. Suggestions: Next time I will not accept so many vectors and low and slow increasing fuel burn when I do not have extra fuel to play.
1778675: Arriving DEN on the CLASH2 arrival from the southeast, I planned and briefed an easterly flow arrival to land 17R. ATIS advertised 17R, 16L, 16R ILS, visual and RNAV Z approaches. I briefed for the RNAV RNP Z 17R. The final point for the arrival was QWIKE intersection and I left a discontinuity between that QWIKE and the QWIKE point starting the RNAV RNP Z 17R. Denver Center gave us a clearance to descend via the CLASH2 arrival landing south.The PM (Pilot Monitoring) and I confirmed that that was what we briefed and the FMC was properly programmed. The PM checked on with DEN Approach and we were told to expect RNAV Z to 16R. The PM installed that approach and I briefed the new arrival points and crossing restrictions on the CLASH2 that coincided with that runway, which were now a west downwind, the final fix being CLFFF. I briefed the approach as well. We did the same thing, leaving a discontinuity between CLFFF on the arrival and CLFFF as the IAF on the approach. The PM pulled the landing data for 16R and we briefed the changes on the engine-out missed approach which was slightly different then 17R. Approximately EVRLY intersection as we were descending through FL180, DEN Approach then said runway change, expect visual or ILS (I can't remember) to 16L. I remember it was at FL180 because it coincided with the altimeter change and the need to verify that VNAV is still able to maintain. The PM installed runway 16L and I did a briefing for the ILS 16L. This changed the FMC to an east downwind, the same fixes as for runway 17R but I did not note the changes in arrival fixes. As we were approaching JURKY intersection, I noticed on the FMC that the next waypoint was not what I was expecting. I had in my mind that we would be on a west downwind for the 16 runways. I said to the PM, it's not the correct fix next for runway 16R. The PM then asked DEN Approach to verify the runway assignment.Approach responded with a frequency change but did not respond to the request for runway clarification. This was at the point where we needed to go left or right depending on the runway. I thought it was 16R, so I went to the next fix for that runway, ROOTZ. As soon as the PM checked on with the next frequency, the Controller asked our runway assignment. The PM said we were trying to clarify. Approach then gave us 16R as a runway assignment. In fact, the previous clearance was for runway 16L. And that runway is an east downwind, not a west downwind even though the runway is on the west side of the airfield. This was absolutely my responsibility to ensure the correct runway and corresponding waypoints for the arrival. Going forward my personal correction will be to write down the runway assignment given by ATC each time it changes, whether on the yoke clip notepaper or on the iPad graphic. I also got complacent after doing 2 full briefings into DEN on a clear day. With the 3rd briefing, I did an abbreviated briefing. A full briefing, stepping through every arrival point would have caught it earlier. Additionally, as suggested by the Jump Seater, instead of clarifying the runway and having to verify the points quickly, I will ask ATC for the next waypoint they are expecting in order to give myself some time to figure out any ambiguities between the FMC and the chart. If we are adding to the data for DEN arrival deviations though...I didn't think this could happen to me. We briefed the threat of runway changes going into DEN. But DEN giving runway changes that impact arrival points without sufficient time for us to properly program and confirm was a contributing factor. Its 11.4 miles from EVRLY where we got the change to JURKY where the arrival splits. To reprogram, confirm, brief, get landing data and brief the engine-out profile changes while monitoring the descent is challenging. CLASH2 RNAV into DEN we initially planned for a Visual Approach to 17R backed up by the ILS. Initial Controller told us to expect 16R so we loaded RNAV/RNP 16R with the CLFFF transition to the approach, per ATIS. Cleared to descend via the CLASH2 arrival so we set 11,000 feet in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). ATC then advised us to expect Visual Approach to 16L. I then loaded the 16L ILS in the box and the Captain continued the descent on the arrival around the JURKEY fix. When the Captain started to brief the new arrival she noticed the arrival fixes did not match up with the new runway.I asked ATC to verify our runway assignment as all 3 of us in the cockpit were unclear at that point. After a pause, ATC gave us a new frequency instead of answering my query regarding which runway. At that point the Captain manually entered the ROOTZ fix. We changed our altitude in the MCP to correspond to the 13,000 feet minimum at ROOTZ while we checked in with the final Controller. Upon checking in the Controller asked us which runway we were planning on. I asked again which runway as we were not certain at that point. He then stated Visual Approach 16R. I updated the box AGAIN to the ILS 16R and, we were then given a heading and new altitude. The rest of the arrival and approach were uneventful.
