1778828: I was approaching F70 from the southeast after a personal flight while making radio calls every few miles as I noticed on my ADS-B in several targets circling around the airport due to intense student activity.Someone made a radio call a few minutes before I was in the vicinity of another aircraft cutting them off on downwind too and I prepared myself for heavy traffic in the pattern and trying to find an opening so I could join the downwind.Upon entering the 45 for downwind I noticed visually an aircraft on the upwind taking off and repeatedly asked his intentions and if he could see me.There was no answer and seeing him proceed on runway heading I continued on the 45 for downwind being confident he wouldn't start a turn to crosswind until he reached close to pattern altitude as is recommended for the noise abatement procedure out of F70 for departures from Runway 18.Then I saw him maneuver for the crosswind maybe 500 feet below my altitude which was at pattern and make a radio call in that regards. At this point I had contacted him several times regarding his intentions and whether he could see me but without any answer.Seeing him turn and put me on the direct collision course with me although 300 ft. below me I decided to execute a 360 degree turn saw him coming extremely near me. Finally he acknowledged my presence in a subsequent radio call.I continued the full turn and reentered downwind.F70 was extremely busy that day with several schools on the field and at one point I saw no less than 5 aircraft in the traffic pattern. Needless to say a Tower is badly needed in that field for the safety of flight as the indiscriminate addition of several aircraft from several schools without any sort of coordination between those schools makes this urgently needed.A bit of courtesy goes a long way too and someone was nice enough to extend their downwind for me earlier in the day so I could depart as I had to hold short of the active runway at least 10 minutes as one aircraft after another was landing with no end in sight.On my side I should have waited outside the pattern on a hold in a safe area until there was no aircraft on upwind and the downwind leg would be fully opened, with adequate radio communications ensuring everyone in the pattern has knowledge of any other traffic with acknowledgement for all.This was my first experience with this field with that many aircraft in the pattern and the lesson learned here is to stay outside an uncontrolled field until there is fewer than a set limit of aircraft that one can set as personal limit.Such a personal limit is not taught at all as part of any training curriculum nor in the AIM in my knowledge.Most uncontrolled field are uncontrolled because of very low traffic but some reach levels just below the threshold needed for a tower and F70 seems to be in that category.Also the schools on the field could coordinate some kind of schedule among themselves so not everyone is up in the air at the same time. Poisson's law dictates things happen in bursts unless there is coordination to avert it.
1778839: I was working everything in the Tower combined. Aircraft Y checked in on a GPS Runway XX approach and I cleared him for the option. A few minutes later Aircraft X called for taxi and I gave him the normal taxi instructions with a crossing at Runway XX, forgetting that I had cleared an aircraft for that runway. While I was making an amendment to a flight plan I hear Aircraft Y ask why there is an aircraft on his runway. He had come to a complete stop on the runway while Aircraft X was crossing. I told him to hold position and once it was clear I cleared him for takeoff from present position. We're reduced staffing due to COVID-19, and having to train forces us to combine positions to accomplish the numbers that management is pushing for.
1778932: We were conducting Aircraft X at night into ABE, vectored from the north, and then given a clearance for a Visual Approach. As always, we had an approach set up, ILS 24, and while descending from the north side of the airport from 3,000 feet, the vectored altitude, to 2,400 feet, at an altitude of about 2,650 feet we received a one time (only 1) 'Terrain' warning from the TAWS (Terrain Alert Warning System), while descending very gently at about 300 feet per minute. We leveled off for a moment, there was no other terrain warning and never a 'Terrain, Pull Up' command, then as we intercepted the final, we continued to the 2,400 feet glideslope intercept altitude. There was a ridgeline north of the ILS course, which we had briefed on, but it did not show an altitude greater than 1,000 feet, so we did not think it would be a problem to start a shallow descent from 3,000 to 2,400 feet, especially at a shallow rate. This is a potential problem at night, as there are no obstacle lights on the ridge line, so I believe Approach should simply provide vectors to the ILS approach instead of just giving a 'visual.' A little more work for ATC but a safer way of operating. Caused by ATC clearing crew to do a night visual instead of providing vectors, knowing that there are unmarked, unlit, terrain ridge lines to the north of the airport. Also caused by crew not requesting full vectors to the ILS at night. Most ATC facilities in small airports don't want to work that hard. Suggest that crews start asking ATC at small airports to provide vectors to the Approach being used to back up the Visual when in night VMC conditions, as a means to improve the level of safety, even if it means that ATC might have to work a bit more.
1779182: My flight began at ZZZ1 with the intent to fly direct to ZZZ for touch and goes and return to ZZZ1. I have flown this particular airplane multiple times with no issues. The start, taxi, and run-up were normal and no different than any other time, except that the strobe lights were blinking slower than usual but working as expected.The airplane was flown earlier, and no issues were reported, hence there was no reason to suspect a problem. I did two take-offs and landings before departing to ZZZ, I had no issues. During a normal approach to landing at ZZZ, all-electric equipment failed at an altitude of 300 feet from touching down on Runway XX. I was forced to immediately clear the runway and exit onto the first taxiway I saw, Taxiway XX, I had a disabled radio, transponder, and ADS-B.Although clear from the tower for a touch and go, I could not continue the flight safely with disabled equipment, therefore a go-around was not an option. Luckily, I have a handheld radio and was able to contact the control tower to explain what happened, and request directions to the parking area. I had to deviate from the touch and go clearance since I dint know what else was wrong with the airplane and continuing the flight would have been unwise.After arriving at the parking area, I talked to the mechanic who was only available by phone and asked me to go through my checklist again to troubleshoot the issue. I made multiple attempts to restart the airplane, loud cabin speaker noises could be heard as the power switch was turned on as if there was a short circuit in the system, but all fuses were okay and there was no power to start the engine. The mechanic determined that I had a dead battery and it could only mean that the airplane suffered an alternator failure on landing, grounding the airplane immediately.The flight club from which I rented the airplane has multiple airplanes of the same make and model and provided me with one so I could fly back to ZZZ1. The return flight was uneventful.
1779583: As background, ZZZ was heavily congested with training and weekend aviators. The approach to the downwind leg was reported via UNICOM as 4nm SE to enter a 45 - downwind entry. We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern.Reported downwind uneventfully and recognized the aircraft we were to follow and minimized their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported [our] base turn to UNICOM, uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 nm from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base to final turn, uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final, I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying), in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine the position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. For clarification, the safety pilot - PNF, is a seasoned 121 CA (Captain) and highly experienced in the PA24-250 with close to 2,000 hours in type. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location, resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile, PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner.At this time, the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude, which was approximately 300 ft AGL. Because of the proximity to us, and apparently being unaware of our location, the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in their base to final turn (RH pattern) with a low wing aircraft [they] would have then been unable to locate us.Additionally, as we both rolled out on final we were both nearly lined up on the centerline, the closure rate was approximately 42 FPS and without evasive action, contact would have occurred in about 30 seconds, short of the runway, all due to the difference in V-ref and approach speeds. The PNF recognized this before I had visual contact with the conflicting traffic and they took control of the aircraft and became the PF.The evasive maneuver was complex in that [the other aircraft's] intentions seemed unpredictable and we did not want to initiate a go-around with the associated high deck angle, which would interrupt visual conflict with the conflicting traffic. Communication from their aircraft was weak and seemed confused as they, on short final, radioed 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you located'. We discussed the possibility that they may begin a go around and that would worsen the conflict since we may have lost visual contact and keep in mind... at this time we were behind their location and out of view.In the interest of safety, we chose to sidestep slightly left and to pass them on the level and then after we cleared the aircraft to begin a go around. The point we were trying to achieve was to maintain visual contact with the conflicting aircraft until we passed clear of their position.
1779586: Aircraft Y had taxied into parking via Taxiway A and was pulling into his parking spot on the ramp. Aircraft X was doing a touch and go on Runway 14L which is directly west of the ramp. During the touch and go Aircraft X was directly behind the Aircraft Y and was hit with jet blast on his left wing from Aircraft Y while they were still under power, idle or taxi power unknown.This happens here often enough and some of us to issue cautionary jet blast calls to Runway 14L traffic. I do not know if the pilot was told or not.We could put a message on the ATIS, create another Hot Spot or at least post it in the Airport Directory.
1779805: We were approximately 20 miles SE of the airport in the mountains on a sight-seeing flight. I was PIC (Pilot In Command) and the only pilot on board with 2 passengers. At 4,500 MSL the AWOS was intermittent because of the mountains. The MEF (Maximum Elevation Figure) on the sectional chart was 4,400 MSL and I was working my around some shorter hills. While experiencing some lighter bumps over a ridge, the 'GEAR IN TRANSIT' annunciator light lit up. I immediately checked to make sure I hadn't selected the gear handle down because we were too far away from the airport to have the gear down. The selector handle was still in the 'GEAR UP' position so my next instinct was to grab the emergency gear override and hold it in the 'UP' position to keep the gear from extending so far out. I checked the circuit breaker and everything seemed normal. I cycled the gear down and got 3 green lights and when cycled back up the green lights went away but the transit light never turned off. The AWOS suddenly kicked in and led me to decide on Runway 8 which meant I would cross the airport midfield and enter a tear drop for a left downwind to Runway 8. On the sectional I saw the altitude as 1,907 and decided to over fly the field at 2,500. In my mind 1,907 was pattern altitude and not the airport altitude. My mind was still on making sure my gear didn't fall down and create more drag for me that far away from the airport. About 1.5 miles to the south of the airport I once again communicated on the CTAF of my intentions to over fly the field at 2,500. One aircraft said they were back taxiing and going to depart Runway 8. As we approached the airport I felt like I was too low even though I was at 2,500 and then realized my mistake by how well I could see details on the ground. I quickly announced my intentions to climb up to traffic pattern altitude of 2,900 feet just before reaching the south side of the airport pattern which meant I was then climbing into the pattern instead of already being at the correct altitude. Directly over the runway we were back to 2,900 feet and I continued out to do a right hand turn and enter a tear drop to the left downwind. The gear came down fine and we landed safely. The combination of trying to troubleshoot an annunciator light while listening to incoming traffic and the intermittent AWOS left me to be distracted and mixing up proper altitudes for the pattern.Better self-briefing prior to arrival to an airport would have greatly reduced the chance of this occurring. Along with remembering that I had plenty of fuel and could have circled at a safe altitude to troubleshoot and then with a clearer mind come up with a plan to land at the airport normally.
1779934: We were established on final a few miles outside of the FAF. All was as it should be. We were stable on the localizer at 170 knots with flaps 15 autopilot on. Winds were 210 at 50 knots, steady. In a split second we went from straight and level to a left hand bank I'm guessing 20 degrees maybe more and the hook came up and we got a momentary stick shaker. As it happened I added power as we rolled wings level. We were about 20 degrees off heading, but the autopilot recovered to intercept the localizer, and we never lost any altitude. Like I said, it happened so quickly and recovered that I saw no need to disconnect the autopilot. We re-intercepted the localizer followed by the glide slope and shot the approach with no other concerns. I'm not sure if the winds were the reason or we hit someone's wake turbulence. I'm guessing it was wake turbulence. [Cause:] not sure - perhaps wake turbulence. The winds were strong but steady. 210 at 50 knots at 3000 ft. Perhaps ATC had us too close, but as I recall my traffic was a 757, 7 miles ahead, maybe it was wake from a plane on the parallel runway.
1780084: We were two hours late due to ATC closure (ZZZ Center). After discussing with Dispatch that we would be very close to Crew day, we launched from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Landed approximately two hours late and took off from ZZZ1 in time to land back at ZZZ within Crew day, however, upon landing (with 20 minutes to spare) there were approximately 10 aircraft waiting for a gate. I sent Dispatch an ACARS telling them that we were going to exceed our 13-hour Crew day. I was told by ZZZ Ops and Dispatch that gates were being issued 'first-come, first-serve.' We waited approximately 45 minutes before making it to a gate. Total day was approximately 30 minutes over allowed hours.
1780179: ATC said there was rain on the field. There was a B737 flight ahead of us on the approach by 5 to 10 minutes. We were listening to both Approach and Tower to monitor their approach and landing. We discussed holding, prior to the preceding aircraft landing. The preceding B737 reported safe on deck, medium braking, and no issues. They said they broke out 300 feet above minimums, 500 feet above ground. This gave us confidence to conduct the approach and landing. We complied with the wet runway requirements on the 10-7 page (max braking).We were fully configured with flaps 30 by the final approach fix with the landing checklist complete. We were stable at both the 1000 feet and 500 feet calls. Approach was mostly smooth in the clouds with no turbulence. Auto throttles moved very little. The rain was moderate, maybe moderate to high. Once we broke out, we could see the runway the entire time. Wiper were keeping up, but on high. We broke out about 300 feet. Saw some ground before that, so knew we were close to breaking out. Saw the Runway End Identifier Lights at 300 feet and the runway edge lights and center line lights shortly after. Captain called 'approaching minimums' just prior to breaking out and I said I had the field in sight. The auto pilot and auto throttles were disengaged around 200 feet.Landed a little left of center line, but the right main gear was to the right of the center line. Nose was pointed down the runway. Landing was firm to hard. Flare was normal. Raised nose to arrest descent at 30 feet and power was at idle at touchdown. We were both surprised by the firmness of the landing. Nose wheel was set down normally. I thought we might have skipped a little bit, but the Captain did not think so. Maybe we hydro-planed then the tires grabbed. We immediately started sliding left. I don't remember us turning to the left. It seemed we were pointed down the runway but going left. I stepped on the right rudder, but it didn't seem to have an effect. The left main mount went off the pavement on the left side of the runway. It seemed to take a while to get it back on the pavement with full right rudder and full manual braking. With both pilots stepping on full manual brakes, the aircraft did not seem to slowdown. Never felt the brakes grabbing, and with max brakes, we should have felt the brakes grab. I do not know if that Captain was using the nose wheel steering to assist getting it back to the right.Once back on the pavement, we started to veer to the right, but never left the pavement on the right side. Once on the runway, we added full reverse. We put in full left rudder to keep it on the runway. We got the aircraft direction under control, but it was still pulling to the right with full braking and full left rudder. I think the Captain was countering the pull with nose wheel steering. The aircraft was still difficult to slow down.We exited the runway on the high-speed taxiway on the right at a slow speed and came to a stop just off the runway. Tower asked about our position and if we needed assistance. The aircraft instruments, indications and controls were all normal. The only noticed adverse indication was an 'anti-skid inop ' light. The Captain released the brakes and rolled forward a little to check for a blown tire and brake function. All seemed fine so we said we can proceed to the gate. The taxi in was uneventful.On the taxi in we informed Tower that we may have departed the paved surface and there may be Foreign Object and Debris (FOD)on the runway. After shutdown, the Captain got up and checked on the Flight Attendants and passengers. All seemed fine. One Flight Attendant said she was scared while it was occurring, but otherwise no adverse comments. They were obviously a little shaken at the time, but not excessively so. We contacted Company maintenance and wrote up the maintenance items that we knew about. Several of the Flight Attendants were working our deadhead flight back the next morning. Theystill did not seem to have any after effects from the event and were friendly toward us.Maybe the initial left drift was due to the right gear hydro planning while the left gear had full auto-brakes using anti-skid. Once the left gear returned to the pavement, it's ant-skid may have been damaged, causing the veering to the right under full brakes. Leg 3 of a transitioning First Officer on a 4 day 15 hour IOE (Initial Operating Experience). The First Officer had just flown the previous leg and done well. He shot the ILS Approach and flew a nice approach to a very nice landing. During the 3 hour sit prior to our flight we discussed the upcoming flight including the special airport requirements and 10-7 pages. Reviewed the flight plan NOTAMs and maintenance status of the aircraft. Noted the sequenced flashing lights to our planned arrival runway were out of service.First Officer made a nice takeoff and climb out to cruise and we continued to update the weather forecasts on the flight. Reviewed 10-7 pages decided to use max braking for training and for possibility of a wet runway. Worst weather report we saw was 4000 feet broken, light rain, and winds 240 at 8. Briefed the arrival and RNAV Approaches due to winds. We also briefed the ILS. Approaching top of descent asked Center which runway was in use. The ILS was the approach in use. Pulled up the landing data. Approaching with radar on noticed a cell and heard [an] aircraft ask for deviations. We asked for and received direct ZZZZZ on the arrival. Descending to 12,000 feet were cleared for the arrival and preceding aircraft ask for direct to a fix. There appeared to be cells just south of the approach. Approach informed us there was rain on the field, we discussed possible holding when we heard [another aircraft] cleared for the approach.I tuned VHF 2 to Tower frequency to get a heads up on the preceding aircraft. They were cleared to land and reported to Tower breaking out a few hundred feet above minimums landed and reported braking action medium. Approach cleared us direct to a fix and to report on the localizer cleared for the approach. Slowed toward 180 kts., flaps 5 auto pilot on LNAV/VNAV, armed the app mode, made 2,500 feet call, reported established and was told to switch to Tower. Called Tower and reported 9 mile final was cleared to land. I believe Tower also said preceding aircraft broke out at 500 feet and braking action medium. Localizer and glideslope engaged set Touchdown Zone Elevation. Approaching the final approach fix gear down flaps 15 rolled speed back then selected flaps 30 and landing checklist.IMC and moderate rain but little to no turbulence or wind shifts. Passing approximately 1,000 to 800 feet saw ground and lights looking down called 1,000 feet then set Missed Approach altitude. Approach was stable and verified at 500 feet. Called approaching minimums slightly early approximately 400 feet to prepare for possibility of a go around. Approximately 300 feet broke out with Runway End Lights, High Intensity Runway Lights and runway center line in sight. First Officer disengaged the auto pilot and auto throttle approximately 150 to 200 feet. Still raining with wind shield wipers on high but could clearly see the runway environment. Short final dipped 1/4 dot low to try and land in the first 1,000 feet. Heard 50 feet just prior to crossing the threshold then 40, 30. At 30 the First Officer began the flare slowing the rate of descent then began reducing power. Everything appeared normal till the last 5 to 10 feet when it felt like the bottom dropped out to a firm to hard landing. Written up as a hard landing.There was no bounce. Power levers at idle and speed brakes deployed. I have used max auto brakes often due to the demo requirement for Operational Experience. Ordinarily they grab and push you forward in the seat. There was no such sensation other than a feeling the anti-skid was cycling and the aircraft did not appear to be slowing. I believe the nose was pointed straight down the runway and the touchdown had the nose just left of the center line. On touchdown the aircraft began to immediately slide to the left. I believe the aircraft hydroplaned after landing. The First Officer depressed full right rudder with no effect. First Officer was slow to go into reverse so I came on the controlsset max reverse and followed full right rudder yet the aircraft continued to slide left and the left main mount left the prepared surface. I used nose wheel steering to bring the aircraft back toward center line. All this happened immediately after touchdown or so I believe. As we continued down the runway with both of us standing on the brakes the aircraft began to slide toward the right side of the runway. With full reverse full manual brakes and what I believed to be full left rudder it required nose wheel input to keep the aircraft from leaving the right side of the runway. At no point in time did I feel the aircraft nose was pointed at or mostly toward either side of the runway from initial touchdown to stop.As we continued down the right side of the runway the aircraft still did not appear to be slowing normally. Approaching the high speed taxiway on the right side of the runway I elected to allow the aircraft to veer onto the taxi way. We had finally slowed where we were able to bring the aircraft to a stop. We were not 100 percent sure the left main mount had left the prepared surface so we discussed the possibility and the possibility of blown tires. Tower asked if we needed assistance. We did not note any usual indications or issues all instruments appeared normal. With the exception of the anti-skid fault light. I allowed the aircraft to roll forward checking the brakes which appeared to operate normally at slow speed and we had no indication of a deflated tire. I decided the aircraft could be taxied to the gate to deplane the passengers safely at slow speed and was cleared by Tower to do so. We also informed Tower there may be FOD (Foreign Object and Debris) on the runway. Uneventful taxi to parking with good clear area all the way into the gate. Performed the parking checklist then left the flight deck to check on the passengers and flight attendants. No injuries were reported. One flight attendant said she was a little shaken. Conferred with base ops then did a walk around with the contract mechanic. Called Company maintenance and made maintenance write ups.
1780466: On a normal approach to landing Runway XX at ZZZ airport, the aircraft experienced a temporary loss of engine power. We were on the middle glide path of the PAPI (2 red, 2 white) on runway centerline at approximately 200 ft. AGL. Approach speed was approximately 85 mph with 20 degrees of flaps deployed. The throttle was at a low power setting and the aircraft was sinking slightly below glideslope, so I pushed it in a bit to increase power. There was no increase in power so I pushed the throttle in further, eventually to full. With no change in engine sound or perceived power I continued the descent maintaining airspeed to the ground. As the aircraft was already low, we struck two approach lights (MALSR) and knocked them over. In inspection afterwards it appears that the lights struck the lower engine cowling and dented it. The plane touched down and at this point I contacted the tower letting them know we had a loss of power. During rollout engine power came back due to the pushed in throttle. I opted to shut the engine down at this point as the state of the airplane was not known. Once crews arrived I had already exited the plane and did not see much visible damage. With the fire crews there we opted to restart the engine to taxi off the runway with no further issue.I believe this incident could be caused by carburetor icing or perhaps a contaminant in the fuel system. The aircraft should have had approximately 20 gallons of fuel remaining at time of landing, and was in a stabilized decent so I would rule out temporary interruption of fuel supply. There was no indication of low fuel on either gauge and the fuel selector was set to both. A contaminant in the fuel system seems possible, though I am not sure what would make this kind of incident transitory. It's hard to say for sure, but I believe we were still hearing the engine running and not just the windmilling prop the entire time, so I don't believe the engine had shut off entirely at any point.Carburetor icing seems like the most likely explanation I can think of, but the symptoms are not consistent with how I was trained to detect it. At no time did we experience engine roughness during the flight, which I believed was a characteristic sign of carb icing. Prior to the descent to land, the aircraft was circling at 10,000 ft. for aerial observation. Power settings during the decent were reduced and I remember thinking that the throttle position used during the cruise descent was further in than I would expect for the observed manifold pressure. I had only flown this plane briefly before, so I didn't think much more of it, but if carb ice was the blame this was probably the main indication. At 2,000 ft. I was reducing to lower power settings and I activated carburetor heat. There was no roughness after this point that I would expect to associate with carb icing as it cleared.The fact that the landing after sunset and starting to get dark was not a major factor, aside from difficulty seeing what was below (besides the lights) as the plane came down short of the runway. Maintaining the approach speed close to best glide after power loss was important in avoiding any injury or more significant damage to the aircraft. Given the long length of the runway (9,800 ft.) I could have avoided hitting anything by planning to land above the PAPI glidepath.
1780518: Initial approach into DIA I encountered two separate large drones that were in the Bravo airspace without authorization. One was at my level off to the right by about a quarter to half mile. The other was while in the descent into the airport shortly after the first encounter. Both created a collision hazard and cause for alarm. The aircraft was in a state of peril and threatened the operation. No further incidents had occurred after entering final for Runway 35L.
1780537: Flight originated in ZZZ as a Part 135 scheduled flight to ZZZ1. There were no passengers on board. ZZZ Center advised us that ZZZ4 Center would be going to an 'ATC Zero' condition for 1 hour 30 minutes at 15 minutes prior to our scheduled arrival due to a COVID situation in the Center facility. I made the decision to divert to ZZZ3 and accomplished training enroute and landing late afternoon. Weather in ZZZ3 was IFR with a report that fog was believed to be moving into the ZZZ3 area. We refueled and departed for ZZZ1. Training was again accomplished enroute...landing was at night with 2,500 broken, 3,100 overcast and 3 mile in R and BR. This was the end of a long day that started early morning for a departure to ZZZ5 from ZZZ1...scheduled time was 1 hour 50 minutes with a 20 minute turn. Due to waiting for a dead heading crew member we left ZZZ5 one hour late, arriving ZZZ1 at noon. I picked up another FO and departed for ZZZ for a planned 1 hour 40 minute flight. Landing at ZZZ, we then departed for a planned 1 hour 40 minute flight to ZZZ1. As noted previously, we were forced to divert to ZZZ3, due to ATC Zero. I exceeded 8 hours but, felt that, per our FOM and the FARs, I was legal to start and finish because the divert to ZZZ3 was not planned and the scheduled times were within legal limits. Note that I had over 14 hours rest before the flying the following day and was off duty after the days flying was complete and no other flying scheduled for several days.The issue that bothers me is that I was accomplishing training at night and in solid IMC conditions...never again. There was some unspoken pressure to get the training accomplished due to approaching holiday and a lack of aircraft to accomplish the training during daylight hours. I also should not have pressed the flying...the start of the problem was the unplanned ZZZ5 turn due to the scheduled Captain timing out and for whom I was asked to cover. As soon as we knew we would have to divert to ZZZ3, I should have terminated any further training and proceeded to ZZZ1 as soon as ZZZ4 Center re-opened. Several 'takeaways'...I will not allow this to happen to me again, even though I believed (and believe) I was legal...fatigue was not an issue. Training should only be accomplished in solid VMC conditions and preferably in daylight.
1780917: We were on a visual approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ at 3,000 feet. Approach cleared us for a visual approach about 7 miles out and we were giving a heading towards the FAF following an airbus. PF set 2,000 feet in the MCP and we began a slow descent heading inbound to the airport. ATC issued a 'low altitude alert' at about 2,300 feet. We leveled off and intercepted the G/S just past the FAF. In addition, we had to rapidly slow since the airbus in front slowed rapidly and ATC wanted us to slow to approximately 150 knots or less. They really did not leave us much lateral room. We slowed and configured while descending. We were never near an obstacle, nor were we a threat to another aircraft. We were still above the 1,000 feet stable approach criteria (1,300 to 1,500 feet) and met the criteria proof to reaching 1,000 feet. We were lower than what was normally flow for that area but still seamed safe. Again on a visual approach. PF stated that he read 2,000 feet at the FAF and misread the altitude. The FAF altitude is 2,800 feet. I did not reverify it since we were visual and I was working on setting up radios and configuration for landing. I assumed he saw it correctly.I can't find where we violated anything. We were a little low for the area but still in a safe position to land and had visual clearance from all obstacles. I know next time to verify the altitude in the MCP from the chart myself. That is that only thing that may have stopped the lower alt in the first place. On receiving landing clearance, I set 2,000 feet in the altitude window and planned to descend to that altitude at ZZZZZ, the FAF. I misread the approach plate. The correct altitude at ZZZZZ is 2,800 feet. The Tower gave us a Low Altitude Alert at 2,200 MSL in VMC and we maintained that altitude (we were nearly at glideslope intercept) until glideslope intercept. We landed uneventfully.
1780939: Cleared for ILS XXR approach into ZZZ outside of ZZZZZ maintain 3,000 until established. VMC but too hazy to see runway at 12 miles final. Autopilot was engaged and LOC was armed but the aircraft did not intercept and we flew thru LOC course. I turned off autopilot and autothrottles to attempt re-intercept of localizer however flight directors were giving far right correction with LOC indices correcting slightly left. We were far right of course, so FD guidance was completely inaccurate and LOC indices should have been making far correction to left which they were not. We attempted to determine source of the problem but were unsuccessful doing so. We cycled the ILS radio panel, but no help. We asked for Go-around and were given instructions by ATC. On second approach attempt LOC and GS captured and an uneventful landing was made.
1780947: While approximately 2 hours from our destination, we discovered that ZZZZ1 weather would not allow us to land at destination. We made a decision with fuel and time to hold and then subsequently divert to ZZZZ2. The communication barrier was difficult with the controllers and while that took place we were also using the radio for Dispatch. I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and was coordinating the divert with Dispatch and the handling in ZZZZ2. Task saturation after a long flight was certainly a challenge. I also was having freezing issues with Jepp FD pro. After being handed to ATC, we had the approach and plan in place for the approach Runway XX. On the decent the controllers left us very high even after multiple requests for lower. The PF (Pilot Flying) was using FLCH and max speed brakes most of the time. We were able to get to an appropriate altitude safely. I had a brief moment of thought about still being in FLCH on decent and through saturation, I failed to mention it. Inside the IAF I set the TDZE as normal and confirmed with crew, as we were cleared the approach. We had still been descending constantly from events before, we never really stopped descending since just after the divert was made. As we were in the arc, we were completely configured for landing and I noticed that we had descended below the published altitude on the ARC. I quickly realized we had been still in FLCH and immediately said to stop decent. We were approximately 400-500 ft. Low. And after arresting settled at about 600 below. The PF and crew were in VMC conditions. CAVOK. We were approximately 1/2 to 3/4 of the way through the arc once I noticed. We had the airport in sight and the PF elected to stay at the approximate pattern altitude as we were over water in VMC and had the airport in sight and about to turn final. The approach continued visually and the PF made a normal landing and taxi to hard stand.
1781036: In cruise I messaged Dispatch and asked the RVR for [Runway] XXR. They told me 1400 for [Runway] XXR. About 30 minutes from arrival we started our brief. We briefed the arrival and the approach plate for [Runway]. We then briefed the CAT2 checklist. We both put 705 feet in our DH and verified it. We did the decent check and verified it again. Did the approach check and was getting vectors to [Runway] XXR. Gear down flaps 45 before the marker. I called 1,000 feet cleared to land when I knew something was wrong. I couldn't grasp why we only had 300 feet left to go missed. Told the First Officer something wasn't right. We hit minimums at 705 feet AGL and I called the missed. Did the missed approach, cleaned up aircraft and did the checklist. Didn't take me long to figure out what I did. The RA for [Runway] XXR is 116 feet. We put the new DH in and took our time to get set up for approach. We got vectors on the LOC and shot the approach to a landing.We both missed the right number for the DH. I knew the approach would be to minimums so I was looking at chart in cruise so I wouldn't miss anything. Ended up on a go around at 700 feet AGL because we had the MDA in. It was first flight of day we both felt good. Just the low visibility at destination caused a threat.Even after the lengthy briefing and checklist usage the DH was still put in there wrong. What I have learned over my career is not to get upset at the moment you realize you did something wrong. Great training over the years and good CRM has trained me to fly the airplane. Run the appropriate checklists and then discuss what happened at a safe time later. We incorrectly set the 705 feet in the DH for a CAT 2 approach and logically got the mins aural alert more than 500 feet early. We executed a go-around, set up the DH properly and flew the second approach normally.
1781502: I was flying with a student pilot, practicing simulated engine failure emergency procedures. Student selected Frazier Lake airport (1C9) as the landing point. We positioned the airplane directly towards 1C9 for runway 5 which is a grass runway. I scanned the area in front and right of us to make sure there was no other traffic nearby. We descended towards runway 5 and ended the practice by going around above runway 5 at about 800 ft AGL. The next day we received a phone call from another pilot who was operating in traffic pattern at 1C9 attempting to land on the hard surface taxiway parallel to runway 5. He told us that he saw us on final flying next to him only approximately 200 ft above. He made few radio calls trying to reach us but no response, because we were not on 1C9 CTAF at the time. What have caused this event was that the student was busy performing the maneuver, forgot to change frequency to 1C9 CTAF and announce our intention. I was too focused on the training but overlooked the safety aspect of the flight. The corrective action is I should have changed frequency to 1C9 CTAF and monitor it when the student decided to head over there.
1781727: Prior to Final approach in ZZZ, approach vectored us very close to the final approach course with a 30 kt tailwind on base and at 4,000 ft just outside ZZZZZ for the ILS XXR, assigned 190 kts. As we intercepted the course the autopilot flew past the localizer at close to half scale deflection, as it would not correct course timely. We also had to descend and slow down to configure for final approach within 3 miles of final approach fix. As the autopilot was correcting for that we set 3,000 ft for the missed approach altitude. A CAS MISCOMP status message appeared and the altitude alerter came on would not stop ringing. When we changed navigation source to green needles, the localizer would not capture with the autopilot, therefore the glide slope would also not capture. During the navigation source change, my flight director on the first officer's side became erratic and I lost the localizer transmission. We decided to execute a missed approach due to being unstable along with the flight instrument errors. Tower assigned us a heading and altitude and we reconfigured the aircraft for the go around all while the altitude alerter was blaring. During straight and level flight, we decided to reassign the FCP to heading and altitude. Once established, we turned the autopilot on and all instruments worked correctly. The altitude alert ringer was still buzzing so we decided to silence using Data Control Unit (DCU) audio buttons to declutter the situation. After completing proper checklists, we decided to continue on with another ILS XXR and executed approach and landing normally. After shutdown the altitude alerter still continued to ring until AC power was switched from the APU GEN to EXT AC. We wrote up the problem and notified maintenance.ATC giving us tight vectors with a tailwind on base along with our equipment malfunctions. The altitude alerter sounding loudly along our flight directors being erratic caused task saturation to the captain who was PF. As PM I helped the captain de clutter the situation and to reminded him to just fly the airplane which he did well as we tracked the localizer and conducted the go around. Once we silenced the altitude alerter it became much easier to fly the aircraft and we were able to conduct the next approach successfully.Possibly asking for a slower intercept speed or lower from ATC. The equipment malfunctions lead to the approach to become unstable and that's why we conducted a go around. I could have possibly contacted tower a few seconds earlier to ask for a vector and altitude but it was quite difficult with the task saturation being as high as it was, especially with the altitude alerter loudly sounding. Overall it was a great lesson in always being able to maintain control and fly the aircraft regardless of the state of automation it is in which I thought we did a great job of despite the system malfunctions during a high work load environment.
1781945: The Satellite position had just been combined with Departure during a relatively slow traffic period. Shortly after assuming control of their traffic an aircraft went NORDO on a heading for an approach. While trying to reestablish communications with the aircraft, Aircraft X was on a vector for the ILS approach into a different airport. The data tag had already been accepted by Tower, so when the new controller assumed the traffic, the tag had already been turned a separate color than usual. Aircraft X was given a descent to 2,100 feet by the previous controller. During the attempts to reestablish communication with the NORDO aircraft, Aircraft X ended up skirting the boundary of a 2,600 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude at 2,100 feet before making the turn back for the approach. No other aircraft were affected. After an aircraft data tag is highlighted green, there should be a way to turn the color of the aircraft back to white.
1782067: On a visual approach to UNV descending through 6500 ft. MSL on a 15 mile left base for runway 24 EGPWS activated over south ridge.EGPWS activated aural alert for Terrain pull up.[Caused by] passing over rising terrain while descending to approach altitude.[Executed a] max power climb at 15 degrees nose up until certain of accurate situational awareness, ridge passage, and terrain clearance.[We should] reduce rate of descent when crossing the ridge approaching UNV valley.
1782162: Suffice it to say that after touching down on a good 3-point landing with full control of the aircraft, on the rollout my left sneaker briefly got stuck on the left rudder pedal and then it started to lose the footing as I did the left-right, left-right continuous tapping that is required to control a tailwheel on the ground. So, with the tapping that is required in a tailwheel, with each tap after getting stuck, the left foot came more and more off the pedal, but I had to keep tapping to control the aircraft. While I slowed the aircraft down a lot, when my foot finally popped off the rudder pedal, the plane did about a ¼ loop to the left and the left landing gear snapped (as it is supposed to do when it receives excess side stress) and the left aileron scraped the runway. There was no real other damage [to the aircraft], or to the runway, or any other aircraft. There were no injuries at all. As soon as the plane stopped, I turned the master and mags (magnetos) off and rotated the fuel lever into the off position.
1782415: While being vectored for the ILS at ZZZ we received several Terrain Terrain pull up! Commands. We were at 2,500 ft. abeam ZZZ on a right downwind leg the autopilot was engaged at the time of the first warning. The autopilot was disengaged and I began an immediate climb and the Captain notified ZZZ approach of the terrain warning. We climbed to 3,500 ft. to silence the warning. ATC cleared us back down to 2,500 ft. after assuring us that minimum vectoring alt was well below us and there was no terrain to justify a terrain warning between us and the airport. After intercepting the localizer we continued to get the terrain warning The controller also heard the warning when he told us to switch the radio frequency to advisory's. We asked the Controller if we maintained IFR separation and he said that we did maintain it. The approach and landing continued normally.
1782726: I was providing On the Job Instruction during the event. I had previously cleared Aircraft X to 17,000 feet prior to the trainee taking position. Another aircraft, Aircraft Y, was also receiving vectors for the approach and was given a descent to 14000 feet and a speed reduction to 210 knots. Aircraft X read back the instructions and then immediately Aircraft Y read back the instructions. On position, I did not hear the call sign of Aircraft X and thought that Aircraft Y read back the instruction a second time. It was clearly a different voice so I just thought that the pilots were confused as to who was talking and who was flying. A few moments later the Developmental recognized that Aircraft X was at 15,200 feet in a 15,500 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) and issued a low altitude alert. The pilot responded that it was blocked and the trainee gave an immediate climb to 16,000 feet. I recognized the the trainee did not use the full proper phraseology by not saying the 'MVA in your area is XXX;' but decided at this point the solution had been acknowledge and it was not worth correcting the phraseology in a third transmission. The aircraft continued to descend to 14,400 feet until we observed a climb. During that time the aircraft crossed into a 14,900 foot MVA, but being in a climb I decided it was not necessary to issue another safety alert since we knew it was being corrected.There was a bit of frequency congestion due to confusion about the weather, and by the time I was ready to issue a brasher warning the aircraft was on a 10 mile final. I felt it was best to let the aircraft fly and have Local Control or Ground Control issue the brasher warning, so I coordinated that with Ground Control.
1782848: We checked on with ZZZ Approach and requested the RNAV Z XX via ZZZZZ. ATC advised unable due to traffic for Runway YY and told us to expect a visual to either [Runway] XYR or YY. The ATIS was reporting a high OVC and a low scattered layer, I think at 700 feet, we did not think we could accept a visual so we requested the RNAV Z YY. The Controller said we could expect that but we would need to be vectored, I said that was fine and also offered direct ZZZZZ1. We were vectored pretty far to the south east, over the river and past ZZZZZ1. We were finally given a vector to intercept final at or above 3,000 and cleared the approach. The CA tried to activate the approach and we discussed not activating RNPs, we had descended some while on the final course in VMC (I recall about 1,900 feet) and decided to cancel approach. We flew the missed and were vectored for the RNAV Y YY, that approach was uneventful.The CA and I had a full debrief and we learned a few things.The first issue was the Controller seemed unaware that we are unable to accept vectors to final on an RNP. After the go-around he asked the reason why and I told him that we can accept direct to or an intercept on a published leg but not vectors to final. He said thanks and I think he just did not know, but perhaps this should be known by all the controllers that work company aircraft.The second thing I learned is that I need to trust my gut feeling in these situations, once we were vectored past ZZZZZ1 I was anticipating that the Controller was going to vector us on to final, perhaps I could have asked him or requested the RNAV Y.The CA was ready to accept vectors to final and activate the approach, he began descending on the final course and I reminded him that we cannot accept that as it may cause issues with VNAV. The CA is a good pilot and sharp but is a newer captain and hadn't flown in over a month so the rustiness probably contributed.Overall I think we handled the situation as best we could and did not compromise safety in any way, especially with a missed approach not at the MAP which is something we rarely do on the line.
1782922: In Mexico City, on Runway 5R, there are no runway centerline markings from 1,000 feet beyond the landing threshold to 3,000 feet beyond the landing threshold. The runway centerline markings are faded and only visible when on top of them from 3,000 feet beyond the landing threshold to Taxiway G where we turned off after landing. A NOTAM needs to be issued to warn pilots.
1782984: While on downwind for a Visual [Runway] 21 we received a terrain caution (that lasted for about one second) while flying over the mountains. We were in visual conditions and clear of all obstacles. We continued the approach into CHO with no further delays. Casual Factor - Terrain around the Charlottesville airport. Made sure we were clear of the terrain and then continued on approach. Be weary of taking the visual around the mountains at lower altitudes. We should have also climbed a little bit to give ourselves some more clearance. While being vectored for a Visual Approach to Runway 21 at CHO on a left downwind, level, at an assigned altitude of 3,000 MSL we received a GPWS caution annunciation of: 'terrain pull up'. The flight conditions were day VMC, so both the Captain and I had the terrain we were overflying in sight. Our vectored flight path took us over steep rising terrain. Upon hearing the GPWS annunciation, we verbally acknowledged the annunciation and the visual steep rising terrain we were overflying. We maintained straight and level flight because we could visual ensure we were clear of all obstacles and/or terrain. Request ATC assigned an altitude of 4,000 MSL instead of 3,000 MSL when vectoring on this flight path for a visual approach to Runway 21 into CHO.
1783290: Flying IFR at 2,000 feet I incorrectly entered the approach information for the RNAV GPS Runway X approach to ZZZ and consequently the aircraft deviated from that depicted on the approach plate for the GPS approach. My flying time has been greatly reduced since the COVID-19 pandemic and I entered incorrect information in the GPS by mistake. I have since taken a course for 'Rusty Pilots' on the internet in an attempt to stay adequate and I have also scheduled my 'Flight Review' with an instructor. I think the reason for the mistake in entering the GPS information was due to greatly reduced flying time experience since COVID-19.
1783578: On flight XX, ZZZ to ZZZZ FO pre- loaded FMC with arrival ZZZZZ XA with Runway XXR. Before descent checklist (6 hours) later briefed STAR and arrival into ZZZZ for both XXL and XXR. ZZZZ ATIS stated both XXL and XXR were in use. Obtained landing data for both runways. Approaching ZZZZZ we got vectors to ZZZZZ1 with expect XXL. On descent ATIS was calling for gusty winds on final from moderate to severe broken clouds at 2,500 feet. We talked about the winds and before we got to ZZZZ1 we got vectors and a decent to XXL we talked about the winds and forgot to change the FMC to XXL. On vectors to XXL with the approach mode armed we intercepted the LOC to XXR. We still were not aware of the error until the controller told us we were lined up for XXR and wanted to give us a heading of 160. We knew traffic was very light so asked if we could continue to XXR and was cleared to continue and land XXR. Landed without incident. Upon returning to the flight deck from break, I was briefed on the ZZZZZ XA arrival and ILS XXL approach. ZZZZ ATIS broadcast that both XXL and XXR were in use. Runway data for both XXL and XXR were had been obtained earlier. Prior to descent we completed the descent checklist. At the FMC's, radios, item on the descent checklist, I intended to check the FMC to verify the approach and checked the item complete, but was interrupted by a radio call and never completed it. I did not catch the error that the FMC had ILS XXR programmed instead of ILS XXL, which had been briefed and anticipated. On the descent we were cleared the ZZZZZ XA Arrival to ILS XXL. Having briefed the ILS XXL, and believing we had ILS XXL programmed, no changes were made to the FMC. We did not catch the error until receiving radar vectors to the final approach. We were given a base leg and shortly after a vector to intercept. The turn to final seemed late and the aircraft but captured and lined up on the centerline. At that point, ATC gave us a 'right turn to 160' and then stated we were lined up for XXR and that we had been cleared for ILS XXL. He said there was no traffic for XXR and asked if we wanted to continue. We were at least 4 miles from the FAF so we accepted the approach clearance. We were able to review the approach noting the LOC identifier, changing the minimums and reviewed the Missed Approach procedure prior to descent on the GS. A stable approach was flown from the FAF to the runway for landing and was uneventful, as was the rollout and taxi-in.On the ATIS, gusty winds were noted and moderate, possibly greater, turbulence mentioned. This was a topic of discussion during the briefing and after. We briefed the cabin crew to have the cabin secured early and to take their seats as soon as possible after the chimes for the sterile cockpit notification. The aircraft was slowed early and we had begun configuring early as well so as to be stable early. The discussion was possibly an additional distraction during the briefing and Descent checklist.While we were able to comfortably get set up for the approach that was incorrectly loaded in and able to fly a stable approach, we should have asked for vectors to a new approach in order to properly brief prior to the initiation of the approach phase. We were lucky there was no traffic conflicts as there was little if any traffic due to time of day and the current state of airline traffic due to COVID.
1783828: Coming to ZZZ on the ILS [Runway] XXR, we were continually slowed by ATC for spacing of traffic ahead and behind. At about 1,200 MSL on glide path still IMC Tower told us to go-around. I was PF and hit GA button and advanced power levers. We went through missed approach procedure, but as flight guidance was attempting to be set the aircraft was also capturing the level off of 2,000 MSL so took a little longer to complete. Meanwhile we were a little late on turning to 195 heading. ATC queried us as we were in the turn. We had also climbed to 2,180 feet before stopping and returning back to 2,000 immediately. After we got settled ATC vectored us back to ILS with no further issues. ATC told us they had to send us around because aircraft on final for parallel Runway XXL behind us had gotten .99 miles from us. Spacing needed to stay a min of 1 mile.I should have paid more attention to altitude and started turn to 195 even if flight guidance wasn't quite set yet. Also pulled back power sooner or not add as much to avoid going through altitude. During our arrival into ZZZ, when told to run base (heading approximately toward ZZZZZ [Intersection]), we were slowed to 170 KIAS. We were maintaining 4,000 feet throughout base turn and intercept turn onto final. Once established on final (approximately 20 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]) we were slowed further to 160 KIAS, with traffic approximately 4 NM in front of us. Once we intercepted the glideslope, we maintained approximately 1,000 feet above the preceding traffic, but gained to within 3 NM distance. Meanwhile, ATC vectored a airline flight onto final for [Runway] XXL close behind us.I told the First Officer (PF) to potentially fly a half-dot high on the glide slope to avoid any potential wake from the preceding aircraft. Once we reached approximately 10 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] we were slowed further to 150 KIAS.As we continued down the approach, the TCAS showed us to be approximately 2.5 NM from the preceding traffic, with the traffic behind us close in trail (unable to tell the specific distance). At approximately 600 AGL, ZZZ Tower issued a Go-Around, with nonstandard missed approach instructions (Right turn heading 195, climb and maintain 2,000). The First Officer initiated the Go-Around and the Captain (PM) proceeded to re-program the Flight Guidance.Due to the light passenger load, the subsequent climb rate caused the Flight Guidance to immediately switch from a Climb indication to an Altitude Capturing indication, which caught the Captain off-guard, and he tried to re-configure the Flight Guidance back to a Climb indication. The Flight Guidance again sequenced to an Altitude Capture indication. At this point, the Captain (PM) noticed the aircraft was off course to the left approximately 35 degrees and was rapidly approaching 2,000 feet. The Captain brought this to the attention of the First Officer while also simultaneously acknowledging ATC stating 'Turn right heading 195.' The Captain also prompted the First Officer to reduce the power setting, as the airspeed was approaching maximum flap speeds. The missed approach up to leveling off at 2,000 feet was all hand-flown (i.e. not with the autopilot).Once the aircraft was established on the appropriate heading, altitude, and configuration, ZZZ Approach vectored the flight around for a second attempt at the ILS 16R, which occurred without further incident. In researching the First Officer's seniority, he has been here less than X years (Date). After debriefing the flight, he stated that that was his first Missed Approach / Go-Around in the actual aircraft EVER.Since we had been slowed down significantly early during the approach, we knew we could expect to be sandwiched in between other aircraft. However, we did not know that ATC needed only 1 mile separation between aircraft on parallel ILS approaches (told to us by ATC during our second attempt). There was no mention of spacing requirements on our first approach.Due to 'COVID loads;' the aircraft type climb rates are very good, requiring steeper than normal attitudes so as to not exceed flap speeds. This factor, combined with the First Officer's relative inexperience with missed approaches, caused a momentary loss of situational awareness by the First Officer.This required the CA to not only re-configure the flight guidance for a missed approach, but also ensure the First Officer did not over speed the flaps, communicate with ATC, and ensure the aircraft was following appropriate flight guidance (which was a non-standard missed approach).Also contributing to the loss in situational awareness was the altitude at which ATC issued the Go-Around: 600 AGL. This caused a significant startle factor in both the Captain and First Officer. Had ATC mentioned anything about a potential missed approach, we would have been much more prepared.Last-minute ATC-issued Go Around instructions (below 1,000 AFE), caused by inadequate spacing with simultaneous parallel approach aircraft.RECOMMENDATIONS:1. ATC NEEDS to let crews know 'be ready for a missed approach' if there is potential for a spacing issue. We were given our Go-Around instructions at 600 AGL. This is a very high-risk area to issue a Go-Around, when spacing throughout the entire approach was tight. Some sort of notification to us would have primed for a potential Missed Approach and therefore could have avoided any loss of situational awareness and subsequent heading / altitude deviation.2. STOP ISSUING NON-STANDARD MISSED APPROACH INSTRUCTIONS. The ILS [Runway] XXR's Standard Missed Approach instructions are to fly runway heading to 900 feet, then climb on heading 195 to intercept the ZZZ 210 degree radial, maintain 2,000 feet. This is VERY similar to what we were assigned (heading 195, climb to 2,000 feet). However, when we're given nonstandard missed approach instructions, not only do we have to interpret what it is ATC actually told us, but also program that into the Flight Guidance. This programming is CONTRADICTORY to what our normal Flight Guidance programming procedures are. Had ATC simply said 'fly the published missed approach;' that could've aided in our appropriate handling of the aircraft.LESSONS LEARNED:Don't trust ZZZ ATC to not screw up. If spacing looks tight, brief a missed approach, even if it's done on the Final Approach Course. Also, do not trust your fellow crew member to fly a perfect Missed Approach. Watch them like a hawk for course, airspeed, and altitude management, and IMMEDIATELY speak up if there is even a minor deviation.
1783930: [Aircraft X] was being vectored for an ILS approach into BFI RWY (Runway) 14R by the Arrival West (1W), Arrival East (1E), Boeing Arrival (1D), and Paine (1P) sectors combined. As [Aircraft X] was being vectored traffic was issued for two VFR aircraft on 1200 codes transitioning both north and south through the localizer for Runway 14R. Due to this traffic I left [Aircraft X] at 3,000 ft. and obtained a point-out with SEA Final (1F). Despite this altitude, [Aircraft X] responded to a TCAS RA and, in an effort to protect the sea final approach course, I turned [Aircraft X] right to a heading 220. As [Aircraft X] turned southbound I observed a C172, [Aircraft Y], being vectored for the ILS Runway 20 approach into PWT. I turned [Aircraft X] further right to a northwest heading, and measured the distance between [Aircraft X] and [Aircraft Y]. I observed approximately 3.3 miles between the two and since I had already issued the turn, I judged that sufficient separation and attempted to continue working to not fall further behind. [Aircraft X] turned slower than anticipated and caused a separation error between themselves and [Aircraft Y]. The root of this issue is the continual constant conflict between IFR jets into BFI and VFR aircraft transitioning through the localizer in both north and south flow. It is a well-known, persistent issue that has been thoroughly reported for several years. Several solutions have been proposed, but none have been adapted.The only fix for this issue is a restructuring of the Seattle Class B airspace to protect the finals in both directions at BFI. I have personally submitted redesigns for this issue that both protect BFI, and in doing so protect SEA, and allow VFR operations in and out of BFI, and are not unduly hindering to the general aviation community. If safety is truly the priority of the FAA and the Seattle region, changes will be initiated immediately. I understand the process for airspace changes take time, however, the changes will never take place if the process is not started. When the inevitable aircraft incident finally occurs, I hope that no one dies and I am not on position. [Aircraft Y] was on vector, at 2,500 ft., to ILS Runway 20 approach at PWT. [Aircraft X], controlled by W Sector, was on final to Runway 14R at BFI and experienced a TCAS RA with an uncontrolled VFR aircraft. The W Controller was already at a high level of complexity and volume as sectors were combined. The BFI Runway 14R final is in close proximity to PWT 20 mile final and is also underneath the Runway 16 finals at SEA. With limited options [Aircraft X] was turned to the southwest towards [Aircraft Y] with only 500 ft. between them. There are many factors that lead to this situation. These include airport proximities, sector overload, traffic complexity. There is also the issue of lack of controlled and protected airspace in and out of BFI. This is an issue controllers have been bringing to local management for years. The workforce is metaphorically beating our heads against a wall as we are asking for help and are given zero assistance in return. The final to BFI is underneath the SEA finals so we are forced to descend large, fast turbojet aircraft out of Class Bravo airspace into a very high VFR traffic area. This leads numerous TCAS situations. Many suggestions have been brought up through established reporting procedures so I will not waste my time typing them out again. The feeling of a lack of support for change is disheartening. There needs to be change made into airspace and procedures for aircraft landing at BFI, and this should be done for both arrival directions at BFI.
1784342: I was on the ground at JNX with my student pilot getting ready for a soft field takeoff. The pattern was very congested with 5 aircraft in the pattern in various places. An aircraft had just landed, and there were a few other aircraft on downwind. A downwind aircraft stated that they were extending their downwind for departing traffic. I told my student that after the landing aircraft had exited the runway to be ready for immediate departure. The exiting aircraft called clear at this point and I told my student to make the radio call and take us out. As we were taxing out the aircraft that had said they were extending downwind was now on a 1.5 mile final. I told the student to accelerate and a radio call over the CTAF said go-around. I took the controls from my student to avoid a confliction with the aircraft going around. The aircraft going around side stepped to the right to avoid conflict. At no time was a G1000 traffic advisory issued, and no aircraft came close to contact. The overpopulated pattern with 4 aircraft doing stop and goes and my aircraft trying to find a spot to get out was a contributing factor to this issue. After the aircraft sidestepped, they immediately departed the pattern, and we continued our takeoff and entered left closed traffic to continue landing practice. Myself and a student who is currently working toward his CFI certificate went out for a training flight. After an hour of practicing maneuvers we approached JNX to practice takeoffs and landings. During our final approach into landing on Runway 21 at JNX my student made a call to let the other traffic in the pattern know of our position and our intentions, shortly after this call another plane pulled out on to the runway in frontof us. We made the decision to go-around and commenced a turn to the west so not to be on a collision course with the downwind traffic. We then proceeded to climb and leave the area.
1784364: Holding short of Runway XX at ZZZ, our aircraft was given a departure clearance void time of 60 seconds from ZZZ Center. We initiated an immediate departure on Runway XX. After climbing via the obstacle departure procedure, we proceeded enroute and contacted ZZZ Center again. We then heard another aircraft call back to ZZZ Center, and stated they were forced to initiate a go-around as they were on final approach to Runway XX. It is my guess that our departure is what caused that aircraft to go-around. I however, do not recall seeing the aircraft on final approach, or hearing a radio call that the aircraft was on final approach. Conditions were VFR at the airport, but IFR traffic load was heavy. I do not recall ATC advising us of the aircraft on final approach. It again is responsibility of us as a crew to ensure the approach/runway was clear for takeoff. If this incident was caused by our departure, we should have more clearly made sure it was safe for takeoff, and will do so in the future.
1784399: I was approaching L52 from the north/west to enter a left downwind for Runway 29. As I was crossing the shoreline at 1,000 AGL (one mile out) and decelerating, my passenger and I spotted two powered gliders crossing the departure end of 29 at approximately 900 feet AGL.They seemed to be transitioning from the southern part of the dunes to the norther part of the dunes through the upwind part of the traffic pattern. I veered the aircraft slightly more to the south to avoid them when I spotted another powered glider transitioning from the south to the north by intersection the downwind leg of the left pattern to 29. He was coming directly toward my aircraft in the opposite direction of traffic pattern. I then had to veer slightly to the left (north/east) to avoid that vehicle. I then landed without incident on 29.When parked at transient space we witnessed another powered glider takeoff from the tarmac and join the other gliders. They continued to overfly the airport at pattern altitude and not seem to adhere by any observable pattern.
1784424: I released Aircraft X for departure from BFI in a south flow. Aircraft X reported climbing to 2,000 ft. on the NIRVANA1 SID. I radar identified Aircraft X and climbed them to 6,000 ft.. As Aircraft X was climbing through 1,800 ft. I noticed that Aircraft X appeared to be making a right turn towards the SEA VOR and not following the NIRVANA SID. I instructed Aircraft X to 'turn left immediately, left turn heading 130.' At this point, Aircraft X was starting to converge with Aircraft Y who was on final approach into SEA descending through 1,100 ft. on the ILS Approach to Runway 16R. Aircraft X was about 1.5 miles laterally separated and 700 ft. vertically separated from Aircraft Y and converging. I observed Aircraft X achieve vertical separation from Aircraft Y, then saw the turn to heading 130 start occurring. I gave Aircraft X the Brasher statement. The pilot of Aircraft X stated that it 'looks like the activation for the autopilot for the NIRVANA1 did not take place.'I honestly don't know how to fix this problem, but it is a recurring, systemic issue. This is not my first event with almost identical circumstances, and many of my co-workers have had very similar events. Attempts have already been made to alter the SID, or issue an initial heading for aircraft departing BFI, but these events still occur. The typical issue is that pilots are filing SEA.J5 and though BFI is issuing the NIRVANA1 SID and a Preferred Departure Route that would join J5 from TAOMA or SUMMA, pilot error including unchecked autopilot actions that result in a turn to SEA VOR will immediately cause convergence at the same altitude as aircraft inbound to SEA within the final approach fix, as well as any aircraft departing SEA during that time. There is very little and very subtle warning, and immediate action is necessary to recover separation and end the rapidly worsening danger of the situation. I believe in most cases it is a result of an individualized pilot deviation, and I don't know how to end those completely. The only other solution I can think of would be to completely remove/decommission the SEA VOR.
1784801: TCAS RA on arrival into ZZZ [airport]. Assigned descent to 7,000 feet and vectors to final by ZZZ Approach. We reached 7,000 feet and noted approach was extremely busy where the Controller was being stepped on seemingly more than half of her transmissions. While level at 7,000 feet the TCAS noted a proximate target converging from 1 o'clock, 400 feet below. We attempted to contact Approach but there was zero opportunity to get a word in due to the sheer amount of communication on frequency. I advised the Captain PF to 'get ready' while we attempted to locate the aircraft visually. A few seconds later the TCAS noted traffic and ordered a very shallow climb. I announced to ZZZ Approach that we were responding to an RA, but I believe I was blocked, the frequency still jammed with constant communication. A very short time later the controller issued traffic to us and I again advised 'Climbing on RA.' Controller replied 'Roger' I believe and the event was over shortly after. We returned to 7,000 feet and were vectored for the visual, but the controller still had to vector us around multiple VFR targets on our way to the runway. Most significantly we were cleared for the visual approach, but were restricted to flying and intercepting between 5 and 7 NM from the airport due to area traffic. This caused a perceived limitation that pilots are not used to. The CA/PF then overflew the Localizer slightly attempting to maintain these limitations. The aircraft was clearly stable by 1000 feet and we continued in to land, but this was following an incident due to the same cause.Cause was due to the intense level of traffic in ZZZ Approach's airspace. I spoke with a contact at ZZZ [Approach] later who noted the Controller had 15 active aircraft not including the VFR targets attempting to get clearance from the closed airspace, Practice IFR traffic, and VFR flight following requests. The Controller was doing an excellent job and maintained a very professional demeanor throughout. There was just no reasonable way for Controller to maintain communications with the volume of aircraft. I am not sure, but this could have been a result of reduced staffing due to COVID. Maybe there was an East and West ZZZ [Approach] sector available, but no staffing to accommodate. My suggestions would be to either split ZZZ Approach or to draw a new arrival for ZZZ airport to reduce the amount of communications and possible routes needed for the controllers.
1784899: While descending into LRU airport, I heard ATC call to another aircraft (Aircraft Y) that was also inbound. I was arriving from the west, and Aircraft Y from the north, North West area. I could see him on ADS-B. While Aircraft Y was behind me, he was much faster, however ABQ (Albuquerque) center had him climb and then hold as I continued my descent. Leveling off at my assigned altitude, I was still unable to see the airfield, despite the field reports of better weather. I was, however, still several miles away. At about the same time, Aircraft Y called in, cancelling his IFR stating that he had the airport in sight. ATC cancelled his IFR as he stated he was now in VMC. I then asked ATC for a report from the Aircraft Y, as he was able to see the field and I was not, despite me being at a lower altitude. (I asked hoping I would break out of the clouds soon, or find an area where I could, such as where Aircraft Y came from). Quickly after, I did get the airport insight below me and was able to descend VFR. I also cancelled my IFR at that time.Being almost over the airport, I extended away from it and then I called entering the Left downwind for runway 26. (The winds at the time were reported as being 240 at 22 - 27, making runway 22 or 26 the best options.) I then called a base turn, and then final. At that time I also heard Aircraft Y call in for the RNAV for runway 12. Being as he cancelled IFR with no mention of practicing approaches, I anticipated his landing before me, with no conflict. As I came on short final for runway 26, I heard Aircraft Y call out that he was going missed from 12, which would then be intersecting my landing path. At that moment I looked up and saw Aircraft Y just ahead and to my right, above me, but very close. I would estimate within 200-300 feet. Already being close to the ground, no evasion action could have been taken. I landed and taxied into the ramp. Shortly after, Aircraft Y landed on a different runway and parked as well. I called the center to report the incident and express my concern and safety issue that had occurred.
1785459: ILS [Runway] 06 circle to land [Runway] 01 just after dark with gusty winds and windshear. Miscommunication in the cockpit dealing with 'programming' the airplane for the approach. Got distracted on the maneuver which got us close to the towers, then got a pull up prompt. Recovered and landed safely.[Cause was] Lack of cockpit communication.[Suggest] Training this approach with bad weather in simulator. Clearance by Approach Control - Intercept the Runway 06 approach course and expect the Runway 06 ILS, circle Runway 01. Clearance by Tower - Cleared for visual approach Runway 06, at TORBY cleared to circle to land Runway 01. During the circle we received TAWS Aural Warning - ''Obstacle, Obstacle, Pull Up'. The pilot flying began a climb from 820 ft. MSL to approximately 1,300 ft. MSL. Message cleared and the approach was continued to a full stop landing. The aircraft was flown too close to obstructions during the circling to land approach. 2 contributing factors: Unfamiliarity with the procedure at TEB and reliance on autopilot.With the frequency that [our company] operates in and out of TEB, it may be advisable to add some type of briefing to the pilot [group]. This is a common procedure at TEB, but it doesn't occur frequently enough to build pilot confidence in the circle to land maneuver.
1785644: In the traffic pattern at ZZZ, my CFI and I were on the right downwind for Runway XXR when we were told to Continue for Runway XXR. We then continued and a few moments later was told to turn right base for XXR. When turning right base we noted traffic, but I didn't think it was a factor at first because we assumed it was for the parallel because we still were told to turn right base. As we got established on base we saw the traffic was close and my CFI took controls to avoid a mid-air collison. We got no warning from the Tower and later found out that the tower told the other aircraft to continue for Runway XXR. Shortly after the Tower told them to continue for XXR that's when the tower said to turn base. I didn't think that traffic that was on final would be a factor for us and thought it was for Runway XXL. In the future, I think the Tower should be more clear and understand the traffic spacing better because if he did then he could've told us to extend a couple of miles so we could've passed behind the traffic instead of passing in front and coming within 1,000 feet horizontally of each other. I believe the talking between me and my CFI also contributed because maybe we would've heard the call for the other aircraft to continue and could've challenged that with the Tower but even then we still were told to turn base. I believe the tower should've noted the other aircraft and looked at the spacing, and told us this isn't going to work and this near-miss could've been avoided altogether instead we got turned directly into the path of another aircraft.
