I was flying with my student in the pattern at ZZZ. When we were downwind, Tower didn't clear us for a touch and go, but told us to continue. We continued downwind and waited for further instructions when Tower then told us to turn base.We turned base. There was some hesitation but then the Controller instructed us to turn directly towards the numbers. At this point, we were on right base unaware we were being turned onto an aircraft that was on final. Before my students turn for final, I always have them look on final to make sure it is clear of traffic. At this point, I noticed the traffic on the left hand side and saw it on my iPad. I took the controls from my student and climbed to offset to the right where we avoided a near miss collision of about 1,000 feet horizontal distance and 300 feet vertical distance over a densely packed neighborhood of City. We never were told to extend or follow this aircraft.Prior to the Controller telling us to turn base, he had spoken to the aircraft on the straight in final and told them to continue. He realized the aircraft was there, but did not communicate the location and told us to turn base onto him. This situation demonstrates that pilots must exercise extreme vigilance at airports where ATC is so busy to provide clear instructions.The term 'continue' can be vague in that…does it mean we're supposed to fly the pattern as regularly, or are we supposed to continue downwind? In that case, the term 'extend' would make more sense.When I talked to the Controller on the phone later, I was told that this situation occurred due to a late runway switch by the other aircraft. However, in examination of the track log, the aircraft was on a straight in approach. The pilot also called up that they were approaching a point on the approach for XXR. The Controller didn't acknowledge the mistake that had been made and the possible deadly consequences that could have occurred from this near miss.This is a serious near miss.
1785678: During a practice RNAV (GPS) [Runway] 35 approach to Colorado Air and Space Port (CFO), we had just crossed the Final Approach Fix (FAF) at ARRES at the charted altitude of 7,500 feet MSL. The student at the controls was 2-3 seconds late in beginning the glideslope intercept, and our glideslope indicated slightly high. Knowing that we had to descend 500 feet in order to be below the upcoming 7,000 feet MSL Class B shelf, I reduced power to increase our rate of descent. There was also an air carrier [Aircraft Y] at our 1 o'clock, approximately 1,000 feet above our altitude according to ADS-B, which was making a right turn from a southerly heading to a northwesterly as it make its approach to DEN. Denver Approach contacted us saying, 'I need you below the Bravo shelf at 7,000 feet.' I replied 'roger, we are increasing our rate of descent, currently indicating 6,800 feet.' The Aircraft Y crossed above and ahead of us, right to left, approximately 1,000 feet above and 200 feet ahead. I did not hear any of the communications between the Aircraft Y and Denver Approach, nor did I notice any maneuvering by the Aircraft Y indicating it was reacting to our presence. The complex airspace around DEN is extremely challenging, and this approach's FAF is approximately 1.4 NM from the 7,000 feet MSL Class B shelf. Descending 500 feet in less than 1.4 NM at small aircraft approach speeds does not require excessive rates of descent, but it does require a timely descent. Any delay, or crossing the FAF above the 7,500 feet MSL altitude, quickly makes it likely that an airplane may violate Class B airspace during the Final Approach Segment. In our case, the timing of the arriving Aircraft Y was coincidentally exactly the same time we were at this critical place. As a CFI-I, I am reluctant to use this approach for training ever again. One suggestion may be to cross ARRES at an altitude lower than the charted minimum of 7,500 feet MSL - if, and only if, it's a practice approach under VFR. The potential negative training this would cause would have to be weighed against the extra margin of separation from the Class B shelf. Additionally, in the future, if I use this approach for practice again, I will have the student execute a missed approach and turn away from the 7,000 feet MSL Class B shelf if the aircraft is high at ARRES, does not initiate a timely descent, or if I notice DEN traffic that could cross above us as happened on this flight.
1785939: I was conducting a discovery flight a requested flight following on the ground with a departure out to the southeast of the field near City X to fly over the house of the client. I was cleared to takeoff of Runway XX. On the climbout I was not sure if Tower wanted me to make a left or right turn towards the south east so I asked for clarification. He said 'you're going to the east right?' And I repeated stating we were going to the southeast. He replied back with instructions to make a right turn to head that way. Right as I turned onto the downwind, Tower switch me to Approach. I switched frequencies and began explaining something to the student as I started to cruise the plane out at 1,500 MSL. About 15 seconds after I switched frequencies to Approach, I gave them a call to check in telling them the altitude I was at and the direction I was headed, southeast. Immediately after I called in, I saw a King Air to my right that was supposedly on final for XX. They were on a track towards us but were in a climb. I saw they were climbing so I immediately started descending. After that is when Approach called in to tell me about the traffic saying that I was intercepting the final approach course for XX. When I looked at my ground track after the flight, I did drift slightly right when I was on the extended downwind, but I never intercepted the final approach course. I did not receive notice from the Tower about the King Air on final before being switched to Approach and it wasn't until after I checked in with Approach that they gave me the advisory. The King Air's TCAS system showed that we reached within 100 feet of each other but myself and the pilots in the King Air agreed that it was much more that 100 feet. I overall feel like there was a lack of communication from all parts that could have possibly prevented this occurrence. I personally could have been more specific with tower on where I was going. I could have been more watchful of my track to stay clear of final. The winds were from the northwest so that could have been a factor in why I was slightly drifting. That is why it is important to know where your winds are coming from to maintain a constant ground track along the ground and prevent drifting.
1786039: We were on approach into CLT [Runway] 18C, level at 4,000 ft. We encountered wake turbulence which disconnected the auto pilot and caused us to take action to correct the aircraft from an upset state. Once corrected we contacted ATC and were able to continue the approach to landing with no other issues. Hard rolling action which disconnected auto pilot. Wake turbulence. Corrected the state of the aircraft and corrected back on course after deviation. As we did keep focused on the airplane and be ready for anything.
1786175: Aircraft X was originally going to land at ZZZ, however, 2 new NOTAMs entered the system just before starting an instrument approach regarding standing water and ice on Runway 20 and the taxiways. Due to the wind and previous icing encountered, he decided to not land at ZZZ. I put him into the published holding at JADGU at 120. We discussed his options for many other close by airports, but due to forecast and known icing and moderate to severe turbulence throughout the area we were having a hard time coming up with a good airport. Aircraft X was also not fuel critical, but did not have a lot of reserve fuel. During this, I was working departures and arrivals into/out of DEN with moderate turbulence. I advised Aircraft X that PUB was 60 miles northeast, and had VFR weather with no known icing. I advised him that he would have to climb to 160, but only for a few minutes and they could descend to 140. Aircraft X decided to go to PUB airport. I climbed Aircraft X to 160 and he asked if it was about a 050 heading. I concurred, but he needed to climb first due to terrain before I could turn him there. He accepted the climb and then asked again about the heading. I told him to remain in the published hold and climb to 160 and I would have the turn on course above 130. He advised me that he was already turning to a 050 heading but was climbing to 130. At this point the MSAW alert was going off, but he was through130 in the 130 MIA. I reiterated the climb to 160 and told him the terrain climbed rapidly and to expedite as much as he could. At this point, Aircraft X was climbing through 140 heading into the 160 MIA. I advised Aircraft X the minimum IFR altitude is 160 and to report reaching. I should have issued a heading south as soon as he advised me he was already turning to PUB. I know the highest mountains in that area are not above 140, but the terrain climbs so rapidly in that area I should have known he would not have topped the 160 MIA even though he did climb above the 130 MIA. He also reported turbulence and icing at this time.The pilot should not have exited the published holding without a clearance to do so. I should have issued a south heading as soon as he told me he was turning out of hold. It was poor service on my end. I know all of the moderate reports and constant transmitter changes did not help the situation.
1786484: On approach at night visual to Runway 26 in the Jacksonville. I was the pilot monitoring with the first officer as the flying pilot. We were given a visual approach and he [turned] off the auto pilot at approximately 1,000 feet. At the 500 feet call he was stable, I don't recall the exact altitude after 500 feet as I was heads up looking outside and I noticed three red and one white on the PAPI. I did observe he was getting low on the glideslope. We had the ILS backed up and when I looked up, I saw four red and instructed him ' four reds, level off' we also received the oral warning glideslope at the same time. He did respond and leveled off approximately two to three seconds later and I saw the three red one white again. Landing was uneventful.It is also worth noting that we were into a 13 hour duty day due to weather delays and rescheduling.Also, worth noting was both Approach Control and Tower stated that they were receiving PIREPs of 40 knot headwinds until a 4 mile final. In actuality the winds were gusting up to 40 all the way to about a 1 mile final.
1786676: Descending via the NIIXX 2 arrival for the ILS Runway 35R in CAVOK conditions. Around the BSTON Intersection we were given a westerly to northwesterly radar vector and cleared to descend and maintain 10,000. As we got closer to the final approach course (somewhere between DEANE and DRUMM) we were cleared to descend and maintain 8,000 and cleared direct to the FRONZ Intersection (FAF for the ILS). The Controller asked if we had 35R in sight, after a pause, we had the runway in sight and advised ATC. We were then cleared for the visual approach to 35R. The FAF altitude at FRONZ is 7,000 so that is what we set in the MCP while descending through approximately 8,800 in FLCH. We had just gotten the '2,500' call from the Radio Altimeter and made our call outs. As we descended through 8,000 I noticed the Radio Altitude around 1,800 and descending. A quick look at JeppFD PRO showed our aircraft position just south and east of the DRUMM Intersection. I called out the altitude and the fact that we need to go back up to 8,000 (our last cleared altitude prior to the approach clearance) until we are north of DRUMM. I reset the MCP to 8,000 and verbalized that we need to climb back up. The Captain selected a V/S climb back to 8,000. We joined the approach course and followed the G/S and landed without incident.ATC never mentioned anything to us about violating airspace or going below the DEN Class B. Though it is nice to get directs, etc. However, I believe the direct to FRONZ clearance, if not really familiar with the DEN Class B, can set crews up to possibly violate airspace and even lead to an unstable approach.Once parked at the gate with all checklists complete, we debriefed and there certainly was some confusion as to exactly where we were when we descended below 8,000. We had a jump seat observer who thought we might have been a little low as he has a lot of General Aviation experience in the DEN area.
1786853: Had a gear up incident. Landing gear would not go down. After manually trying to pump the gear down for over an hour I decided to belly land the plane at ZZZ. All precautions were taken and an emergency landing was made on Runway XXR. No injuries but plane has extensive damage. My student and I took off in his airplane from ZZZ and flew to ZZZ1 where we added some fuel to the airplane. Then we took off and flew to ZZZ2 where we began an ILS practice approach. On final the gear would not extend. We went missed and flew around for an hour and forty five minutes trying to get the gear and flaps to extend. Only the nose gear came down. We decided to land at ZZZ2 so called approach for landing. They immediately turned us over to the tower where we explained our situation. WE then landed on [Runway] XXR on the nose wheel and the tail tiedown ring. It stayed on the tiedown ring until it was almost stopped then came to rest on the left wing. We departed the airplane with no issues. There was very minimal damage to the plane. Later we discovered the ELT battery was due for replacement 60 days earlier.
1786996: On final [Runway] XXL ZZZ we were paired up with traffic on another runway in visual conditions. I thought the FO had selected TA on the transponder. After debriefing on the ground he told me that he was telling me to set TA on the transponder, but what I heard was transponder is set to TA. Inside ZZZZZ [Intersection] at about 1,200 feet we got an RA Climb. I verbalized 'We got to go.' I surmised that the TCAS RA would be followed by a go-around. My communication was unclear. The traffic was in sight throughout the approach. The FO continued the approach and landed uneventfully. We should have gone around, but after debriefing I understood that the FO thought it might be unsafe to climb and go-around with the other traffic so close. With the A.P. and A.T. off, I was P.F. on the visual approach to Runway XX. ATC calls out traffic at our 2 o'clock that will be close to us for another runway. We call the Aircraft Y traffic in sight and proceed inbound. Both the Captain and I are wearing masks (COVID), which I believe muffled my request to 'Set to TA only.' The Captain later said he thought I said 'We're set to TA only.' The approach continued normally with us going to managed speed, gear down, as we started down the glide slope inside the FAF. Just after I called for flaps 3 around 1,400 feet AGL, I noted the Aircraft Y a little above us and the appropriate distance to the right joining up with us. I was still slowing the aircraft at that moment, and the RA went off 'Climb, Climb.' I asked the Captain 'We are not in TA only?' He responded 'Well we are going to have to go.' I momentarily considered going around, but thought continuing the approach was actually the safest course of action when the RA immediately stopped. We continued the approach and landed uneventfully. The RA happened the moment the Aircraft Y was joining the other localizer course. What I should have done is gone around. Following the RA is the right thing to do unless it is unsafe to do so.
1787050: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions, crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach, but was able to reach the 5,000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance, the PF initiated descent to 4,500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle, and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4,500 ft. is within 1,300 ft. AGL of field elevation, and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles), the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around), disconnected the autopilot, and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions', and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred, and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape, with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape, PIC noted an 1,800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude, the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal, and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape, which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight, crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM, go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed, and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations, including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF, this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach, crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power, and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received, decisive, immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation, having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.
1787266: Performed a go-around on [Runway] 30R at MSP. We queried controller that we saw an aircraft sitting on runway while we were on short final approximately 900 feet. He told us to go around which we did - then thanked us for the query due to him being distracted or involved with a disabled aircraft on Runway 30L, this occurred during VFR conditions at night.
1787756: On an ILS approach to Runway 16L at HEF, at approximately 300-400 ft AGL, while scanning for approach lights, the crew observed two bright white steady burning lights located to the northwest of the approach lights to Runway 16L creating a momentary impression of REIL lights for Runway 16R. The lights were shining directly into the approach path. Crew continued the approach on localizer and glideslope, identified the MALSR for Runway 16L and landed normally.
1788176: We had been vectored off of the WAZKO1 RNAV Arrival toward the final approach course for the RNAV Runway 4 at ELP. We broke out of the overcast around 9,000 ft. and were approaching KANTR at 7,500 feet. There was a lot of ambient light from the city below and the reflection of that light from the overcast above as well as the fresh layer of snow on the surface. Approach cleared us for the approach and gave us 'Direct KANTR, Maintain 7,200 ft. until KANTR;' which I read back, with an emphasis on the '200'. The FO (PF) selected vertical speed mode after I set 7,200 ft. in the altitude preselector and called '7,200 ft. set!'. The published altitude at KANTR is 7,500 feet, which is located above terrain at 5,851 ft. We leveled at 7,200 ft. and she called for Flaps 18, and we joined the final approach course with the runway, and the terrain below in sight since descending out of 9,000 ft. Just then the GPWS System chimed in with 'Terrain! Pull Up!'. The FO dutifully disconnected the autopilot and I told her NOT to go around, as we were on a published segment of the final approach in good VMC (ELP was reporting 10 SM Vis) and I had the terrain in sight the whole time. We were not descending, and we had been level for some time. We landed without incident and taxied to our gate. Upon docking, I asked Ground for the phone number to the folks at approach control. The fellow who answered offered that he was indeed the Controller. I told him what had happened and he said that it was not at all uncommon, and that 7,200 ft. was their Minimum Vectoring Altitude in that sector. I told him that I would be filing a report with respect to the incident, for his own information.If there are other similar incidents here a communique should be distributed to the pilot group.
1788331: We came to land at ZZZ airport, executed ILS Runway XX to approach to it even the weather conditions where completely Visual. Everything was normal, we touched down and begun our landing roll, lowered the nose of the aircraft to the ground, deployed reverse thrust and applied brakes, suddenly master warning illuminated indicating a failure, I was not able to determine the source of the failure at that very moment, I have increased progressively the pressure on the brakes and reverse thrust, aircraft begin to decelerate rapidly and begin to veer slightly to the left side, condition I counteracted with differential braking and thrust reverse power reduction, reached for the steering wheel to continue counteracting the veering tendency and steering wheel was stiff and locked unable to move it, I mention to my First Officer we have lost steering control, continued counteracting with rudder pedal and differential braking, but rudder aerodynamic capability diminish with speed reduction, I mention again to my First Officer that we had lost steering control and felt diminish braking action, airplane slowly overrun into the grass to the left side and lost braking action, I went to and transfer to emergency braking and recover partial control of the aircraft finally stopping on the grass.Executed passenger evacuation checklist to secure aircraft, passengers and crew evacuated through main door, no injury occurred to any one onboard, airplane is in good condition, we called FSS to advise of our incident during landing.
1788339: As I was setting up cruise at 11,500 ft. I noticed my speed was not what it should be with a bit of a tailwind and the plane was yawing severely to the right. I used a fair amount of left rudder to keep the ball centered for the whole flight. I tried to figure out what could be wrong with the plane to cause this, but could not come up with a plausible explanation. Checked the trim, looked at the flaps, ailerons, elevator where visible and could see nothing. [On a previous flight] there was pretty substantial turbulence and I thought maybe something happened to the rudder that I missed on the preflight. Other than being slow and requiring the constant pressure on the left rudder pedal, the flight was uneventful. Approach cleared me through the Bravo airspace utilizing the west transition to get to the south side of the Bravo airspace. Once clear of Bravo, they terminated VFR Flight Following and I contacted Tower about 10 miles west and indicated inbound for landing with ATIS. I believe Tower had me #2 with a 2 mile final. I had nice stable approach utilizing a fair amount of left rudder to align with the center line at a 90 kt. approach. I crossed the numbers at about 84 kts. and mains touched down at about 76 kts. When the nose gear settled, the aircraft immediately shot straight right off the side of the runway. I worked the left rudder pedal and brake to try and regain control and got the plane back on the runway fairly quickly. Tower asked if I needed assistance and I told them no. I tried to explain what happened but really did not know. Tower said to contact ground. I did so and they said the pilot waiting to depart said my nose wheel was canted 45 degrees to the right as I came by them. That would explain the yaw and the plane shooting off to the right on landing. I contacted a mechanic and he will be looking at the plane to [determine] what the issue is and what it will take to repair that issue. The mechanic said there is a pin on the strut that can break and cause this issue. He said I was very fortunate to have regained control and the nose gear released and was able to track again. He said when that pin breaks, very often the nose gear will not release and allow straight forward movement. I had no idea that this is a not uncommon occurrence with these aircraft. I had googled a description of what happened and got nothing coming up that would explain what the mechanic told me.
1788373: I am a CFI and I was flying a training mission with my client who is a licensed private pilot working on transition training to a new model aircraft (Aircraft X). This was my client's first flight in a Aircraft X. The lesson started with a detailed preflight, followed by a similarly detailed run-up. Once ready, we departed Palo Alto Airport for a familiarization flight in a practice area south and west of the airport. During our time in the practice area we maintained visual separation from another aircraft in the training area (each trying to stay in our own section of the training area, while we also maintained appropriate distances from scattered clouds in the area, and staying below the Bravo which starts at 4,000 in that area. During this time, we stayed in contact with the Tower having asked them for advisories during our training mission.After approximately 1 hour of Hobbs time (including the taxi and detailed run-up), we copied ATIS Quebec and informed the Tower that we would like to return to the field for the option, and closed traffic. We were instructed to fly over Stanford and enter the pattern for left traffic for Runway 31. We made our way as instructed and entered the left downwind for Runway 31. The Tower then told us that we were number 4 cleared to land, and that the traffic that we were following was roughly abeam us in the opposite downwind. We acknowledged the instruction and reported negative contact with the traffic to follow. Meanwhile, the Tower was very busy with numerous other traffic entering, leaving, and in the pattern. We were then told to extend our downwind, that we had extensive extensions into Moffett Field's airspace (it is very common for Palo Alto to have and use extensions into Moffett's airspace - this extension was even further than usual) and that the Tower would call our base. While extending, we saw our traffic to follow turn base and then final. But we continued downwind since the Tower said that they would call our base.Moments later, the Tower instructed us to fly 'straight towards the 31 numbers' which was a bit strange since we were so far from the runway (probably at least 3 miles at this point). But the frequency was very busy and it didn't seem to make sense (or even possible) to ask to verify the instruction. We turned left onto a long final and proceeded towards the runway. We were holding approximately 1,000 feet (+/- since my student was flying and this was their first time in the aircraft) this entire time on downwind, base and long final.Not too long after we turned long final, the Tower told us to climb 500 feet immediately for traffic. I immediately took the controls of the plane, quickly (re)checked nearby traffic on the G1000 MFD (with ADS-B traffic) and did a visual scan for traffic as I went full forward on the throttle, prop, and mixture and pitched the nose back for the climb. The quick scan of traffic (visual and ADS-B) did not indicate any traffic below or next to us, but it did indicate one aircraft above our altitude but not in the immediate vicinity. None-the-less, we tried to visually acquire the above traffic as we climbed.Moments later, the tower told us to stop our climb immediately and to turn right and fly directly towards Leslie Salt. Again, we immediately complied with the Tower's instructions as we continued to try to acquire and track any immediate threats visually. Just then, we saw another aircraft pass directly above us, slightly off to our left side, in very close proximity to our aircraft. The Tower then instructed us to make a right turn back to final for landing.I've been flying at PAO for nearly XX years, so I am familiar with how busy it can get. But even with that experience, it was particularly busy at this time. One of the things that I think was a factor in this situation was a partial callsign conflict. Our aircraft callsign ended in [--] while the callsign of another aircraft on frequency at the time ended in [--]. In fact, it is possible that the aircraft above us when we were instructed to climb, and the one that nearly collided with moments later, was the aircraft ending in [--]. My theory is that the instruction to climb was actually intended for Aircraft Y and not Aircraft X, and that the controller tried to stop our climb as soon as he noticed the error. Unfortunately, these problems were all compounded by the heavy radio traffic making it virtually impossible to verify instructions, especially in a timely fashion.My client and I replayed this whole incident both while still in the air, and during debrief on the ground, and we are both quite certain that we responded to our correct callsign and that this wasn't a case of us improperly (and unintentionally) responding to someone else's callsign. I wanted to use the G1000 PLAYback feature to check/verify the radio call, but, unfortunately, the radio traffic was so heavy that there was no way to use the replay feature successfully. I have replayed this entire situation a number of times trying to analyze what I could have / should have done differently to avoid getting this close to another aircraft. Unfortunately, I haven't really come up with a good answer given the details of the situation.Given that the only nearby traffic that I could observe at the time was the one above us, I could have held my attitude of 1,000 feet, in defiance of the Tower Controller's instruction, until I could verify that the climb instruction was for us, or until I could verify another nearby traffic threat. But this seems like a very bad idea. I have always operated that when ATC gives you an immediate traffic avoidance instruction that you follow that instruction immediately. There could have very well been another nearby aircraft that I was unaware of that was an even more of a threat that I was currently unaware of. Hence my immediate response as instructed.I believe that the similar sounding callsigns, heavy radio traffic, and large number of aircraft operating in the class Delta, all contributed to the confusion for all parties. I know that it made our task (mine and my client) much more difficult, and I believe that you could hear that in the voice and instructions of the Tower Controller and the other pilots. After landing, we opted to terminate rather than continue pattern operations. Once back in the flying club, we talked with another CFI and student who was flying (and returning to the airport) at the same time. I asked them if they heard the Tower 'trying kill us' and the CFIs response was 'yeah, the Tower Controller was clearly overwhelmed!' We asked him if he heard any indications that we responded to the wrong callsign. His response was 'no' and that, again, he thought that whole problem was that the Tower Controller was simply overwhelmed by the overall situation.I know that Palo Alto is an FAA Training Tower, and I'm fully understanding and supportive of that. But perhaps in this case maybe there should have been additional oversight of Tower operations, or at least a senior controller stepping in before the controller got too overwhelmed.
1788927: We were transitioning in VFR conditions on the ZZZZZ3 arrival to the GPS approach to XXR. We loaded the approach into the FMS and set bottom attitude for the approach. I was in right seat flying and CA was in the left who is a CE510s rated pilot also. I was off auto pilot and hand flying with a different flight director display than normally used. The issue was when engaged the appr mode on flight director while still in Vnav instead of waiting until the GPS switched to LPV mode just outside of the final approach fix. The controller advised us that we had descended below the minimum vectoring altitude for that segment of the approach. The clear message here was that better crew coordination was needed.
1788957: Aircraft X was uneventful leading up to the approach at ZZZ. We had been cleared for the approach to Runway XX and were established on the localizer and glideslope. The autopilot and autothrust had been disengaged earlier in the approach and the aircraft had been configured to Flaps 3 when Gear Down was requested. When the gear lever was selected down the three indicators on the landing gear panel indicated red UNLK (UNLOCKED), no noise from the landing gear doors opening was heard. Captain [Name] and I communicated and confirmed on the Landing Gear Systems page that the landing gear had not extended. We decided to level out at 6,000 feet MSL while we confirmed the situation and attempted to cycle the gear. We communicated to the tower we would be going around for a landing gear failure approximately 3mi prior to the runway. Tower provided vectors and a climb to 9,000 feet, we initiated a go around over the threshold per ATC instructions and cleaned up the aircraft per SOP. The autoflight was re-engaged after the go around. During this time after the failure of subsequent attempts to cycle the gear and with the lever still down, we eventually got the L/G GEAR NOT DOWNLOCKED ECAM. The ECAM was run according to SOP by Captain [Name] while I flew the aircraft and handled radio calls. We [received priority], stated our intention to return to land on Runway XYR and requested CFR (Crash Fire Rescue Equipment). Gravity extension was successful and we were vectored to the approach. Approach and landing were normal with the exception of the gear doors remaining open. We landed with 8000 lbs. of fuel. We stopped on the runway and Operations was standing by to tow the aircraft back to the gate.
1789215: On initial approach to TRM I was announcing the arrival quite often and very diligently, in a descent of approximately 1,600 feet per minute another plane was observed on the ADS-B and was in sight. I continued the descent to fly well under the plane which was obviously VFR and as I approached the plane it turned into me with a sharp turn. The TCAS had a TA but not an RA as I had descended well below the other plane. The other plane must not have been monitoring the UNICOM or monitoring their traffic ADS-B.I realize now that I should have changed course at an earlier time, to give a much wider birth to the crossing plane. Also, I can not take into account other pilots listening to the CTAF or UNICOM frequency for area traffic. In addition, as I approached the airport to fly over and enter a left downwind, another plane was spotted that had just flown over the field with no announcements. VFR traffic in this area are not listening or announcing their intentions in the airport environment.
1789312: During flight testing of an experimental, retractable gear aircraft, the landing gear failed to extend. The failure was first noted at 2,500 feet AGL while configuring for landing stalls. The left main gear failed to lock down, as noted by the left main gear indicator light remaining red. The gear would retract normally. Several attempts at extension were made, including during pitch and yaw, to no avail. Manual extension of the gear was attempted following POH (Pilots Operating Handbook) checklist procedures, but the manual pump handle would not move. The decision was made, as recommended by the POH emergency procedure, to land with all gear retracted. The aircraft returned to the airport of origin, which also had a grass runway. Landing was made with full flaps at stall speed, and slid about 250 feet in the grass before stopping. There were no injuries to the single occupant of the aircraft.
1790605: We were flying from ZZZ to ASE and I was the pilot flying. As we approached Aspen, which at that time was reporting VFR, we were given vectors to intercept LOC DME E into ASE. I looked over and noticed the LOC approach was not properly set up. I warned the monitoring pilot of this but at that point we made visual contact with the airport. We accepted clearance to maintain 13,000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC DME E approach. Having visual contact with the airport we started our descent. A layer of clouds moved in below us as we made the final turn inbound. At the entire time we had full visual contact with all the terrain around. We lost sight of the airport due to the cloud layer, at the same time ATC issued an altitude alert. I emphasize that we were in full visual contact with all the terrain and that visibility at our flight level was unrestricted. The pilot monitoring advised that we had terrain but lost a visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked for vectors to give time to decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ1 airport afterwards. We were NOT in IMC conditions at any phase of the flight and we maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. The mistake was communication breakdown with ATC and in part CRM in regards to the intentions to execute a visual approach. At no time aircraft was in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. The aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition. I learned from this how CRM and communication has to be mastered the entire time.
1790677: Landing Runway XX in ZZZ experienced a bump on the runway after landing which was coupled with a wind shear causing a directional control problem. Pilot made control inputs to correct situation. Wind speed and direction varied greatly. Pilot was unable to maintain directional control. Aircraft ground looped to the right approximately midfield. No human injuries were sustained.
1790681: Tower closed, multiple airplanes in pattern using Runway 14 for favorable winds (170 about 15 knots). I was on short final, less than 200 AGL over clearway for runway. Jet lands straight in on Runway 32. No calls were made from the jet on CTAF announcing position or intentions. Jet landed, I added power and went around, overflying the jet. All other airplanes in the pattern were using 124.125 as the CTAF as published. Brief phone conversation with Houston Approach confirmed that the jet landed straight in apparently on an RNAV 32 approach. Jet would have landed with excess of 10 knots tail wind. ASOS was broadcasting at the time.
1790703: Aircraft X was inside of a quarter mile final on the ILS Runway 31C approach. I turned around for a second to tell the supervisor about the visibility getting better on final when the supervisor noticed an airport vehicle going onto Runway 31C. At that point I issued a go around to the aircraft and to climb and maintain 3,000 ft. MSL and turn right to a heading of 110. I also let the aircraft know the reason of the go around. They were able to respond in time and were re-sequenced for another approach and landed without incident. I understand it was snowing and airport markers are difficult to see. I suggest airport vehicles be more vigilant of their position on the airport before moving anywhere. Driver refresher course recommended.
1790720: My second report regarding aircraft from the Palm Springs area performing erratic maneuvers in the face of IFR arrivals. Aircraft Y departed Palm Springs and terminated services outside of the PSP Delta. They proceeded to fly just north of UDD and start performing aerobatic maneuvers between 050 and 060. This aircraft climbed right in front of Aircraft X, who was cleared for the RNAV visual 31L approach. Traffic alert was issued to Aircraft X and while the pilot did not say 'near midair', they did say 'he's right in front of us!' and the altitudes were the same.The pilot for Aircraft X said they had to respond to two RAs for that one aircraft.The pilot of Aircraft Y may have also been in violation of FAR Sec. 91.303 which prohibits aerobatic flight within 4 miles of a federal airway (V137) and over an area of congested population.I am requesting, again, for the PSP airspace to have a Charlie or Bravo airspace. My colleagues and I deal with dangerous situations every day that could easily be avoided by having non-voluntary protected airspace. This is the second event in one day where PSP Tower has terminated a VFR aircraft who ultimately got much too close to an IFR arrival. A Class C/B airspace and a requirement for Tower to hand off departures to approach, would allow the radar Controller to determine if a dangerous situation is imminent.As of now, the only controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley is the Tower's Class D. Class E airspace exists around TRM, but only prohibits flight for poor weather. This airspace is a free-for-all with half of the aircraft talking to ATC and the other half are not, and just blasting through everyone else. This needs to change.Also, the local pilots should know better than to be flying in these congested areas doing aerobatics. The safety culture of these pilots is questionable and should be discussed.
1790790: I was working a sector and Controller in Charge combined during the event. I cleared an aircraft for the approach to maintain 13,000 feet until established on the localizer. As I was about to switch the aircraft to Tower I noticed that they were at 12,100 feet on the approach. The crossing altitude at the fix they were cleared to is 12,900 feet so I issued a low altitude alert and the crossing altitude. The aircraft responded that they did not have the runway in sight and wanted to go around. Since they were on an instrument approach I told them to execute the missed approach. I noticed the aircraft continued to descend, so I issued another low altitude alert, this time using the 12,100 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude as a reference since they were at 11,700 feet and advised they climb to 14,000 feet immediately. Once the aircraft was above MVAs I issued a heading and eventually notified them of a possible pilot deviation and gave them the tower number.
1791485: On final at the final approach fix for Runway XXR at 170 knots we configured aircraft with gear and final flaps of 25. We received and EICAS message of TE Flap Disagree", the flap indicator was between 20 and 25. We evaluated the situation and discussed how the go around would be executed, then informed ATC and performed a go around without flap retraction not exceeding 137 KTS. We successfully ran the QRH and were vectored back to [Runway] XXC to an uneventful landing with a reference speed of 127 KTS and taxied to the gate. We notified ATC knowing we would be in a non-normal landing configuration. Emergency vehicles were not requested but present for the landing." On Runway XXR at the final approach fix at 170 KTS we configured aircraft with gear and final flaps 25. We received an EICAS message of TE FLAP DISAGREE" the flap indicator read between 20 and 25 degrees. We evaluated the situation, discussed how the go around would be performed not exceeding 137 KTS. While being vectored back to land we ran QRH successfully and were vectored back to [Runway] XXC to an uneventful landing with a reference speed of 127 KTS and taxied to park. We did notify ATC knowing that we would be in an abnormal flap configuration. Emergency vehicles were not requested but present."
1791555: I am a private pilot, multi-engine student. I was working with my instructor on a variety of things that morning in the practice area. We came back to the airport and proceeded to perform some touch and go landings on Runway XX, left traffic. We performed two touch and go landings, then a full stop landing. We taxied back and performed two more touch and go landings before the tower asked us to switch to right traffic (five landings in total). On downwind, the nose gear light didn't come on immediately. The hydraulic lever would kick back telling us it was pressurized and I had visual confirmation that the front gear was down.We performed three more touch and go landings to do our best to confirm that the gear was down and locked. I recall the nose gear light would flicker from time to time. We performed the checklist items accordingly but could not get the nose light to stay on when extending the gear. Every time the hydraulic gear lever would return to neutral and the gear was visible in the mirror. My instructor requested to the tower that we switch to the non active Runway (XY) so that he could land and get out to see what was going on with the gear. With the instructor flying, he chose to feather the left engine after the gear was lowered. No flaps were used. Upon landing, he shutdown the right engine. The plane initially acted normal but started to veer to the right as we continued down the runway. I could feel that he had very little directional control. He also has no brakes on the right seat position so he yelled 'left brake!, left brake!' I pushed the left brake as hard as I could and the plane turned left enough to stay on the runway, however shortly thereafter the nose gear collapsed. We skidded to a stop, shut everything down and exited the plane. The right engine hadn't stopped in time so the prop was damaged from contacting the runway. The left engine was feathered so there didn't appear to be any damage to it. The plane was removed from the non active runway and brought back to the hangar. I have no idea what we could have done differently as we had hydraulic pressure and visual confirmation that the gear was down (bad switch?). The previous touch and go landings were fine with no adverse steering issues. Perhaps the nose gear wasn't getting a lot of contact during the touch and goes but I still had directional control prior to him landing. Feathering the left engine obviously saved that from damage. The intent was to only gently land and inspect prior to taxing back to the hangar, but due to other circumstances the plane veered right, was corrected with left brake and the nose gear still ended up collapsing.
1791749: I am writing about two events that occurred at ZZZ. I do not believe either event was a violation of FAA policies but I wanted to be sure I reported both of them to protect myself.On [Date] I was preparing for a 45-degree entry into the left traffic pattern for Runway XX in ZZZ. I made my second CTAF call 4 miles from the airport and announced my intention to enter the pattern 'on the 45, left traffic for [Runway] XX.'A few minutes later, a pilot flying a Diamond announced he was 'turning left crosswind for [Runway] XX.' He asked whether I was in the left downwind or still 'on the 45.' I replied that I was still on the 45 but would be turning left downwind momentarily. He then announced that he was 'turning left downwind for [Runway] XX.' Just to be safe, I announced that I would perform a 360 degree turn for spacing. The other pilot flew the downwind leg, then I entered. No issues.A few days later I received a call from an FAA POI asking about a 'near miss' that had been anonymously reported, probably from someone on the ground. She kept coming back to my 360-degree turn. I explained the situation and referred her to ATCLive, a web site that archives radio calls.I also expressed my confusion over why this was a concern. I had been trained that using spacing maneuvers is the conservative and correct approach at uncontrolled fields if the pilot is in ANY DOUBT about the safety of entering.The second event occurred 15-20 minutes later. This did not come up in my conversation with the FAA POI. It only occurred to me later that this may have been the near miss she was inquiring about. Here's a summary:I was on a one-mile final for Runway XX at the same airport on the same morning, about 20 minutes after the entry I described above. I was flying patterns that morning to maintain proficiency. I looked to my left as I flew the final approach and saw a glider landing on the 'Glider XX' runway to my left.He was descending from above me and he was slightly ahead of my aircraft. It is very difficult for me to measure feet in this situation so I cannot be certain of the distance. But it did not feel like a near miss in any way. No evasive action was taken by either one of us. We were both flying straight in to our respective runways and lined up on our center lines.Let me be clear about something -- while I do not believe this was a 'near miss;' I don't believe two aircraft landing on parallel runways, with one aircraft being a glider, is a safe practice and I normally would have extended my downwind and/or base to create more room. However, I never heard the glider pilot's CTAF calls -- if indeed there were any. Also, the glider was above me so I couldn't see him until he descended in front of me and to my left. Some conclusions:I have flown in and out of ZZZ for five years. For an uncontrolled field, it is one of the most dangerous airports I have ever flown, and that includes ZZZ2 inside ZZZ3 Class Bravo. Traffic on any given day is packed with student pilots, private pilots, traveling pilots coming to ZZZ and -- worse yet -- gliders on a parallel runway to the active non-glider, powered runway. It's a mess. Making matters worse, there are five airports in a narrow corridor between the mountains and ZZZ1 Class B airspace -- four of which are uncontrolled. And to finish this night mare off, a very active parachute operation at ZZZ4.It's a disaster waiting to happen.
1791820: It was a typical busy day with many requests both inbound and outbound. Aircraft X called Ground Control on Taxiway Lima between the parallel runways requesting taxi to the northwest ramp. I issued 'taxi via Lima, Kilo, cross Runway 21 and hold short Runway 26 right at Kilo.' As the pilot read back the taxi route he appeared to hesitate and start a slight right turn onto Runway 21. I asked the pilot if he was familiar with taxiing between the parallel runways to which he replied 'no.' I then issued plain language instructions 'continue straight ahead and taxi kilo is the last right turn. As you make the turn the hold bars come up really quick so as you turn, slow to a stop. The pilot acknowledged my instructions. As the pilot turned on Taxiway Kilo he passed the hold short bars. I immediately reached out to Aircraft X and told him to stop. At that time another aircraft was calling Ground Control with a request. Aircraft X stopped prior to the runway edge line. I then made Local Control - North aware and advised the Controller to send around the traffic that was on about a 1-1/2 mile final. I had issued the hold short instruction but in his confused taxiing I missed the hold short readback as I was attempting to stop the aircraft from turning on to Runway 21. The airport recently painted a yellow taxi line that leads off of Taxiway Lima and onto to Runway 21. I've seen several pilots get confused while taxiing and follow that yellow line inadvertently. The airport also painted some enhanced taxi lines and runway markings on the ground. I believe the yellow line leading off Taxiway Lima is and will continue to confuse pilots. I think additional signage in the midfield clearly showing taxi routes would help the pilots who continue to 'get lost' while taxiing in these hotspots.
1791911: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X from ZZZ2-ZZZ1. I flew the RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach with rain and wind in the vicinity. I attempted to configure early but a strong tailwind made it challenging. I encountered a wind gust which caused me to counter increasing airspeed by pitching up and slightly reduce power to maintain airspeed and continue configuring. This resulted in a position higher than anticipated. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed this also and we articulated that. About that time, ATC directed a go-around. We executed the missed approach and climbed to 3,000 [feet] on vectors for another approach.Noting the conditions, I configured early for the second RNAV RNP XX approach. Rain and wind were still predominant throughout the approach but fewer gust excursions and we remained stable throughout the approach all the way to minimums. At minimums, we both had the approach lights and runway environment in sight and I continued the approach. As I turned final aligning with Runway XX, I lost sight of the runway environment due to the weather. The PM called go around and I initiated go around procedures. We climbed to 3,000 feet on vectors as directed by ATC. We communicated with one another and ensured we were both in the green, we had ample fuel, and agreed to attempt a third approach. On the third RNAV RNP XX approach, I configured early again and remained stable throughout the approach. The wind was still a factor though and required careful monitoring and aircraft correction to maintain a stable approach. Fully configured and in the vicinity of arriving at minimums, ATC advised a wind shift on the field of 330 degrees at 26 knots of wind. ATC asked for our intentions. Due to airline limitations on Maximum Tailwind Component for Landing, the PM told ATC we could not land and we would go-around. ZZZ1 Tower handed us off to ZZZ Departure and they advised us that they 'turned the airfield around' and they would give us vectors for the ILS RWY XY approach and we would be 'number 1' to the field. Again, the Captain and I communicated that we were both in the green, we noted that we had ample fuel, and we prepared for an ILS approach to Runway XY.After intercepting the localizer for the ILS to Runway XY, I configured fully and continued down the glideslope from the final approach fix. It was raining outside and was windy but we remained stable. Shortly prior to 1,000 feet AGL, it grew increasingly difficult to maintain a stable approach. I told the PM that I didn't feel comfortable, the weather was worsening, and it was likely that we would not be stable at 1,000 feet. We agreed and elected to go-around. Just as I began the go around procedure, we encountered a Wind Shear Warning and I proceeded with the Wind Shear escape maneuver. We exited the conditions quickly and transitioned to ATC's directives. We quickly agreed to divert to ZZZ3 and the PM informed ATC of our intention to divert. We climbed to 3,000 feet and flew vectors to ZZZ3.We flew the ILS RWY XYC approach and landed safely at ZZZ3 and taxied to the gate. We shut down the aircraft with approximately 7.4k pounds of fuel remaining. During the deplaning process, the Captain coordinated with the Maintenance and Dispatch and agreed to continue on to ZZZ1 as the weather cleared the area. We added fuel departing with 11.8k pounds of fuel. The Captain flew as the PF and I was the PM for the return flight to ZZZ1. The Captain maintained appropriate communication throughout the event. He communicated with the passengers explaining as best as possible what occurred and what we were doing to ensure their safety while doing our best to land at our intended destination. He kept the flight attendants apprised of the situation after each approach and we discussed each approach, verified we were both in the green, and maintained situational awareness at all times. Flew RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and was configuring the aircraft early. He was at gear down, flaps 15, and we encountered a wind gust that drove the airspeed indication almost to redline. The FO raised nose slightly and reduced power to slow the airspeed in order to continue configuring the aircraft. As this occurred, aircraft got a little high. As PM, I noticed this and was in process of informing FO when ATC said that we looked a little high and to just go around. We executed the missed approach as directed by ATC and climbed on a heading to 3,000 ft. to vector for another approach.On the second RNAV RNP XX, FO configured the aircraft early and shot approach to minimums. At minimums, approach lights and runway lights were visible, but as we turned to final approach, visibility was lost. I called go-around, and FO initiated go-around. We climbed on a heading to 3,000 feet. We communicated with each other that we were both in the green, had plenty of fuel, and prepared for another approach.On the third RNAV RNP XX, the FO had fully configured the aircraft, when ATC advised that the wind had shifted out of the north at 330 degrees and we had 26 knots of wind at our tail. ATC asked our intentions, I told them that we could not land with those winds and that we were going around. At that point, ATC handed us off to departure, and departure immediately advised us that they had turned the airport around and could give us an immediate left downwind to be number 1, shooting ILS Runway XY. FO and I communicated with each other that we were both in the green, had plenty of fuel, and prepared for an approach using the new runway.On attempt to Runway XY, we intercepted localizer and G/S. We had continual high winds indicating to me that the aircraft would not be able to remain stable throughout approach and landing. As PIC, I called for a go-around. FO communicated to me his agreement, and I immediately notified Tower of our intention to divert to ZZZ3. FO initiated the miss. As he did, we encountered a brief Wind Shear Warning. FO finished cleaning aircraft up and we diverted to ZZZ3 without incident.We were vectored to ZZZ3 and landed on Runway XYC and taxied to the gate with 7.4 pounds of fuel. I called Dispatch and she said we had plenty of fuel to get to ZZZ1 but as a precaution due to the frontal weather passage, she added more fuel and brought us up to 11.8 pounds. After the front passage, I flew the aircraft as PF uneventfully to ZZZ1. During all of the approaches and the divert I kept the flight attendants up to date and communicated with the passengers at all times. We exercised good situational awareness and followed SOPs during the entire flight.
1791916: Green laser event, continued to landing. Still had symptoms the next day but flew one leg as pilot monitoring, ZZZ to ZZZ1. Still having pressure symptoms in left eye.
1792218: I was on short, short final for Runway XX at ZZZ with a touch-and-go clearance. At an altitude of approximately 400 ft. AGL and about 0.4 SM from the runway threshold, ZZZ Tower cleared a Cirrus for takeoff. As the Cirrus began entering the runway, I rejected the landing and began to apply full power before the tower instructed me to go around and side-step to the right. I acknowledged the go-around, and requested a north departure, which was granted to follow the Cirrus that had just taken off. I'm unsure whether ATC inattention, loss of awareness of spacing, or simply the desire to get that traffic out caused this unsafe clearance to be issued. I would expect that controllers be aware of traffic on final and not issue conflicting releases of departing traffic.
1792268: 8 miles south of FNL we contacted the FNL Tower to request a touch and go then a departure to the east after the touch and go. The Tower requested that we contact them for a right downwind for Runway 15 when 4 miles south of the airfield. At the 4 mile mark we were unable to contact the Tower due to the fact the frequency was so busy that each time we tried to contact them we were stepped on. We were midfield right downwind by the time we were able to talk to the Tower. They were very upset yet there was nothing we could have done. We were cleared for the touch and go on Runway 15 then an east departure after that.The Tower requested we let them know when we were 4 miles east of the airport on our departure leg. At the 4 mile mark we contacted the Tower to let the Controller know. At the exact same time there was a helicopter that flew over us at less than 300 feet. We told the Tower we had the traffic insight. We had the helicopter in sight yet the Tower did not inform us about this traffic.FNL is a remote Tower and ATC (Tower) has limited visibility around the airport. My experience with this remote Tower is they do not have the same situational awareness that a full manned Tower would have. Congested airspace at FNL. Verbal traffic overwhelmed controller and was unable to get word in edgewise. Our comms were being stepped on constantly. Flying with a CFI we were unable to announce our 4 mile location until actually in a 3 mile downwind for Runway 15. Controller was verbally upset, but was still able to sequence us for arrival to complete a touch and go and make an east departure.
1792290: I was flying solo in an experimental aircraft and just as I was touching the ground on landing experience a wind gust from the right side. I ran out of right rudder and the plane tipped onto the the left wing tip starting a ground loop at approximately 15 mph ground speed. The tail spun around, a prop-strike occurred, then a tail-strike. I climbed out of the aircraft after shutting everything off and was uninjured. The airplane sustained some damage to the empennage and a propeller. No property damage or harm to any person occurred.
1792327: Private pilot student working toward a commercial certificate, practicing a simulated engine out within 1 mile of the runway from 2,200 AGL. The student was guiding the aircraft toward the runway. We had passed the threshold and were still high. I (the instructor) was directing coordinated S turns in order to not overshoot the available runway. We were using Runway X with winds approximately 330 at 7kts. On the last turn back toward the runway we were just west of the runway and I then noticed that airspeed was getting too low, we attempted to still land the plane, at this point only about 20ft above ground. We continued the descent and were touching down on the runway but not aligned with the runway. The student initiated a bank to realign the aircraft with the runway and the left wing apparently scraped the runway without any indication on the flight controls. I took the controls and leveled the wings, controlling the aircraft through a bounce. We departed the runway at an angle into the grass median between the runway and taxiway A. We continued the ground roll in the grass, crossing taxiway G before coming to a stop. Upon shutting down and inspecting the aircraft we found the scrape on the left wingtip and corner of the left aileron.
1792355: Visual to 27 at SAN using RNAV Z. Ceiling was BKN015. Crew briefed visual procedures at altitude but was informed that ATIS had changed late in the descent, crew adjusted minimums to account for the updated ceiling. Earlier I had queried the Captain if he preferred flaps 40 for SAN and he said he wanted flaps 30. Vref was 141 knots, wind component added 6 knots for a VTARGET of 147 knots. Captain configured early and we were stable at 1,000 feet AGL with a slightly high VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) due to SAN Runway 27 3.5 degree approach and the high weight and subsequent high approach speed. We were visual at that point, I think we broke out at 1,000-1,200 feet. Every time I crosschecked the speed and VVI, the Captain was stable, with the knowledge that the 3.5 degree approach and speed (as mentioned in the Safety Alert) would result in VVI rates over 1,000 feet. I was crosschecking radar altitudes and glideslope guidance more than I usually do, but this is my personal habit for SAN. As I did the normal 'in and out' visual crosscheck, nothing seemed amiss. Directly over or slightly after the parking deck on short final, the Captain slightly adjusted his visual aim point as is common technique at SAN. My eyes were outside at this point. We both heard a 'sink rate...'. I don't know what the second phrase was, as the Captain acknowledged the first sink rate forcefully and almost instantly. I quickly looked inside and I think I saw 'pull up' on the bottom of the PFD for what seemed like an instant. I can't be certain, however, and it can't be understated how fast it went away if indeed it was there. I looked back up and we were two red and two white on the PAPI, slightly fast, and Captain was in what looked like a good position to land. We made a safe landing and applied moderate braking and exited the runway. In the postflight, the Captain and I disagreed about what the second term was at the aural system annunciated. He thinks he heard 'sink rate, sink rate.' I actually don't know what the second term the aural system annunciated was, as I didn't hear it clearly due to the Captain's acknowledgment of it. I do think I saw a very fleeting 'pull up' on the PFD, but I can't be perfectly certain, and Captain is adamant that we didn't get the GPWS warning, only the sink rate caution. I want to be clear that I understand the limitation with regard to the warning annunciator. In hindsight, I can see now that a go-around could have been a prudent decision even though the aircraft appeared to be a safe and normal position for short final at SAN. I want to highlight this issue for a few reasons. It bears repeating that phase of flight, temporal distortion, and flight deck confusion can all conspire to create a situation where two trained and alert crew members can see different things. The other thing I want to highlight is how heavy -800's, going into SAN, can potentially be affected by a flaps 30 approach. I don't know why we don't have recommended flap settings for certain situations. We've all been flying light aircraft for almost a year now and perhaps it would help to remind crews about heavy aircraft with higher approach airspeeds and subsequently higher VVIs in higher altitude environments or steeper approaches like SAN. On approach to SAN when transitioning outside, we briefly received a sink rate call. At the gate, the First Officer was unsure if it was just a sink rate call or sink rate pull up. I adjusted sink rate and landed normally.
1792417: This was me and the First Officer's first flight together. He hadn't had a landing for approximately a month and hadn't been flying a lot recently. It was a beautiful day in ZZZ and we were cleared for the visual to XXL at about 7,000 MSL. We were established on the localizer as a backup and had the runway in sight holding around 210 knots. Approach control handed us off to tower and I checked in. We were cleared to land and told that there would be fighters departing out of ZZZ1, but they would stay below us. The First Officer started too slow and I extended flaps to 2. I started searching for the fighters and saw 2 of them takeoff. I keep my eyes on them to make sure we were clear. First Officer called for the gear and I extended it. I noticed we were still at flaps 2 and we were too fast for flaps 3. We were inside the FAF by this point and it was going to be close for a stabilized approach. The first officer had previously selected the approach mode and we were on course about 300 feet high on the glide path and fast so not correcting. I noticed the power on the engine instruments was not at idle which was strange because we had the approach selected in managed speed and the speed tape showed the target speed well below our current speed. I pointed the power setting out to the first officer and it was also confusing to him why the power was still up. We got to flaps 3 around 1,000 AGL and were still high on the glide path. We leveled off a little to get the flaps to full and then started to correct to glidepath. When we got to 500 feet we were still a good 200 feet high and 15-20 knots above our target speed. The First Officer asked me if I wanted him to go around. There was no traffic and the runway is 2 miles long so I said to continue. We ended up touching down at target speed well within the touchdown zone and cleared the runway. After getting to the gate and shutting down the engines we debriefed the approach. The First Officer said that all along he thought he was setting himself up nicely for the approach and thought it would work. I agreed and then I took myself out of the SA loop when I started searching for the fighters and didn't pay close enough attention to our energy status. When I finally did get back into it I wasn't forceful enough to help. When I pointed out the engines not being at idle I assumed he would disconnect the auto thrust and put the throttles at idle. When he didn't I should have told him too and that alone would have probably made us stable as there was still some time. At any rate I didn't and we were clearly unstable and we both knew it. The only correct option was to execute a go-around. Fuel was not an issue as we ended up landing with 6,500 pounds. I told him that I should have told him to go-around but he should have just executed a go-around without asking. That is the procedure. You don't need permission from the other pilot and permission not to go-around is still wrong anyway. We agreed that the biggest factor that got us going down this path in the first place was his recency of experience and that in order to fix that he should in the immediate future at least, slow down and configure earlier then he thinks he needs to. Going back to our departure briefing I should have taken the first leg anyway since I knew he hadn't flown in a while. This way he could have eased back into it.
1792587: I was traveling from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I experienced radio and GPS problems when trying to activate the runway lights at ZZZ1 around XA:00 local. After 3 attempts to activate the runway lights, I contacted Tucson Approach to see if there were any other ideas to help get the runway lights on. They called the airport to see if Customs was there. As no one was there, I was reaching my personal fuel reserve of 1 hour. The radio I have installed is GNS 430W. I had also had intermittent GPS signal, which resulted in no ADSB. Tucson Approach offered ZZZ2 as an alternate, but the airport was closed for the night. I felt it was much safer to go to TUS, as it has a host of FBO's and services available 24/7. I estimate that my radio at that time had about a 5 mile range. I lost contact with Approach several times, but I was able to hear the transponder code.As I got closer, Approach advised me that I was to enter a Right Downwind for Runway 11L at 4,000 ft. or above, and that I was cleared to land. They also told me to expect light gun signals from the Tower. I was able to acknowledge that transmission and was handed off to Tower. Tower also had a hard time hearing me, describing it as broken and scratchy. I was receiving Tower just fine, as I was close enough to the airport. I landed on 11L without incident and was given progressive taxi to FBO. Once I arrived and shut down, I asked if they had Maintenance available, which they did not. I parked there overnight until I was able to get an Avionics Tech to look at the airplane the next day. The Technician noticed that the 430W was not seated completely due do the design of the radio stack. He was able to quickly solve the problem. We did radio checks with TUS Ground and listened to the ATIS both over the cabin speaker and headsets. This particular aircraft is new to me, and I had not noticed the issue before as I normally operate out of an uncontrolled field. Now I incorporate a visual inspection of the GNS 430W, the audio panel, and the transponder as part of my preflight inspection, specifically looking to make sure they are seated properly, not loose, and functioning as they should. I took for granted that they had been installed correctly from the previous aircraft owner. I trust Maintenance shops to do work and repairs correctly, but it is now a trust but verify as I am the one responsible for the operation of the aircraft and systems.
1792798: Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1, on decent into ZZZ1 at about 7,000 feet the gear warning audio went off 'landing gear-landing gear-landing gear' in a very loud tone in both headset and speaker. A quick troubleshooting of the system showed #2 radar altimeter 0 feet to -5 feet and #1 normal for 7,000 feet (hidden) no CAS message or other evidence of a fault. Left us with no direction for check list. We tried selecting the gear override switch but that was of no help silencing the audio. In my 35 years at this airline I have experienced many in flight emergencies including 5 engine failures however never in all those experiences has it been so hard to concentrate on dealing with the problem with the continued very loud 'landing gear-landing gear' over and over with no way to turn it off. It was also very evident to the forward flight attendant and most likely front half of the aircraft passengers. When we have a fire we get multiple warnings but we can silence the audio warning wile we work the problem. The other part that bothers me from a safety standpoint is we have two radar altimeter systems #1 and #2 if both are in agreement that's one thing but in this case only one was faulty. We should not get to this level of alarm during a disagreement or miss-comparison. I propose that we find a solution or fix so in the future crews can have an option in some way to silence this type of warning after they have acknowledged the problem. In our case we lowered the gear to silence the warning, this might not always be the best course of action.
1793225: The FO (First Officer) was flying and we were on the visual approach to RWY (Runway) 22 and we got a Caution Obstacle message. We started a turn and visually kept clear of the obstacle. We continued the visual approach and were stable. We descended to 2,000 [feet] MSL before turning on final and a tower off the right side of the aircraft caused us to get the alert. In hindsight we should have maintained 3,100 feet until passing BRIDL. Transferring from Approach to Tower and upon passing Lexington VOR (HYK) we were asked to descend to 3,000 [feet]. Flying towards the departure end of [Runway] 22 we were asked if we had a visual of the airport. The Captain was non flying and answered yes. Then the Tower said that we were cleared for visual [Runway] 22 and a helicopter on the north end of the field was operating. That put us on a 45 downwind and once on the downwind, I then put 2,000 [feet] on the altitude selector. As per procedure 1,000 [feet] AGL is the lowest we can put in the selector. I then gradually decreased my descent from 3,000 and called for flaps setting three at speed 160 [knots] then gear down to be configured by the Runway 22 touchdown zone point. My descent was shallow and we did have the ILS 22 in the MCDU as reference. Turning within the outer-marker BRIDL we got an obstacle call. I was referencing an obstacle as referenced on the approach plate at 1,997 [feet] marked with an arrow at 1,997 [feet]. We were at 2,500 feet still descending as I looked to the right. I was about to call obstacle and perform the go-around procedure as per SOP but the call quickly ended. The call as per SOP is the trigger call 'Obstacle, Pull Up.' The call ended and we continued the standard turn. We were configured flaps five on the base leg and the continued on final. We descended once we captured the glide slope. We put 3,100 [feet] which was the missed approach procedure. The startling part of the flight was the obstacle call which we then started to look for something else, since we already had the tower obstacle in sight and we both confirmed the sighting.I think that in the future it's best to enter the traffic pattern and just follow the approach itself.
1793441: Upon the execution of normal gear extension, flight crew observed the nose gear indication displayed on the aircraft systems page, the nose gear was not down and locked. PIC communicated to the ZZZ Tower that the nose gear indication was not down and locked. PIC asked for a low approach and for the Tower to visually check if the nose gear appeared to be down. Tower Controller confirmed the gear was not down. Flight crew executed QRH procedure associated with gear up/unsafe condition multiple times noting the hand gear pump would not move and there was no hydraulics CAS message. Flight crew then requested an additional low approach and ZZZ Tower indicated that the nose gear still appeared to be retracted, but that the nose gear doors were open. PIC executed missed approach and departed traffic pattern to complete speed turns in attempt to lower the nose gear. Procedure proved to be unsuccessful. Another low approach was conducted and ZZZ Tower said the nose gear still appeared to be up, with the gear doors open. PIC requested priority handling, then gave passengers onboard an additional briefing. Flight crew briefed the landing procedure multiple times and then entered an approximately 15 mile final for Runway XXL at ZZZ. Flight crew fully configured aircraft for landing (with the exception of three gear indicators in down and locked state) at 10 mile final and briefed landing procedure again. PIC landed disabled aircraft on Runway XXL at ZZZ in accordance with procedure for nose-gear unsafe state. Flight crew and passengers evacuated aircraft after it came to a stop on Runway XXL ZZZ. While ground personnel and local responders worked to remove the aircraft from the runway, a police officer came into the FBO with an (estimated 9-10' long) chrome socket/ratchet extender in his hand, and informed the flight crew that he had removed that item from the retracted nose gear. Police officer stated he removed the tool from the location where the aircraft tow pin/head is supposed to be installed for towing and that it was almost as wide as the nose gear door opening on the aircraft.I suggest an additional line item be added to the aircraft's certified Pre-Flight Inspection Checklist and Before Start Checklist that includes wording/verbiage to identify and confirm that a certified tow head, tow pin, or otherwise foreign or unapproved object is not in the nose strut of the aircraft. I also suggest the identification of a clear nose strut tow-pin location be added to the PIC's final before flight walk-around. I suggest additional training and oversight of FBO line personnel that includes a mandate of using certified, tagged and visually identifiable, approved tow pins for the aircraft they are moving and the importance of removing them immediately after ground movement/towing is completed. Upon initial extension of the landing gear, the nose gear did not extend. The flight crew performed QRH procedure. QRH procedure was unsuccessful in extending the nose gear. The flight crew executed a landing on Runway XXL at ZZZ.
1793705: My student and I were flying a C172 on the RNAV XY at ZZZ, planning to circle-to-land on Runway XX. We made radio calls on CTAF for 10 miles, 5 miles, 3 miles, and when starting to circle.
