We only heard calls from a plane on short final. During the circling procedure, before we were established on downwind, my iPad with ADS-B In (via Sentry) alerted that there was traffic 10 o'clock, less than a mile. Both my student and I observed the other aircraft, a C152, pass less than 200 feet above us and less than 500 feet horizontally away. I made another call on CTAF and the C152 finally made a radio call that they were performing a teardrop maneuver to the downwind. My student and I proceeded to do a touch-and-go and fly the missed approach procedure on the RNAV XY. We did not hear any more radio calls from the other plane.
1793739: Upon landing at night from ILS Runway 16, we were given right turn onto H1 from Tower. We saw the H1 Taxiway sign on the right and turned inadvertently onto Runway 11/29. Recommend this intersection be labeled a Hot Spot as it's difficult to see at night.
1793788: I was climbing out from Runway XX during a 'Go Around' turning from left crosswind to a left downwind at 800 ft. I heard another aircraft reporting entering a left downwind to the same runway. Right after entering downwind I broadcast in the blind looking for a position of aircraft and he told me I had just passed below his belly at about 200 ft. away from his aircraft. I apologized and told him I never saw him until after his call and he was about 1/2 mile off my left wing.A safer practice would have been if I sidestepped to the right during the initial phase of the go around and climbed to 1,000 ft. AGL before turning left into the crosswind. This action would have put me farther away from the airport and would give me a greater view of the area I was turning into.
1793827: Aircraft X, cleared Visual Approach off a downwind turn behind a Heavy. Aircraft X was pointed away and behind Heavy when cleared to follow the traffic and issued caution wake turbulence. The pilot turned to follow the Heavy at his discretion towards the traffic and the field to a dog leg at about 5.5 miles in trail of the Heavy. Aircraft X joined final approach behind the traffic and I, the Final Radar Controller, observed what looked like a quick radar track anomaly. Quickly followed was an observed turn and quick descent and climb by Aircraft X back towards the field. The pilot promptly advised of a 'complete upset' and that he was back on the turn towards the traffic and on the Visual Approach with out a chance for me to issue any instructions.Later to find out this verbiage meant the aircraft had been sent into a complete roll to the right in which the pilot continued to recover the aircraft. No official cause but I can only guess wake turbulence from the Heavy traffic sent him into an uncontrolled roll. I acknowledged, inquired if any assistance was required to which the pilot responded in the negative, and I continued to work the traffic to include breaking out a Heavy behind him to allow him to continue the Visual Approach. The aircraft continued on the approach and double confirmed that everything was okay and no assistance was required before sending him to the Tower for landing.No recommendation, but awareness for all pilots of potential wake turbulence induced events. I personally could have ensured the aircraft was at a higher altitude to possibly prevent the wake trajectory, but I was originally setting up Aircraft X for an ILS Approach to follow at the appropriate wake turbulence minimums. Only after the pilot called traffic and field in sight was he given the Visual Approach clearance to follow. If the pilot did not feel comfortable with this, I did not know or could have recommended a different method of approach.
1794298: After landing at ZZZ on the roll out towards the taxiway exit the aircraft landing gear system failed and buckled in. Consequently the aircraft fell to the ground causing the propeller to strike the ground. Damage observed and assured by A&P was the propeller, aux tank drain sump fell off, scratches on the bottom of fuselage, side step and landing gear. Airport operations did not want us to load the plane on a flat dollie and insisted on using a crane. When the crane was used the flaps were bent. No further damage was observed.
1794523: Winds were moderate, variable, and gusty, but within limits for the aircraft. In accordance with accepted technique, half the gust factor, approximately 6 knots, was added to the final approach and landing speeds. Just after touchdown on the centerline, with all three gears established on the runway, a gust was felt and corrected for. As the correction was made with what was perceived as moderate aileron and rudder input, the airplane veered sharply to the left. With the thought that over-controlling back to the right could lead to the left wingtip dipping and then digging into the runway resulting in the aircraft tumbling (worst case) or a ground loop at high energy (best case), I elected to input enough control to keep the aircraft tracking as straight ahead as possible. This resulted in departing the runway surface to the left of the runway. Once in the gravel that was lining the left side of the runway, my entire focus was on maintaining enough control not to hit obstacles or dig in gear or wingtips so as to cause tumbling. In the process of dissipating energy, I crossed two high-speed taxiways at almost a perpendicular angle and at a still relatively high-speed resulting in the aircraft becoming lighter on the struts. The struts compressed again on the other side of the taxiways resulting in enough energy depletion to safely steer back to the runway surface.Upon re-establishing safe contact with asphalt, the aircraft was taxied a short distance to parking. Upon the post-flight walk-around inspection, there was visible damage to two of three propeller blade tips (of composite material made by Hartzell) from contact with gravel likely occurring when the struts compressed after crossing the taxiways. No other visible damage to the aircraft was observed nor were fluids observed to be leaking. It is very likely the root cause of this event was the application of too much rudder for the capabilities of the aircraft in countering the cross-wind gust after landing.The PA-46 line of aircraft is known to have very sensitive nose wheel steering, especially at higher speeds, and while being aware of it and managing it were trained to extensively, it's entirely possible that too much rudder was applied as was appropriate for this aircraft type. Habit pattern transference is a likely contributing factor in that I have several thousand hours in other type aircraft, to include very recent and continued professional flying experience in the Pilatus PC-12, and all of which do not exhibit the level of sensitivity in nose wheel steering that the PA-46 does. In instinctively applying the crosswind gust correction I'm used to, it is very possible that I applied an amount that was too much for safe control of the PA-46 at the time of occurrence.I do not feel training was a contributing factor as I received very thorough Piper-authorized training and initial conditioning in the aircraft with a Piper-authorized instructor. However, overall low time in type is definitely a contributing factor. Up to the time of this event, I had logged 20 landings in the PA-46 and several of which were in gusty conditions and or crosswinds similar to what was experienced during this event. In the future, the biggest take away from the event for me for flying the PA-46 is to concentrate on keeping the nose wheel off the runway as long as possible as energy depletes so that when the nose wheel does contact the runway, it's at the lowest speed practical. During this event the nose wheel was centered upon initial contact with the runway, as was emphasized in training. Any application of nose wheel steering at higher speeds should always be done very lightly at first to ensure the aircraft remains under control.

1796869: We had been flying on an IFR flight plan with a destination of ZZZ, a non-towered airport just north of ZZZ1. Per the appropriate checklist, we took the action of turning on the fuel pump on the fuller side. In spite of taking this action, the indication of the problem got markedly worse (increased to 6 and then to 7 segments) within only 2-3 minutes, yet we still had no controllability issues. We then ended up getting a 'Fuel Balance Fault' CAS message as well. In sum, we were close to the ground, in the vicinity of Class B, near a practice area, trying to deal with this issue. We elected to focus primarily on doing the most important things: aviate, navigate, and communicate. We flew the airplane and began a diversion towards ZZZ1, which we could clearly see. It has a longer and wider runway, which would be important in landing a bit faster than normal to avoid potential controllability issues, and it also has emergency equipment available as well. Notified ATC since the issue had happened so quickly, and the fuel monitoring device depicted that the problem had gotten markedly worse so quickly as well -- felt it best to get on the ground quickly before a controllability issue developed. Landed without incident. If we hadn't been so close to landing (instead being enroute at altitude in the middle of nowhere), we could have obviously spent more time analyzing and dealing with the issue in flight. After landing and thinking about it a bit, we believed it was an indication problem, and not an actual fuel imbalance after all. Upon further reflection overnight of our actions during the flight, we concluded that we wouldn't do anything different than we did. In general, we were pleased with what we did. It was a particularly busy time with the nearby traffic, and we quickly focused on the most important things of aviate, navigate, and communicate. The notifying ATC might be questioned, but only with hindsight, I believe -- I am comfortable with this judgment call.

1798250: This flight was the first leg of a four day for the Captain and I. The Captain said he would be the pilot flying, that I would be pilot monitoring and he briefed everything up, including threats. We made each other aware of our lack of recent flying experience and lack of proficiency. I informed him that I only have a little over 700 hours on type, that most of that time was trans-cons prior to the pandemic and that I haven't flown much in the past twelve months. I also informed him to the best of my knowledge this would be my first time flying into ZZZZ [Airport]. We agreed that we would take things slow and that we were doing everything correctly. Our taxi out, take off, departure and cruise were routine and uneventful. Approximately twenty minutes prior to the Top of Descent the Captain briefed our descent and approach into ZZZZ and we ran the descent checklist. Center gave us a descent, followed by descend via the X Arrival. We were handed off to approach and told to expect the VOR [Runway] X, after ZZZZZ [Intersection] to fly present heading for a vector to the VOR approach. Prior to ZZZZZ the Captain called for flaps 1, After ZZZZZ he called flaps 5, slowed to 190 knots and approach gave us the vector and cleared us for the VOR X approach. We were at or near the final approach fix when the Captain called gear down, flaps fifteen followed by flaps 30 landing checklist. I set final approach altitude, we were VOR/LOC and VNAV descending per the approach and slowing to our vref of 156 knots. At 1000 feet we were fully configured, and I believe we were at 165 knots. I called 1000 feet, the Captain was task saturated so I said 1,000 feet, set missed approach altitude and said cleared to land. I noticed VNAV had kicked off, I verbalized it and re-selected VNAV, I thought it went to VNAV PTH, but in our debrief I learned it went to VNAV SPD. Between 1,000 and 500 feet the fastest speed I saw was 170 knots. At 500 feet I called 500 feet and saw 171 knots and almost called a go-around. I called 15 knots fast, the Captain said correcting and I saw the speed slowly begin to decrease. I was focused on airspeed as we were at the limit for a stabilized approach and I was looking at the runway as I was concerned, we were going to be high. We continued our approach and I was beginning to become uncomfortable, at approximately 200 feet I noticed we were at 170 knots (it may have been a couple knots faster) but 170 is what I recall. At approximately 200 feet I called that we were high and fast, the Captain said correcting and I saw the speed slowly begin to decrease and he pitched down to correct. At approximately 100 feet I wanted to call for a go-around as we were fast, 170 knots or faster, however I was unable to verbalize it. We touched down hard and flat, we may have had a small bounce, but I don't believe that we did. The Captain deployed the reverser's and we made a normal exit onto taxiway and proceeded to parking. Upon parking, we debriefed this event, we both conducted thorough post flight inspections of the exterior. To the best of our knowledge the aircraft was nott damaged. The Captain contacted Maintenance and they wrote up the hard landing. The Captain also called the Duty Manager.Factors that led to this event were both of our lack of recent flying experience, unfamiliar airport, night operation, Runway X PAPI out of service, the change from VNAV PTH to VNAV SPD and I did not call for a go-around.I have learned from this event and will call for a go-around if I become uncomfortable or we become unstable in the future. We were flying into ZZZZ [Airport] on the VOR [Runway] X approach at night. I had not flown for a year. Currency was a factor. While on approach I configured on time and landing checklist was called for and completed. At 500 feet we were 15 knots fast (171 knots) and the FO said we are fast. I said correcting. At 200 feet I was 17 knots (173 knots) fast the FO said we are fast, I tried to correct. Also, at 200 feet the FO called out high. I over corrected and landed abruptly from 50 feet to touch down. I do not believe this was a bounced landing but may have been. Our pitch was flat, and we landed main gear first. Our descent rate from 50 feet to 0 feet was extreme. The failure of myself or as a crew to not call a Go Around was the primary mitigating factor. Also executing an off center VOR approach with a PAPI OTS at night was a factor. I felt I was not high but in reality, it was due to lack of visible surroundings. Furthermore, the VOR approach only gave guidance to 1,054 feet MSL. To further complicate issues the VNAV disconnected. So, in essence we were left minimal visual guidance. Winds were 20 knots reported and was another factor. My FO stated he was about to call for go-around at 500 feet and 200 feet, but neither of us did. After landing we taxied in normally. We both did several post flight inspections. I also notified Maintenance and the Duty Pilot of the events. This was the first leg of a 4 day with an FO I've never flown with. All briefings were completed. The FO and I discussed before departure how infrequently we have flown due to the pandemic. He had never been to ZZZ [Airport]. I had not been in 2 years. All approach briefings were concluded in a timely manner. The STAR in use was the X arrival. After ZZZZZ [Intersection] we were instructed to fly present heading for radar vectors to join the VOR X LOC. The VOR approach X is a very tricky approach. It is offset with limited visual guidance. Flaps 1 was initiated prior to ZZZZZ. Flaps 5 was initiated after ZZZZZ. Best to our knowledge we were configured by the FAF. The FMA was showing VOR/LOC and VNAV path commencement to approach, at some point we lost VNAV path and went to VNAV speed. I accomplished a LAVS check but did not add 2 and 4 mile rings. I may have gotten very close to exceeding flaps 30 speed. I also believe my flare was minimal at best. Having a PAPI would have been beneficial.
1798253: We were flying the ILS 27R to ORD. When cleared for the approach level at 4,000 ft, we twice had to disconnect the autopilot from the aircraft wake ahead of us. Spacing was the usual 3 miles and winds were straight down the path at 40 kts. Other aircraft were radioing similar issues with wake. I decided to hand fly the approach the rest of the way to better control the speed and avoid the wake. The Final Controller told us to slow to 170 kts and contact Tower. We were cleared to land by Tower and continued the approach at 170 kts. Spacing was holding at 3 miles, but as we approached the marker I noticed our spacing was closing faster than normal. At about 2.5 outside the marker I made the decision to start slowing to avoid going around. (Full disclosure, I have been in the exact situation before and had to go around twice on this approach.) What I misjudged was how fast the 737-700 slows down. We were at approach speed too early and the Tower asked our speed and instructions. We made the aircraft behind us go around from my error in speed control. While on ILS 27R into ORD, we were experiencing wake turbulence from the aircraft ahead of us and appeared to be quickly closing the distance between us. We had been assigned 170 kts until the final approach fix 'SIBLY' and began slowing 2 miles prior to the fix to stop the closure. The Tower Controller queried our speed, and emphasized we were to hold 170 until the fix.
1798411: We were flying and cleared on the IFR approach and had 3 flight school planes come within 500 feet. One of the planes pointed straight at us at our altitude within 100 feet at us. I read their tail number. We veered immediately. All three planes climbed straight up out of an adjacent airport. I notified ATC and they said it's a beehive there right now and he can't tell what's happened there.
1798694: Neither one of us had ever been into ZZZ. We both took the opportunity on the flight to review the company pages. Acknowledging that it is a special qualification airport and after review of company documents, we realized that controls needed to be transferred to the Captain due to my low time in the aircraft. Control of the aircraft was transferred at approximately 13,000 feet MSL. Traffic was landing XXL. We briefed and set up for the RNAV for XXL. Center handed us off to ZZZ Approach. We were asked to advise when the field was in sight. Conditions were VFR and remained so. We had the field and were cleared for the visual. We recognized immediately that we were high. We had a tailwind which made it exceptionally difficult to get configured. The Captain continued to descend and try to reduce speed. He called for gear, however, I was unable to extend the gear because we were not at the appropriate speed. We were switched to Tower. The Captain continued the descent all the while attempting to reduce speed. Best guess we were at approximately a 7 mile final. We received an EGPWS 'TERRAIN TERRAIN'. The Captain shallowed the descent. It was then followed by a 'TERRAIN TERRAIN PULL UP' and I called for the go-around. We followed the escape procedures, were vectored around the pattern, and landed without incident. Neither pilot had been into the airport. We had reviewed documents, however once cleared for the visual we did not comply with the prescribed speeds on the arrival. In retrospect, we should have continued on the RNAV arrival since we were unfamiliar with the airport. Additionally, better awareness of wind may have assisted in getting configured.
1798844: AIRCRAFT 1 was in the downwind. I decided I was going to turn my traffic on to base leg above my traffic to the parallel runway. AIRCRAFT 2 was downwind ahead of AIRCRAFT 1 descending to 7000 feet. I vectored them to join final, no clearance to use altitude leaving. AIRCRAFT 3 was straight in to the parallel runway. I based AIRCRAFT 1 the first time with the wrong call sign XXX , no response. AIRCRAFT 3 and AIRCRAFT 1 were head to head at same altitude with 8 miles of separation. I transmitted three additional times for AIRCRAFT 1 feet twice no response before 'say again' and finally got a read back. AIRCRAFT 1 had divergence with AIRCRAFT 3 by about 1/2 mile. I shipped AIRCRAFT 2 to turn heading 050, more panicked each time, finally got a response. Told AIRCRAFT 3 to expedite with a speed restriction, not realizing I had not cleared them for an approach. They said nothing because [of] my near miss seconds before. Local Control called and asked if they were landing, I said I thought they were cleared. AIRCRAFT 2 went around because of this mistake.This was a tight hole to get into. I pushed to get in it because without, AIRCRAFT 1 would have flown 10 more miles. If pilots would have listened, this would be a non-event, but I instead was panicked and forgot to clear AIRCRAFT 2 I feel terrible for the go around, and scared that I barely had separation, head to head, between two aircraft. I think I will be much more hesitant to attempt to get general aviation aircraft their preferred runway. Just a few minutes before this, I made another general aviation land on a different runway because I deemed it not worth the risk. It's not that I don't have cutoffs, in fact, I'm less aggressive than a lot of my coworkers. This exact situation has been completed without incident numerous times by myself and others. Plain and simple, this happened because the pilots didn't hear and then I allowed a distraction to make me forget to clear AIRCRAFT 2. That being said, at least for a while I won't be accommodating general aviation aircraft quite as much. That situation could have been much, much worse and that's going to be playing in my head for quite some time.
1799059: We did night currency at our home airport. There was one Controller for Clearance [Delivery], Ground, and Tower. It was pretty busy with military aircraft doing night landings and airliners coming in. I had to ask the Controller to clear us to land each time. Usually they say report downwind or base and then will clear us to land or have us extend after we report. He was probably overwhelmed because he was constantly talking while working three frequencies. I wanted to report just in case it was unclear at any point if we were actually clear to land. The second landing he sounded annoyed when I asked if we were cleared to land - I had to ask because he had not cleared us. It didn't help that we were going 150 knots over the ground because of the 40 knot tail wind. It would help if there were separate people working Ground and Tower.
1799214: On the LIBER 3 arrival, ATC instructed 'after GLOWS fly heading 020 descend 4200 ft. for traffic, vectors for the approach.' Approximately 15 miles from the runway, ATC instructed '5 miles from CIGNI left turn to intercept the inbound course, maintain 4200 until established, cleared approach.' PF (Pilot Flying) tuned heading, drew a line out from WUNDU, set 1700 in the altitude alert and armed the approach.As course came alive and captured we noticed path continuing to drop below us on the vertical guide. As course came alive, PF pushed VS then VNAV. ALT turned to FLCH and the aircraft began to descend. Rather than capture, it descended through the path. PF pushed VS in attempt to regain the path. We heard 'Terrain warning.' PF turned off AP, began a climb and asked PM (Pilot Monitoring) to rest 4,200. ATC questioned the low altitude alert and asked us to confirm we were established on the approach due to the MSA of 4,200. We confirmed due to laterally established and visual contact with terrain. PF leveled at 4,200, engaged AP and we worked to re-engage the APP while continuing, landed and debriefed.After being vectored off the arrival, it may have been a better course of action to load the RNAV Y for 20R due to better altitude protections. Also need to wait for LNAV to be in magenta. Due to traffic we were on a heading and descended to 4,200. 5 miles from CIGNI turn left maintain 4,200 until established, cleared approach. I turned to the heading, pressed approach and spun the AA down to 1,700 and lined out from WUNDU, entered in the inbound course and activated.Waiting to intercept I noticed VNAV path was dropping below us. I as saw the course come alive I pressed VS and VNAV, ALT turned to FLCH. Aircraft began a descent to capture PATH but we went through it. My first reaction was to press VS and climb back to path. We heard a terrain warning, I clicked AP off and began a climb asked PM (Pilot Monitoring) to spin AA to 4,200. ATC notified us of a Low Altitude alert, he said if we were established we were okay, We were laterally established and had visual contact with all terrain. I leveled at 4,200 and engaged autopilot. We worked to re-engage APP and continued.We landed and debriefed. Mistake was lowering AA to 1,700 until fully magenta.
1799610: During the approach briefing for the ILS approach to Runway 15 at LCH, the First Officer (Pilot Flying), informed the Captain that he had problems with the Runway 15 localizer on two previous flights for this runway. The FO (First Officer) said that on both previous flights, the Runway 15 localizer did not stay centered. The FO explained the Localizer Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) had swung left and right of course. After discussing this, the Captain and FO agreed that the FO would remain on GPS guidance while the Captain would monitor on the localizer radio guidance. After being cleared for the approach, The FO intercepted the inbound course on GPS guidance. The Captain's localizer guidance initially appeared stable. Approximately three miles prior to the final approach fix, FIDGA, the FO switched his course guidance to the localizer. The approach guidance was stable. We passed FIDGA, intercepted the glide slope, and began our final descent. At approximately 1,300 feet MSL, the localizer began deviating left and right of course. The autopilot was engaged. The FO disengaged the autopilot and we immediately descended below the cloud ceiling, which was approximately 1,100 feet MSL or 1,200 feet MSL. The Captain and FO both sighted the runway at 1,100 feet MSL. At some point below 1,000 feet MSL, the localizer appeared to be stable. The remainder of the approach was uneventful. During the approach, the winds were 40 knots from approximately 200 degrees, prior to the FAF. After clearing the runway, we reported the problem to the Control Tower. The FO informed the Tower Controller he had problems with the Runway 15 localizer on two previous occasions. The Tower Controller said he had not received any other notifications about problems with the localizer from any other aircrews. At no point was the approach unstable. [Request] inspection of the localizer antenna. A query to the LCH Control Tower to determine if other aircrews have experienced the same problem. A notification in the daily read warning aircrews they might encounter the same problem.
1800001: This event happened While training was in progress on the local one position. Aircraft X was sequenced to follow Aircraft Y in the pattern. The trainee did not observe that Aircraft X was much faster and had turned in too close behind Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y was on short final approximately 100 feet AGL. Aircraft X was off the left wing of Aircraft Y at approximately the same altitude. It was apparent that Aircraft X had offset to the left side of Aircraft Y in an effort not to land on top of or create a collision with Aircraft Y ahead. This being said, Aircraft X never attempted to query ATC. It was not until the ground controller said 'what is happening' That the trainee, trainer and the Controller in Charge even looked out the window. The trainee was staring at the radar, the OJTI and the Controller in Charge were not paying any attention and we're engaged in a non ATC related conversation. Neither one of them were looking out the window. At the time of the incident, the Instructor had his back turned away from the runway threshold. Once the incident was brought to everybody's attention, the trainee who looked out the window but did not make any attempt to send the aircraft around until the Instructor instructed the trainee to send the aircraft around. I saw the incident, however, I chose not to say anything.After this Incident, I brought it to the Supervisors attention. That said, at the time of the incident the Supervisor was not in the tower cab. I later heard that the Controller in Charge stated to a management official that the situation was 'not that bad.' In fact, the situation was incredibly dangerous. The aircraft probably were only separated by maybe 200 to 300 feet laterally and 0 feet in altitude. I do believe this statement was made by the Controller in Charge in an effort to cover up the situation considering that the Controller in Charge was distracted in a non ATC conversation and did not see the situation developing. I believe the only thing that needs to change from this incident, is the Controller in Charge and Instructor paying attention. There is too much trust put in a trainee that has a history of dangerous happenings.
1800353: I was instructing while my student was performing a touch and go on Runway 36 at SLN when a Helicopter turned over the runway head on with me and passed roughly 200 feet above my aircraft during our initial climbout. SLN Tower had advised the Helicopter that there were three aircraft on Runway 36, which the Helicopter pilot acknowledged. However, SLN Tower did not call out the Helicopter traffic to my aircraft or the other aircraft in the pattern for Runway 36. The traffic alert popped up on my GPS, at which point I instructed my student to take evasive action by leveling off over the runway and staying below the Helicopter until it was behind us.
1800416: It was a very busy day coming into DAL. We were being vectored from the northeast for a Visual Approach. We had Company traffic in sight and were told to follow them and cleared for the Visual Approach. We ensured clearance from them and began maneuvering for the runway with a more direct path to ZZZZZ. It was about that time I noticed a TCAS target ahead. I cannot remember if we had already been switched to Tower or not at that point, but ATC told us about the traffic ahead. I responded, 'looking for traffic.' Shortly after that we heard ATC tell Aircraft Y [the traffic ] to turn east immediately. We were given no more instruction and weren't sure which way would be best for avoidance. I told the Captain that we may get an RA here and he prepared. We then got a climb RA. The Captain responded immediately and we avoided the conflict.We were able to regain approach stability and land uneventfully. We have no idea why a small aircraft was in Class B airspace between us and our line to the airport while we were cleared for a Visual Approach, or why we were given no instruction by ATC other than a traffic notification. By the time the traffic was noticed by us as a threat, the rate of closure was so fast we only had a few seconds to process what we may needed to do. We never got Aircraft Y in sight, but I noticed on the TCAS indication that he was 300 feet below us at what looked like our position on the 2.5 NM display.I am not sure what needs to happen to prevent this from happening again because I'm not sure why this happened. I'm hoping this report brings some attention to this event so we can find out why something like this happened. I know they were busy but I feel this incident should have been prevented by either keeping us in their control until we were clear of Aircraft Y or keeping them out of Class B at such a busy time.
1800479: When on arrival and approach the flight was put 5nm in trail of a 757. This caused the aircraft to experience wake turbulence intermittently for the last approximately 100nm of the flight. While focusing on mitigation strategies for the wake, a loss of situational awareness occurred causing the pilot flying to become high and fast on approach. Aircraft was configured by 1,000 feet AGL, however was still stabilizing airspeed. Aircraft landed without incident. Increased spacing between heavy jets and regional jets would reduce the pilot workload on arrival and approach and thus minimize the chance of fixation on that issue.
1800957: Approximately XA:11, Pilot Flying and I were on the ILS 27R to OPF. Weather was good, we could see the runway from 10+ miles. I was Pilot Monitoring. About 3-4 miles from the runway, on course and glide path with autopilot engaged, I saw a bright reflection to our left, about 10 o'clock low. It was obviously not air traffic, nothing on the TCAS. It quickly moved left to right across our flight path. Passed under the right wing. Appeared to be climbing. It looked no larger than a lunchbox, but was certainly flying, not just blowing in the wind. It was a shiny metallic color, not a bird.Aggressive enforcement of laws concerning drone flights in vicinity of airports. I was on an ILS approach to Runway 27R to OPF. The weather was VFR and we could see the runway from 10+ SM out. I was the Pilot in Command - flying pilot. About 3-4 miles from the runway Pilot Monitoring and I saw a bright reflection to our left, about 10 o'clock low. It was obviously not air traffic, nothing on the TCAS. It quickly moved left to right across our flight path. It passed under the right wing. It appeared to be climbing. It did not look very large but was certainly flying and not just blowing in the wind. It was a shiny metallic color and not a bird. No evasive action was needed on our part and none was taken. Pilot Monitoring reported this object to the OPF tower as we continued on the approach. We landed safely without incident and cleared the runway and taxied to the ramp. Possibly this was a drone.If this was a drone being flown around and just to the east of the OPF airport, try and find out who was doing this.
1800996: I was taking off on my 3rd and final takeoff and landing for my first solo. I had 3 great landings with my instructor and had landed twice solo and was going in for my final takeoff and landing. I was climbing in the pattern and was at 800 feet when I turned right over [road] then leveled the wings. Waited 3 seconds and turned parallel to the runway at 1,100 feet. Powered to 4500 RPM got the clearance to land from Tower and radioed back for clear to land. I pulled the carb heat and when I got to ¾ of the runway I powered to 3000 RPM which is normal for a descent. I put in 2 seconds of flaps and took out the trim. I noticed I was a bit high at 900 feet when I turned over the shopping center so 100 feet above where I normally am. Put in some more flaps to about 20 degrees and turned in to final. I saw 3 whites and 1 red light, so I knew I was a bit high, I reduced power to get the plane to slow and reduce elevation. This gets me to the railroad tracks and descending in normally. Power is reduced to idle over the railroad tracks near Runway XX airplane starts to decent quicker than the last 2 times that I landed solo. As a result, I pitched up to get the glare shield on the horizon as that happened, I touched down and bounced on the runway. As the aircraft rose, I pitched for a decent angle thinking I was high above the runway, as the nose came over, I was surprised how close to the runway I was. Then I pitched for level flight, as I did this the aircraft touched down for a second, I thought It touched flat. But the nose dropped even more, this is when I heard the prop strike the runway. The aircraft went out of control veering to the left, as it departed the runway the nose gear collapses and digs into the dirt. The forward momentum of the airplane has the tail lifted off the ground before aggressively landing on the mains. the aircraft has come to a full stop, after stopping I paused for 3 seconds and then I contacted Tower and let them know what happened. After contacting Tower, I Opened my door and took off the seat belt, took the headset off and stepped out of the plan. I went out of the aircraft for 30 seconds before going back and turning the ignition off and turning off the master switch. After that I was met by airport ops. After the initial shock and recuperating my thoughts I have found what mistakes I made on this solo and how this should have been avoided. Firstly, there is the initial bounce and when I caught air, I should have pushed into full power and pitched up to have the glare shield on the horizon which allows me to climb and then radio into Tower for a go-around. Definitely do not pitch down like I did and try to save the landing but rather go full power and pitch up for a climb. I was very appreciative of the airport ops and their quick action to make sure that I was safe and getting all the information to see how I didn't land correctly.
1801314: Just below 1,000 feet AGL, ATC directed us to go-around, due to previous aircraft still on the runway. I performed the soft go-around procedure. I called for go-around flaps and the FO selected flaps 2, but the correct flap setting for go-around was flaps 3, as this was a flaps Full approach. I noticed the incorrect flap setting when I saw the airspeed was down in the aircraft's amber 'hook' indication. Normally we would be five knots above the top of this hook, the top of which is Vref. I manually selected a higher airspeed and accelerated before commencing the turn away from the runway. The rest of the go-around and subsequent approach and landing were normal.Lack of recency of experience due to short term leaves of absence may play a role. My FO hadn't flown a lot since returning from a six month hiatus. I also had close to a month off, due to COVID. I feel that I could have reduced my approach speed earlier and thereby increased our spacing. However, we had been assigned 160 knots to a 5 mile final. We complied with that ATC instruction.When I am pilot flying, I brief that a go-around is a successful outcome and encourage my FO to call it out if I don't meet stable approach criteria. I think in the future I will include in my approach briefs which flap setting corresponds to the 'go around flaps' call. This aircraft family uses flaps 3 and flaps full for landing, but 'go-around flaps' is a command to go either from flaps full to flaps three or from flaps three to flaps two. We don't do that many go-arounds, so a quick review might help. Additionally, watching the preceding traffic more closely on TCAS could have prompted an earlier speed reduction and notice to ATC that we were unable to comply with the previous speed assignment. During go-around I inadvertently selected flaps 2 instead of flaps 3 during the flap retraction sequence. The PF noticed and compensated, and we continued with the cleanup and subsequent climb and re-vector back runway for a landing with no other issues.I inadvertently selected single engine go-around flap setting of flaps 2 instead of full flaps to flaps 3 go-around.Continue training go-around procedures in training and being more mentally prepared for a potential go-arounds in the landing phase.
1802052: During our approach briefing, First Officer pointed out that there was an antennae approximately nine miles to the southwest of AVL that is 5,049 feet tall and that Approach Control would leave us high until we were clear of that. While approaching the airport, we were given a descent from 6,000 feet to 5,100 feet. It was during this descent that we received our 'Terrain' GPWS caution alert. We were on vectors at this time due to the First Officer requesting vectors for our RNAV 35 approach. This was done because Center had left us at a high altitude until about 15 miles from AVL and we needed time to descend. Our position at the time of the GPWS caution was approximately 2.5 miles to the southwest of the fix ZICZU. Immediately upon receiving the caution, we notified Approach Control, and added that we were now climbing to 6,000 feet. I then reminded the First Officer that there was a note on our Jeppesen REF plates that says that high rates of descent could result in GPWS alerts (our descent rate was approximately 1,500 FPM). The cautions did not stop until we were at 6,000. Approach Control replied that the Minimum Safe Altitude in that region was 5,100 feet and that we were fine. Upon reaching 6,000, we informed Approach Control that we had AVL in sight. We were cleared for the visual and turned towards the final approach course. Once we were established, we descended down to 4,200 feet for the fix ZICZU and continued the approach. We received no further GPWS alerts.We complied with the GPWS caution directive to 'Pull Up' that we received during our climb to 6,000 feet. Perhaps the northwesterly winds had blown us close enough to the fix AVEBE which is about 13 miles to the southwest of AVL that the terrain database triggered the GPWS alerts. The Minimum Safe Altitude in this region is 6,200 feet. In the future, I could not descend as fast as 1,500 FPM and can be more proactive at requesting a lower altitude from Center well before entering the terminal area.
1802132: It was a routine flight. On approach, the First Officer called for 'Gear Down'. The gear was lowered and showed '3 Green'. Several seconds later, the message 'Steer Fail' appeared. Because of the proximity to the runway and time constraints, a go-around was initiated. Once the gear had been retracted, the message cleared. However, the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) procedure for 'Steer Fail', was accomplished. While this procedure was being completed, ATC asked for the nature of the go-around, fuel on board, and souls on board. The Captain provided this information to ATC and also stated that we are not declaring [an urgent situation] as of yet because we were still troubleshooting the problem. It was later discovered that ATC elected to declare [this situation] for our aircraft (ATC informed us that Airport Fire Dept. is standing by). We informed ATC that our procedure had been completed and that there was a possibility that the problem would reappear when the gear was lowered. We further explained that the procedure indicated that the runway centerline would be maintained but we may have an issue turning off the runway. A second approach was performed (the message returned with the lowering of the gear) and a normal landing was the result. Centerline was maintained via the rudder pedals and differential braking. As tiller steering was attempted, there was no response. The aircraft was brought to a stop on the runway. At this point, the flight crew attempted one ground reset per the Ground Reset Guide. This reset was not successful. Because we are unsure of the ability to negotiate turns (verifying smooth radius turns) the decision was made to have the aircraft towed into the gate by high-speed tug. This was proactively put into work by Dispatch prior to our landing. We were in constant contact with the Fire Crew Chief who relayed pertinent information to the tug crew. The APU was started and the engines were shut down. The gear pins were put into place. Maintenance was on scene as well to verify the aircraft was safe to be towed, and the tow to the gate was started. Communication was maintained with the tug crew and they informed us that all tower communication would be handled by them at this point. The aircraft was successfully towed and parked. Appropriate notifications were made, passengers deplaned via jet bridge, and the aircraft was handed over to Maintenance. During the entire approach, go-around, second approach, landing, and tow to the gate, the passengers were kept informed as much as possible. Both flight attendants were updated throughout the incident and were told that this should be a normal landing with a possible tow to the gate. The flight attendants stated that the passengers remained calm and patient throughout the event.There needs to be a clearer definition of 'Smooth Radius Turns.' Trying to decide what qualifies a 'smooth radius turn' in the midst of this event is somewhat difficult.I was informed well after this incident that the CodeShare Company had asked Dispatch why we had issued a 'Brace' command. I stated that at no such time was a Brace Command issued and I further confirmed with my flight attendants that no Brace Command was heard in the cabin of the aircraft by either Flight Attendant. Passengers were calm and patient throughout the event. Information was presented and updated to the passengers as much as possible.
1802319: Intercepting the unstable Localizer on a 225 vector, approximately 16 nm final, the aircraft started to join the Localizer. The Localizer shifted to the right and the aircraft began a hard right turn to intercept passing of approximately 240 degrees. I instructed the FO to stop the turn and come back to the left toward final approach heading. He did not reply to my direction and did not act. As the aircraft passed approximately 255 degrees, I took command of the aircraft, disconnected the auto-pilot and started a turn back to the Localizer. I was concerned about the numerous aircraft on final for Runway XX. In my turn back to the Localizer I overshot the Localizer and deviated from the assigned 900 meter altitude by approximately 100 meters. I intercepted the Localizer, got back on altitude, and flew an uneventful ILS and normal landing. This all happened unexpectedly. The hard right-hand turn to intercept is unprecedented in my XX years of flying [this type aircraft].Unstable Localizer and Autopilot aggressive turn to intercept. Fatigue affected my flying after taking the aircraftThe current schedules to service this country during Covid leave no extra margin of safety when things like this go wrong. Multi-leg days, with long turns between flights, after crossing X time zones leave little margin of safety. Also, the very long trip extensions for crew members leads to fatigue. I was the PF for the 2nd leg of the night which was a night recovery. At altitude I had briefed the STAR and approach, and once the descent started, we received numerous altitude, heading, and airspeed clearances as the controller was trying to work what appeared to be a fairly large recovery into ZZZZ [Airport]. ATIS reported that simultaneous ILS approaches were being flown to [Runway] XXL as well as [Runway] YY. Approaching ZZZZ, we were being vectored for the ILS Y, Runway XXL and at about 20 miles were cleared 'heading 215, maintain 180 knots to 8 miles, maintain 900 meters until intercepting the Localizer, report established.' We were already configured at flaps 15 with the ILS tuned and the approach checklist complete. The assigned heading provided a comfortable 15 degree cut, but with winds of about 120 at 25 knots at our altitude (overshooting crosswind), and parallel approaches being conducted, with the autopilot still engaged, I was diligently watching the automation. I pressed the APP/LAND tile and initially the aircraft maintained heading, but after a few seconds, it started making some gentle (level) turns left and right. Initially these turns were mild and we even chuckled at what a poor job the AP was doing to maintain heading to intercept. Suddenly, the magnitude of one of the turns to the right increased markedly and the aircraft was in a level turn to the right of approximately 25 degrees angle of bank with the heading coming through approximately 230 degrees. As I spent just a few seconds (no more than 4 or 5 I would say) trying to determine what the autopilot was doing, the CA called out, 'turn left, turn LEFT, I have the airplane' and executed a maneuver that I would describe as similar to a PRM breakout maneuver. He disconnected the AP, added power, and reversed our turn, climbing and accelerating in the process. The maneuver was aggressive enough that I thought it possible the CA had SA to something that I was missing since I had already started to reach for the heading selector in order to get the plane to level its wings and come back to the left (note: things were happening very quickly now and I did not verbalize this FMC input since I would have just been trying to talk over the CA telling me to turn left even though the airplane did start to shallow its turn to the right once I pulled the selector). I verbalized 'you have the controls' and monitored his inputs. As former fighter pilots, the CA and I both have fairly wide comfort zones and although the maneuver was fairly aggressive, I was still comfortable with the aircraft's attitude and remained quiet as I monitored the aircraft's flight path. I did not want to add to the confusion of the moment by asking questions or saying anything unnecessary since the CA was very purposeful in his maneuver. Now things became quite busy because in addition to receiving a 'bank angle' audible warning due to our steep turn to the left, the approach Controller began talking to us rapidly. He made several transmissions and told us repeatedly that he had us on a heading that was not going to intercept the Localizer and that we were above our assigned altitude and asked what we were doing. I replied that we were still below the glidepath at approximately 930 meters, and maneuvering to intercept the Localizer. After a few more moments the CA stabilized the aircraft's attitude, I selected FMS speeds (since we had accelerated to approximately 210 knots and needed to slow back to 180 knots), and he began a turn back to the right to intercept the Localizer. The CA re-armed the approach (but never re-engaged the AP), slowed to the assigned speed, returned to the assigned altitude, and leveled the wings on an appropriate intercept heading. The FD provided what appeared to be valid guidance to shoot the rest of the approach. The aircraft was configured and stable before glide-slope intercept and the remainder of the approach proceeded normally with me remaining in my role as PM.We went from conducting a routine controlled approach, to one where I think we had widely differing perceptions of what was actually occurring in the space of literally about 4 or 5 seconds. This rapid breakdown of CRM resulted in actions that were perhaps more aggressive than they needed to be, and a deviation from the ATC clearance. I would actually say there were two separate events. The first being the aircraft's unexpected and overly aggressive turn to the right to capture the Localizer for ILS Runway XXL, and the second being our response to it. The first I would potentially attribute to a software issue, a problem with the ILS tune, or some sort of RF interference. As far as the second I would suggest the following, 1) Even though I did not feel fatigued during the approach, it was at the end of a long day and it's possible I underestimated my level of fatigue. That said, I did have some coffee prior to Beginning of Daylight (BOD) for this reason and, I felt like the CA and I were both alert and engaged and don't feel like my response to the aircraft was unacceptably slow or inappropriate. 2)The CA believed that the intercept angle was excessive (he referenced 45 degrees during our debrief) and that based on his prior experiences, there was no way the airplane was going to be able to capture the Localizer. Since I had not experienced the automation act in the manner it did during our approach, I was perhaps more comfortable than I should have been with the AP's ability to capture the Localizer, even with the admittedly substantial intercept angle that we had before the CA took the controls. 3) The CA stated during the debrief that he thought we had already flown through the Localizer, and that he was therefore worried about a lack of separation from the traffic that was flying the ILS to Runway XX, to our right. I did not perceive that we had flown through the Localizer for the following reasons: a) We were in a phase of flight where we both (certainly I was) monitoring the raw Localizer data in anticipation of Localizer capture, and neither of us ever called 'Localizer alive'. I felt like I was hawking this for the reasons listed above (overshooting crosswind and proximity to other landing traffic). b) The AP commanded a turn to the right, which in my mind it would have only done if it were trying to intercept the Localizer from the left. c) When ATC contacted us, it was to say that we were not on an intercept heading. He did not indicate that we had flown through the Localizer or were encroaching on the protected airspace between the approach corridors for the active runways. He never issued a vector to East which is likely what he would have done had he perceived there to be a risk of loss of separation. d) When we finally got the situation under control, the aircraft intercepted the Localizer from the left.Again, this entire narrative took place in what I suspect was less than a minute. Between the uncommanded turn to the right and the CA taking the controls, maybe 5 seconds passed. That said, I could have acted sooner and certainly should have verbalized when I reached for the heading selector to stabilize the heading, since that may have precluded the CA from taking the controls and executing the 'escape' maneuver. I think in the CA's mind, we were probably already past the point where that was going to mitigate our situation since he perceived that we had already crossed the Localizer, but it might have helped. I wish the CA would have verbalized why he was maneuvering as aggressively as he was. I thought that perhaps he saw an impending collision that I did not have SA of, and so I stayed quiet for longer than I should have before I started to rebuild the picture and work to develop a CRM. Ultimately, he was well within his authority to act in the manner he did and fully adhered to the company's three step intervention process. This was a tough one for me to analyze and I welcome any feedback you might have.

1802626: Aircraft X was IFR and requested the RNAV [Runway] 35 approach into CVO airport. I cleared them for the approach and advised them of traffic - multiple targets in the vicinity of CVO indicating 040 and below. There were probably about 10 VFR targets in the vicinity of CVO, all squawking 1200 not receiving ATC services. Several of the VFR targets were maneuvering near the IAFs for approaches into EUG Runways 16R and 16L, which could have easily caused more problems for arrivals into EUG if they had come then. I switched Aircraft X to advisory frequency at least 10 NM south of the airport. My focus then switched to other traffic I was working. After a few minutes, Aircraft X returned to my frequency to report that they were flying west to avoid traffic. They were not flying the published missed approach due to multiple other aircraft in that path. I also had to immediately issue a traffic alert to other traffic near them. They were flying on an IFR plan and maneuvering on their own below the MVA to avoid multiple other aircraft. Once they were above the MVA I vectored them further away from traffic.From what I could tell, there was not any orderly flow of the VFR traffic at CVO.CVO airport needs to have an air traffic control tower. There is too much VFR aircraft flying disorderly on their own in that vicinity, many of them student pilots and foreign, but also mixed with air taxis and jets, as well as regular aerobatic activity. This is just one example of pilots not being able to sequence themselves and pilots needing to take evasive action.Also, EUG should be upgraded to a Class C in order to require VFR aircraft flying at dangerous altitudes in the approach path of EUG to talk to ATC.
1803042: Conducting flight training at ZZZ. There was a near miss involving myself and another plane on final.Prior to the incident, radio traffic around ZZZ became distracting for both my student and I while we were practicing steep turns, so I turned the volume down to where I could still hear the other traffic, but could focus on my lesson.Conducting left traffic Runway XX, on the takeoff roll, I instructed my student to apply take off power, and climb out at 85 kts once gear was retracted and propeller set to 2500 RPM. We turned left crosswind 500 AGL, then left downwind for [Runway] XX. Proper radio calls were made on left crosswind and left downwind. Visually scanning the area, I did not see any other traffic. Midfield downwind landing gear was set to the down position, green gear light verified. Once abeam the numbers [Runway] 21, power was reduced to 2100 RPM, flaps 10 degrees, and 75 kts established. 45 degrees off our landing point, left base radio call was established, then left base was turned, and 20 degrees of flaps established. Final call and turn was made, 30 degrees flaps and a normal landing.Once parked and shut down, a gentleman walked briskly up to my plane and informed me that we had just turned final 'a quarter mile in front of him'. He also explained he heard my radio calls, and was responding. I had not heard him so I inspected my volume knob for com 1, finding it turned down too far to have heard him. 1803068: Unremarkable landing on centerline, when applying brakes aircraft drifted right, unable to correct drift. Exited runway at low speed. Struck embankment with horizontal stabilizer when turning aircraft back to runway. Performed normal shut down.
1803093: I departed ZZZ, for a VFR flight to ZZZ1. The estimated flight time was one hour and ten minutes. The aircraft had been at ZZZ since Month 2021 for some touch up paint work. The fuel on board the aircraft was 28 gallons, as indicated by the installed JPI Instruments 450 fuel management computer, installed in the aircraft two years previously. Prior to this flight, I had on numerous occasions verified the accuracy and calibration of the JPI by comparing its data to actual fuel used. This occurred over about 100 hours or more of flight time. When connected to a GPS source the JPI also provides two parameters in addition to total fuel used, and fuel remaining. Mine is connected to a Garmin 430W. They are, fuel needed for the remainder of the trip and fuel remaining at the end of the trip. This is updated on a minute to minute basis. The estimated fuel burn was not more than 14 gallons, leaving a 14 gallon reserve, well within VFR flight requirements. During the flight, I continually monitored the fuel usage and the fuel remaining parameter never changed from 13 gallons. About to enter the downwind leg for Runway XX, at ZZZ1, the engine abruptly stopped. I made a successful off airport landing, which caused no injuries and minor damage to the aircraft, per the NTSB. On landing, the JPI indicated 12.9 gallons remaining.
1803113: I was conducting instrument flight with a student flying a VOR approach circle to land. We were circling to land and making all appropriate radio calls for the circle. Both my student and I visually cleared the runway before touchdown. We were planning on doing a touch and go. After visually checking the runway and making two final calls, we touched down on the runway to conduct a touch and go. On the rollout when the student was getting ready to add full power, we saw an aircraft coming right towards us on their takeoff roll opposite direction down the runway. I immediately took controls from my student and got us off at the intersecting runway. The other aircraft realized what was happening and stopped as well. I made several attempts to contact the other aircraft with no response. We can only surmise that this aircraft rolled onto the runway while we were on a very short final leg and initiated a takeoff roll without checking to see if the area was clear, making a single radio call, or checking to see what other traffic was doing. The winds were heavily favoring the runway we landed on and there were several other aircraft using the same runway we were. I feel as though that there is nothing else that I could have done to prevent this other pilot from entering a runway and taking off opposite direction right into another aircraft.
1803852: Traffic was busy, there were more than 5 planes in the pattern when approach handed us off to tower. The approach phase was uneventful, the incident mentioned occurred after our landing. Spacing got really tight between us and a Seminole before we exited the first taxiway from the runway, I turned around and saw a Seminole in ground effect about to land maybe 600 feet or so away from us before we got a chance to exit the runway and join the taxiway. This runway incursion should have never happened. Had tower asked us to slow down and put the faster Seminole in front of us, had the pilot for the Seminole performed a go around, or even if tower had cancelled their landing clearance. Had I taken even 5-10 more seconds to exit the runway I believe that plane would have hit me.
1804019: I was acting as a flight instructor on board Aircraft X, a Cessna 172S on a local IFR flight practicing approaches. My student is a Certified Flight Instructor (CFI) candidate who was gaining instrument currency and proficiency. We began with an ILS approach at ZZZ1 with my student flying the aircraft and me handling ATC communications to reduce his workload in the hard IMC conditions. We crossed a cold front while receiving vectors for the ILS approach where we encountered light to moderate turbulence and precipitation. We completed the ILS approach without incident and proceeded to the VOR for the VOR-A approach into ZZZ, planning to complete a Low Approach Only. We experienced severe turbulence which forced the autopilot (GFC700) to disconnect and I took the controls of the aircraft and requested deviations to the north as necessary to track clear of the progressing cold front. Once we got into smoother air, I gave my student the flight controls and we proceeded direct ZZZ2 [VOR] for a procedure turn. Our plan was to complete the VOR-A approach and then receive radar vectors for the RNAV 01 at ZZZ. My student had proclaimed that he wanted to avoid going back through the cold front while getting vectored for the RNAV 01 approach and suggested we circle to land at ZZZ and cancel the IFR flight plan. When my student suggested this, we had passed the Final Approach Fix inbound and began a descent to the Minimum Descent Altitude and were switched over to advisory frequency. I switched frequencies back to Approach to tell them our intentions to try and circle to land since they were expecting us to go missed on the practice approach. When I told ATC of our intentions, they replied in the affirmative and added 'Aircraft X, low altitude alert, check altitude immediately, altitude indicates 1,800.' I replied the altitude checks and requested an altimeter setting. ATC replied with an altimeter setting of 29.58 and we had a setting of 29.67 set in. I figured this was why they gave us the low altitude alert but then quickly realized that the Minimum Descent Altitude for the segment of the approach we were on was 2,020 feet and we were at 1,720 feet with the new altimeter setting. I informed my student to return to 2,020 feet and we continued on the approach without issue and proceeded with the missed approach with vectors to the RNAV01 at ZZZ. During the missed approach, I was surprised at myself that I did not catch that the student had descended below the Minimum Descent Altitude and I assessed why that had happened during a period of smooth flight and during the post flight discussion with my student. During the lead up to the approach, the encounter with the severe turbulence had shaken both me and my student. We also had a back seat passenger who was an instrument student who had never been in IMC before. I was concerned with the safety of my student and the back seat student and began thinking about the circle to land approach and how we would request vectors for the RNAV Approach if we were unable to circle to land in order to stay away from the front line. I had determined from the weather when we departed ZZZ that circling for the runway at ZZZ would have been nearly impossible with the current ceilings. I told my student this and informed him we would need to execute the RNAV Approach in order to make it back into the airport.The workload at the moment was very high and the effects of the turbulence certainly could have impaired multitasking skills for both my student and I. When we began the descent on the approach, we left 3,000 feet for 2,020 feet which is the Minimum Descent Altitude until a fix which then the Minimum Descent Altitude decreases to 1,760 feet. My student did not reset the altitude select when we ran our Final Approach Fix check and the altitude select remained at 3,000 feet. Additionally, when I recognized we were below the published Minimum Descent Altitude, I should have instructed my student to execute the missed approach as 91.175(E)(1)(i) states, rather than just climbing back up to the Minimum Descent Altitude.This flight was also my third flight in hard IMC this day, and this VOR approach was my 8th approach in IMC in a span of 6 hours. I am an experienced Flight Instructor with over 45 hours in actual instrument conditions and over 150 approach logged, but never before had I completed so many IMC flights in such a time span with the challenging conditions of the frontal passage. My self-assessment prior to this flight determined I was able to complete the flight successfully with good quality of instruction to the student, but the extraordinary conditions we experienced during the flight quickly eroded that ability for me, in addition to the highly divided workload situation we found ourselves in while inbound on the VOR Approach which led to the descent below Minimum Descent Altitude and failure to execute the missed approach immediately after. I think also a more comprehensive briefing of the approach would have aided in my student's short term memory of the initial difference of Minimum Descent Altitude. Even though I briefed the Minimum Descent Altitudes, I do not think they were retained due to the stress and workload of the situation. If this event were to occur again, I would better instruct my student to execute the missed approach rather than working to reclaim the missed Minimum Descent Altitude. The aircraft had 3 people on board for a local approaches flight in IMC conditions in Aircraft. This flight took place while a stationary front was passing through the area. This caused for almost constant moderate turbulence at times during the flight close to the frontal passage. The flight started with an ILS approach into ZZZ1. After the ILS approach we were vectored to go to the ZZZ2 VOR . Along the way, we had to deviate twice for turbulence. This, as well as IMC conditions, was causing a good amount of sensory overload for myself and the flight instructor with me. At times during the flight the autopilot was being used, but at one point, the amount of turbulence actually caused the autopilot to disengage. Because of this, at the time of the deviation, I was hand flying the aircraft while the other pilot was loading the VOR Approach. When we proceeded inbound on the approach, there is a step down to a minimum of 2,020 feet until an 8 DME fix. Then the minimum goes lower to 1,760 feet. With the sensory overload that both I and the other pilot were experiencing during the IMC flight, we ended up descending below the altitude minimum below the fix. ATC had not updated our altimeter setting in a decent amount of time. We were called by ATC letting us know for a low altitude and to immediately recover. They gave us an updated altimeter and our altitude after the correction showed it being right at the approach total minimum. Instead of executing an immediate missed approach we climbed back up to 2020 feet then re-descended to the 1,760 minimums. By doing this we unfortunately broke 14 CFR 91.175 (c) 1, 3 and (e) 1. The proper action would have been to either, not conduct the flight in the first place or, to immediately execute the missed approach once realizing the descent below the step down. We also could have stopped the flight after the ILS approach into ZZZ1. The rest of the flight utilized great CRM, but during this approach, a better action to even ask as the approach started would have been to double check the approach and its minimums including each step down.
1804585: After an Instrument Proficiency Check and Biennial Flight Review with the aircraft owner the last landing of the day was proceeding normally with the owner/operator pilot-flying. There was a crosswind on final approach but nothing abnormal. As the aircraft was entering the flare and about 5 feet above the runway (with power at idle, on centerline, at 75 knots) the aircraft nose suddenly slewed about 45 degrees left immediately taking the aircraft off the runway and over the grass. The pilot initiated a go-around with full power. The aircraft touched down on the grass and rolled straight for several hundred feet before the right wing settled to the ground and the aircraft rotated 90 degrees right and stopped.As instructor I did call for a go-around as directional control seemed lost, but that call was simultaneous with the pilot initiating a go-around. I cannot explain the initial sudden yawing moment. I speculate that the plane was hit with a gust during the flare and there was inadequate energy, even with full power, to keep the plane from contacting the grass. The attempt to prevent the plane from settling onto the grass caused a nose high attitude, along with full flaps, probably created excessive drag preventing acceleration.The METAR at the time showed wind 30009KT The 3 METARS before the incident showed wind 24011G17KT to 28009G14KT. The landing METAR was well within the Demonstrated Cross Wind for a Cirrus SR-22, but perhaps unexpected gusts were starting as we landed.There were no injuries but the airport was closed for several hours. Just prior to touch down on Runway 20 a wind gust pushed the airplane extremely hard to the left, I initiated a go around but was unable to climb and regain control. I pulled power back and landed in a grass area. The airplane slid and the right landing gear dug in to the ground and separated from the airplane. The airplane came to a stop in the grass. There were no injuries. I was flying with a CFI at the time and had just completed a Biennial Flight Review and an Instrument Proficiency Check and everything had gone fine, the day was done and were landing at my home airport. I feel the cause was a combination of a strong wind gust and wind shear.
1804752: MYF RNAV28R approach, circle to land 23. On final approach between fixes NESTY and PENNY aircraft descended to 2,000 feet prior to 2,500, the descent minimum at PENNY. MYF tower controller issued altitude alert and I corrected back to 2,500 feet. Continued approach and airport was visual, above minimums.Circled to 23, tower was trying to clear previous arrived aircraft off runway and I had to execute a missed approach. Tower stated to execute missed approach procedures. I looked at chart and it was to fly straight to 3,000. Raised gear and flaps and climbed to 3,000 feet. At 1,000 feet I engaged autopilot and contacted approach on a new frequency. Autopilot was having the aircraft descend and I disengaged autopilot and it was seemed to be still engaged and I struggled with controls to climb again. Departure control commanded that I climb to 3,000 and I stated that I seemed to be having trim issues as I was fighting to climb. I continued to the headings that were issued by Approach and returned for another approach without further incident. Suggest not using the autopilot until all desired settings are set, and review of missed approach procedures for circling approaches since they are not the same as depicted on the missed approach plate.
1804760: We were flying back to ZZZ on a clear dark night, arriving on day four. It was my leg (Captain), PF (Pilot Flying). About 20 miles out we were given a vector to ZZZZZ which is about 6 miles south of ZZZZZ1, the final approach fix for runway XXL. The controller asked us to keep our speed up to 210 or better until final as she had other inbound aircraft that she was sequencing in. We switched to green needles and sequenced the approach according to our normal procedures. When we were about 10 miles from ZZZZZ, approximately abeam ZZZZZ1, we called the field in sight. The controller gave us a heading of 080, cleared us for the approach and switched us to tower. She noted that the other aircraft would be following us and to keep 170 or better to final. At this point we were about 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 at about 90 degrees intercept. The heading the controller gave us would take us inside the final approach fix before we intercepted the final bearing. Seeing this, the FO (First Officer) noted that we had not begun our decent to final approach fix altitude yet. I called for the descent, flaps 20 as we slowed to final approach speed. As PF, I noted that the flight guidance would not give us a good intercept because the intercept was too great. At this moment, the autopilot began the turn to final too soon. I turned off the auto pilot and began hand flying. As we began the turn to final I called for flaps 30, and then flaps 45 as we neared the final bearing. As we were completing the turn, the FO (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were still high and that we should increase our rate of decent, we were about 2000 MSL, I steepened our decent and he selected 1000 fpm as we rolled out. I called for and we completed the landing checklist. Tower came up and checked us in. We had not called at the FAP (Final Approach Path) as we were busy flying. At this point, we were about 4 miles from the end of the runway at about 1800 MSL. The tower gave us landing clearance and noted that we were low as the PF I called for us to stop our decent, and I leveled the aircraft at about 1500 MSL. I noted that I had not completed the turn correctly and we were not quite on final bearing. I corrected and called for zero VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) and adjusted to get on final. The FO complied and we continued inbound. At about 3 miles from the runway on final bearing our GPWS alarm went off, PULL UP. As PF, I called for a climb and began a climb at about 5 degrees nose up. As we began our climb, the GPWS alarm went off again, saying PULL UP, I increased the climb, and we climbed about 200ft, as we were very close to glideslope. I was about to call for a missed approach, when I noted that the climb had put us on glideslope, and the PAPI's confirmed us on glideslope. Seeing this, I reestablished our decent and the FO called stabilized at about 3 miles. We landed normally, completed our checklists and shut down the aircraft in accordance with our normal procedures. We have procedures and training guidance that should have prevented this. In this case, there were several errors I made on this approach. As PF, I should not have accepted the vector inside the final approach fix with such a large intercept heading. As Captain, I knew that the flight guidance would be unable to make the turn correctly and we would need more room to make the turn to final. I should have asked to continue our course and give the controller other options. This likely would have prevented the whole series of errors. I should have started my decent to FAF altitude sooner. We were at 3,000 feet, 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 as we turned, and I delayed our decent to 2,400 ft. for several seconds as I turned off the flight guidance and began the turn. If we had been at 2,400 MSL we would not have required a large decent in the turn to final. When the tower checked us in at 4 miles and noted that we were low, I should have called for and established a climb back to glideslope instead of just leveling out. We were very close to glideslope and we should have re-intercepted it first. When the GPWS alarm went off, I should have immediately called for a Missed Approach. We were low (hence the alarm) and there is no space or time for altitude errors on final. Any delay calling for a Missed Approach puts safety at risk. Finally, there was probably some 'get-home-itis' in our minds as we were flying. Arriving late at night, at home field on day four, we were tired and wanted the trip to be over. Going missed would have delayed our landing. Also, we were also trying to satisfy the controller who was sequencing us in front of another aircraft. We needed to focus on our flight, not her decisions or problems.
1805063: First Officer, Pilot Monitoring. Captain, Pilot Flying. 3,000 feet MSL inbound to AWLEE 210 KIAS or greater assigned. Cleared for a visual approach approximately 5 miles from AWLEE 170 or greater to 5 mile final assigned. Continue on heading, allow spacing for visual approach at 210 KIAS. Abeam CRDNL given 080 heading and still cleared for visual and switched to Tower. 080 heading gave a perpendicular intercept course for final. Captain armed approach mode. Aircraft began an early turn to final simultaneously the Captain input a command that caused the plane to enter into pitch mode. I called out pitch mode and he turned autopilot off. I advised the Captain that he needed to begin a descent since we were inside the final approach fix and were 600 feet high. I entered vertical speed mode and put in a thousand ft per min rate of descent and dialed in a 45 degree intercept into the heading. Captain began slowing down and called for gear down, flaps 30, and flaps 45 at appropriate speeds I called for level off when I realized we were at 1,500 feet MSL (acceleration altitude). Simultaneously we received a call from Tower advising us that we were low for our area. I informed Tower that we were leveling and continuing our visual approach. At this point I went outside the cockpit and became focused on looking for towers that would pose a danger to our flight. I didn't recognize any threats. I thought that we could maintain this altitude and intercept the glideslope without issue. We then received a call of terrain. I said we needed to climb. No climb was initiated. We then received the audio alert of woop woop terrain. Pull up. At this point I stated we needed to climb. I began pulling back pressure and a climb was initiated. The audible signals ceased and we continued to intercept the glide slope. Once established on glide slope and on course I called out 1,000 feet stabilized and we completed the approach to a landing. As soon as we were at 1,500 MSL I should have called for a go around. I knew the Captain was disoriented and was confident that I could act as a back stop to get him onto final. I didn't call for a go around after we stopped getting the audible warnings because we were at that point established within the safe and standard parameters of the approach. However, a go-around may have been the pertinent thing to do to increase everyone's situational awareness.
1805215: While flying practice ILS XX into ZZZ I experienced a loss of throttle control. This occurred when leveling off at 5,500 while being radar vectored to final approach course just outside of ZZZZZ waypoint. I requested priority handing with Approach Control and clearance given to land Runway XX. The engine RPM remained full power when throttle was reduced. I climbed to gain altitude and keep RPM below redline. Once at safe altitude and able to reach airport we begun to lean mixture to reduce RPM. Once runway was assured and at about 200 feet AGL we pull mixture full off and preformed an engine out landing to Runway XX. Was able to clear the runway and depart the plane. Safety pilot Mr. X was the only other person aboard the plane.
1805438: Initially reported to Tower my position and I was cleared to enter the right downwind.
