Adjacent to the Class D boundary common with the Class D airspace boundary with the adjacent airport, I was given a traffic advisory of a small aircraft inbound. I had that aircraft in sight and reported so. I was then instructed to 'Turn left and follow that traffic' I refused the left turn as that would have taken me into the adjacent airport Class D, so reported 'negative left turn, I am turning right and following the [small aircraft]'. When approaching there were three planes on the right downwind for the runway. Aircraft Y who was cleared to land short approach with a long landing, the small aircraft I was following and myself who was cleared to land number 3.Shortly after that, something caught my eye in my right peripheral vision. As I scanned it was an airplane broadside to me, northerly heading, at the same altitude as me, in a slight climb. As a collision was extremely possible, I took evasive action by chopping power and nosed over going negative G to miss the aircraft. I contacted the Tower of who was that airplane and why was he in my vicinity and not called for traffic. Controller went into meltdown about who was who and who was where. By this time the small aircraft I was following had landed. I did not follow the previously issued landing clearance to land number 3 behind the small aircraft, but rather followed this mystery plane which was finally identified as an X type plane who had been in the left closed traffic pattern doing touch and goes. Apparently, this plane made a right pattern after takeoff and went right into me on the right downwind. Controller and any supervisors should be watching that aircraft comply with the proper traffic patterns, and if there is a deviation, notify other aircraft that such non-compliance could create a traffic conflict. Due to a staffing shortage, the other two controllers in the cab were both Supervisors, which one was on Operational Supervisor and the other on Ground Control. [This was] an abnormal configuration at this time of day. Aircraft Y had been in the pattern with minimal traffic before I took the local position. Aircraft A reported inbound from the northwest. Aircraft A seemed unfamiliar and I provided him extra assistance. When Aircraft X checked on, inbound from the northwest, I had him follow Aircraft A as I preferred not to give Aircraft A more instructions than I deemed he could handle. Aircraft Z checked on inbound from the south. TRACON called with a direct for Aircraft B. I instructed Aircraft Y to extend climb straight out to a point and make right traffic to avoid Aircraft B's expected left downwind entry at a high rate of speed.The Supervisor stated that Aircraft C was inbound from the east for a hospital. I asked if Aircraft C was coordinated by TRACON or did I miss the check in. The Supervisor said TRACON had coordinated it. The Supervisor and Ground Control continued to debate with each other the intention of Aircraft C, the background noise can be heard in the background. Traffic on final needed to extend downwind, and thus, created a problem with Aircraft C's trajectory to cross the runway final. I asked the Supervisor to find out Aircraft C's intentions. Aircraft X reported a near mid-air collision with a small aircraft which was not the correct aircraft. This prompted me to verify Aircraft Z's position. Aircraft Z confirmed his position. Aircraft X mistook Aircraft Y, as Aircraft Z. It was at this time that I realized Aircraft Y had turned in front of Aircraft X. I allowed my attention to be drawn away from my pattern. I appreciate other controllers/ supervisors willing to provide assistance, but because all the information was not known it added another distraction to the operation.Aircraft C ended up entering the airspace without coordination. Aircraft C contacted MRI as he exited MRI airspace. Do not expect aircraft to fly the left and right downwind the same. Extend aircraft further if necessary. Tell aircraft to extend further out even if it extends the pattern. Do not allow others in the cab to distract you. Other controllers and supervisors' assistance is needed in the cab and appreciated. If, however, you do not have all the known information, before distracting the local controller, confirm with the appropriate facility/ sector the intentions of all aircraft.
1805744: [We were] cleared for the visual approach. Pilot in Command hand flew the visual approach. Switched to Tower and was cleared to land. During the descent to land Pilot in Command got too low. Second in Command informed Pilot in Command to climb as aircraft was too low and almost hit terrain Pilot in Command said he was good, Second in Command advised Pilot in Command to immediately climb. Pilot in Command was reluctant to climb. Tower informed us that we were too low for that sector of the approach and to Immediately climb. Pilot in Command climbed back up to 3,100 feet from 2,000 feet, then landed normally. Pilot in Command lost situational awareness during a visual approach. Pilot in Command initially did not react and did not listen to advice from Second in Command that the aircraft was too low on the Approach. It was not until the ATC Tower Controller told crew to immediately climb to 3,100 feet, did the Pilot in Command react and then climb back up to 3,100 feet. Suggest that the company discusses and better trains flight crews in performing visual approaches at day and night and to somehow incorporate improved Crew Resource Management Training so that if a Second in Command tells the Pilot in Command to climb or descend Immediately, he or she will listen and react immediately, and then ask questions later when the risk factor has been mitigated.
1805918: I was training on Local Control and Aircraft X was switched to me from Approach. As soon as Aircraft X checked in, I issued traffic 11 o'clock 2 miles northwest bound 2,700 feet climbing to 3,300 feet. I then called over to Approach and informed them I was climbing the IFR Aircraft X to 3,300 feet. Aircraft X said how that's nice of them they are going underneath. The other aircraft had climbed to 3,000 feet and Aircraft X was leaving 3100 feet. I'm not too knowledgeable on getting new procedures, but something where planes don't cross [over] final Approach fix without talking to Approach or the Tower.
1805938: The lead Flight Attendant was so uptight with a passenger not complying with the Mask policies, [Flight Attendant] thought it was prudent to chime the cockpit during landing rollout and advise the flight crew to notify a Supervisor to meet the aircraft. This was a direct violation of sterile cockpit procedures. Because flight crews repeatedly experience chimes from the cabin while in simulator training, they are most associated with fire or critical aircraft issues. This is never a good time to chime the cockpit unless it is an emergency. Especially for a mask compliance issue.Relaxed emphasis from Leadership on the tattling on passengers for improper use of masks (never saw this type of behavior from FA when it came to early seat-belt releases. Reissued sterile cockpit etiquette with a bulletin on scenario that are and are not acceptable for chiming the cockpit during landing rollout.
1806166: While descending into ZZZ we were given a vector to the right of the arrival. Later, we were given direct ZZZ1 VOR. The First Officer, and pilot flying put ZZZ in the FMS and executed the change. I thought I saw him select LNAV, but I began looking at the approach plate to review our arrival. A minute later I noticed we were still in heading. I immediately told him to turn to ZZZ1 VOR and select LNAV. ATC contacted us at that time and gave us direct ZZZ1 again. I told them we were in the turn.This was both our first flight in the 737 Max and we were a little distracted at some of the newness of the aircraft. Attention to flying the airplane when given a clearance even while Pilot monitoring is necessary at all phases of flying airplanes.
1806517: While on the ENDEE 6 Arrival to MDW we encountered a near midair collision and the following is a narrative of that event. Time stamps are from 'Flightaware' app and may not be 100% accurate. I added these to recreate the event to the best of my knowledge.I was the Pilot Flying on this leg. At about XX:26Z ATC began to vector us off the arrival for spacing. During these vectors we were cleared to descend to lower altitudes. I had even made the comment jokingly that we were being 'over-controlled' by ATC after several heading, altitude and speed changes. At approximately XX:45Z we were cleared to descend to 5000 feet. Our flight path at the time was approximately over top of Morris Muni airport (C09) about 6.6 miles southwest of STKNY on the arrival. Crossing altitude at STKNY is published is 6000 feet. We were then cleared direct to ALQUE for the ILS 4R at MDW. While still level at 5000 feet at approximately XX:47Z we had a TCAS TA (solid amber) showing an aircraft in front of us and +100 feet above our altitude. I do not remember the scale set at the time on my navigation display but it was very 'close'. This was this first time we had seen a Traffic Advisory of any kind on the display (no open white diamond) and had not been advised of traffic from ATC. One second later ATC told us we had 'glider traffic' ahead and to 'deviate as necessary' to avoid the traffic. I immediately began a right hand descending turn. About two seconds later we received a Resolution Advisory RA to descend and the First Officer told ATC we were responding to an RA. At about 4500 feet, I saw the glider slightly higher and to our left. Once clear of the conflict, ATC cleared us to descend to 4000 feet and stated he was not in contact with the glider and asked if it was clear of clouds. ATC warned aircraft behind us on the arrival about the glider and it's altitude. We estimated the distance from the glider was 150-200 feet as it passed to our left. The event happened in the proximity of Channahon, IL Glider Club (IL59) south of STKNY on the arrival.The takeaway from this event:The TCAS did not operate as we would expect in time regarding a TA caution providing 40 seconds warning and an RA providing 25 seconds warning. It's hard to tell if the glider had just turned on its transponder or if the slow speed of the glider had an impact on our TCAS. The glider was in Class E airspace and outside the 30 mile equipment requirement (transponder) from the ORD Class B. What rules apply to gliders here, to me, is unknown to be honest.ATC had vectored us off the arrival and was assigning altitudes lower than published crossing restrictions by 1000 feet (5000 feet abeam STKNY).Vectors took us almost directly over a glider airpark with no warning about that on any chart we would ever use readily available. Some warning symbology or quick access information would assist considering the low altitudes we fly over these areas.In hindsight, I would have made clear to ATC we experienced a near mid air collision in that language as described in our FOM.
1807279: Since Typhoon Yutu in Saipan, the PAPI lights have been out of service. After advising the company last year, the Jepp chart was finally changed. However, it now says there are VASI instead of PAPI (but there is no visual guidance). After I made several queries with SPN ATC, they said there is no plan to install any visual guidance lights (PAPI or VASI) on Runway 07. There is a plan to replace the PAPI for Runway 25.
1807324: Night VFR RNAV Y XXR approach. Approaching FAF ZZZ tower advised us of Cessna traffic on downwind turning base for short parallel runway XXL. Traffic in sight. As we passed our FAF, fully configured and stable we saw the Cessna pointing right at us on base and both remarked 'I hope they don't overshoot'. At approximately 800 feet AGL the Cessna was still pointing at us and I could see they were clearly going to overshoot slightly above us as they turned to final. I felt it was way too close and pushed over slightly as I estimated them to be no more than 100-200 feet above us as they crossed right over us and slightly behind. As our approach was now unstable in my estimation I executed an uneventful go-around. We advised tower of the close pass. We returned for a second, uneventful approach and landing to XXR. I called tower controller after landing and he said he would contact the Cessna pilot and talk to him about the incident. Cessna not keeping us in sight and possibly lining up on incorrect runway. Light VFR traffic maintaining better situational awareness with a large air carrier with approximately XXX people on board and all landing lights, fully configured on final approach.
1807543: On the RNAV Visual 31 L between fixes WEMIR and CEKMA, SOCAL Approach witnessed a target (aircraft he was not talking to) pop up that was a threat to us. He instructed us to stop descent immediately, the First Officer did a great job of arresting the descent, then Approach told us to immediately climb as TCAS instructed us to descend. We followed TCAS and saw the single-engine turboprop pass over us by about 400 feet and in front of us by about one-half mile. The FO re-established us on the approach and we landed without incident.The beautiful weather in Palm Springs and general aviation aircraft not talking to ATC was THE factor in this TCAS RA. ALWAYS follow TCAS.
1808423: I departed with one passenger to ZZZ on an IFR flight plan. The flight was uneventful until on a 5-mile final when I heard the Tower clear a 'Heavy' cargo plane to take the runway for departure. As we got closer to the runway, we noticed that the heavy cargo plane was just getting off the runway as we were on short final. With traffic behind us in the pattern, I continued the approach opting to land slightly below the glideslope on the first third of the runway so as to avoid any potential wake turbulence put off by the departing aircraft beyond its rotation point. While in the landing phase of flight, approximately 1' off the ground and near stall speed for a normal landing, we encountered sudden turbulence that caused the plane to destabilize resulting in a brief touchdown followed by a balloon and a subsequent stall that caused the aircraft to bounce on the runway. As I saw we were losing directional control, I added full power to initiate the go-around maneuver, regained stability, and completed a left traffic pattern. We came in shortly after another Cirrus on short final and had a normal smooth landing. It was not until after taxiing to [FBO] and performing engine shutdown that I noticed the tips of the props were frayed as the obvious result of a prop strike on our initial attempt.It is my opinion that the cause of the turbulence encountered on the runway was the jet blast from the departing heavy jet rather than wake turbulence as we landed well before its point of rotation. While I do not have a copy of the Tower's audio, I do not recall any warnings from the Tower. Apparently, the 'heavy' jet took an extended amount of time to take the runway after being cleared and departed less than a minute before our touchdown. Since we could not see the plane delay taking the runway from a distance due to haze, the Tower should have warned us to avoid wake turbulence and jet blast during our approach. This would likely have prompted a decision to break off our approach at a safe altitude to allow the jet blast to dissipate, and follow trailing traffic to an uneventful landing.At 120 kts. approach speed, our ETA to land on a 5-mile final was approximately 2.5 minutes. Had the Tower held the 'heavy' cargo jet for the additional few minutes, substantial loss of property and the potential for loss of life could have been avoided. In hindsight, as PIC I could have made the decision to break off on short-final and abort the landing when I noticed the heavy cargo plane had departed so shortly before we were to land. I trusted the Tower to provide safe and adequate separation for our arrival and it could have cost us a lot more than a prop strike. I will not make that mistake again.
1808443: Called landing intentions on CTAF frequency on approach to airport and prior to entering traffic pattern. No other traffic heard. On downwind leg, observed another aircraft nearby flying approximately same heading but heard nothing on radio. I called my position and intentions on my radio but heard no response. I watched other aircraft continue on course and I landed after flying base and final legs of the pattern and calling my position on the radio. While taxiing on ground after landing, discovered volume of my radio was turned down. Turned volume up and heard the other aircraft calling landing intentions at the airport. They had apparently been flying the pattern too, and extended their downwind while I landed.Factors involved were my inadvertently turning volume down too far, and distraction of passengers (the radio was active with lots of faraway traffic and passenger asked question, so I turned radio volume down to hear better). As a side note, did not see a traffic alert on ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast), suggesting other aircraft was not ADS-B equipped.
1808680: [Pilot] was flying her Aircraft X as Pilot in Command at the ZZZ airport, landing Runway XX. I was monitoring from the right seat. [Pilot] was cleared for the option on Runway XX by the ZZZ Tower from the left downwind of Runway XX approximately midfield. She initiated proper airspeed and flap configuration for a stabilized approach from pattern altitude. She applied correct airspeed, pitch, bank, and flap configurations while flying base and final approach. The aircraft maintained proper airspeed, pitch, and crosswind correction while on final maintaining the centerline of the runway as it flew a stabilized glide angle down to the runway. When transitioning into the landing phase, she began a flare and proper attitude to land the airplane. As the airplane was about to land, the attitude of the airplane changed suddenly in a way that was consistent with large rapid change in the characteristics of the wind, [Pilot] attempted to initiate a go-around with my immediate assistance. However, the plane lost directional control, veering to the right and eventually coming to a stop with a nose down attitude.
1808687: I conducted a routine pre-flight of the aircraft and no anomalies were noted. I requested that the aircraft be fueled, and that was done. I also checked weather and NOTAMs for my solo flight. I noted some wind indicated in the forecast - clear, unlimited visibility, wind variable 6 G 13, 30.01 altimeter - but well within aircraft and pilot limitations. Actual weather at take-off was clear VFR and unremarkable.I then had a routine flight for approximately one hour focusing primarily on use of the Garmin avionics system. I did an approach and landing which was uneventful.I returned to [home airport]. My initial approach was stabilized, but I was alert because of wind guests. On touchdown, the aircraft became airborne after a wind gust. I executed a balked landing procedure as the aircraft settled on the runway and went around.On my second approach to land, the aircraft was again on a stabilized approach through flare and touchdown. I was conducting a no-flaps approach because of the wind. After touchdown, there was an exceptional gust of wind which caused the aircraft to veer sharply to the left. I immediately applied full right rudder and heavy braking to maintain control of the aircraft and avoid exiting the runway. Despite my best efforts, the aircraft exited the runway. I immediately released hard braking to avoid flipping the aircraft and focused on maintaining control, which I did.The aircraft came to rest adjacent to the intersecting taxi-way. I could tell that the left tire was flat so I stopped the engine and exited the aircraft to inspect it and assess the situation.
1808930: This was not a good flight because of compounding errors that happened and the negative effect that they had. The good part is that the flight remained safe, but here below are several things that I learned. The events started when on decent into ZZZ when the lights on the autopilot mode selector began to flicker erratically, however the autopilot appeared to perform normally. This was in IMC descent thru layers with occasional moderate turbulence. (The was second flight after the power supply to the EFIS system failed resulting in loss of the primary attitude indicator and HSI which was repaired and return to service. I mention this only because it attributed to my increase lack of trust in the flight instruments.) The autopilot was on altitude preselect with a vertical speed selected. During the decent I was evaluating the autopilot issue and I think, after the fact, I pushed the altitude capture twice, resulting in me disengaging the capture and descending below the desired altitude. At the time I attributed this to a malfunction autopilot and I decided to disconnect the autopilot and manually flew the plane. This increased the workload. Weather was also a significant factor. There was a line of thunderstorms that were moving over ZZZ (destination) and I was watching the satellite radar utilizing a portable GDL52 communicating to Garmin pilot on my I pad. For this flight I was using ForeFlight for navigation/charts and Garmin Pilot for weather, because the GDL would not communicate satellite radar information to ForeFlight. I have been using ForeFlight for charts and weather in previous aircraft for many years, but this aircraft has only ADSB-out and is scheduled to have an avionics upgrade to a GDL69a (sat WX) and Garmin 345 (ADSB IN/Out) installation in Month. I was also utilizing the onboard radar, but am learning to use this system. Bottom line was too many nav / weather systems in use that resulted in unnecessary and additional workload. Another factor was that I had transitioned from a piston to a turboprop and had about 80 hours in the TBM time at the time of this flight. So I was still low on the TBM experience curve. Based on the weather I requested GPS XX and activated the approach on the 530s. However, as I proceeded to ZZZ GPS XX, the weather changed and the IAF for GPS XX was near the line of thunderstorms and center offered ILS XY and left turn to heading for the IAF - I made a right turn to that heading. I should have recognized that I was starting to make small mistakes. During this time I also was varying from assigned altitude due to increase workload. I entered ILS XX in to the 530S and activated and Center vectored me to the approach. I began the approach and was able to see the ground occasionally. I was handed off the Tower and I waited to capture the glideslope. I continued the approach, my position and altitude were not cross checking, and I began try to determine why. I was high when I was on a 2-3 mile final. While making this evaluation, I was able to see the runway lights and able to make a visual decent and landing. I was not confident after this flight, there were too many mistakes in this flight. When I was on the ground I contacted my flight instructor and went over flight and discussed the avionics and my reaction/ decision I made. We made a plan of how to determine the effect of the flickering light on the mode selector and insure that it was safe for flight. I altered my plans so that weather would have a minimal impact and returned back to ZZZ1. To learn and avoid these errors in the future, I did a full debrief with my instructor when I return home. This focused on both the avionics and cross reference that he recommended to determine status of the navigation system. We also spent a considerable time on how I responded to the apparent situation and decision making. It was at this time, I realized how much some minor errors in my part had a large impact onthe flight. The avionics have also been evaluated by Company in ZZZ2 and determine that the malfunction was limited to the mode selector display and that the autopilot is functioning normally. It is schedule to be repaired. Further I have also flow approaches in VFR conditions to verify operations of the navigation and autopilot systems and apply some of the procedures that my instructor and I discussed.
1809205: After a normal flight from ZZZ we descended for the visual approach to ZZZZ, due to no response from anybody on the ground at ZZZZ, I elected to do an over flight of the airport at pattern altitude of 1,500 ft. with the autopilot disconnected, crossing over midfield from north to south on the east west runway to enter a left hand crosswind for the left pattern landing east, we started configuring the aircraft for landing by selecting flaps to the #2 position, on the left downwind leg we selected the gear handle down, at that point we received an amber CAS message of GEAR MISCOMPARE R The nose gear and left main indicated down(GREEN) the right main gear was an AMBER X. While the First Officer (FO) looked for the message in the Emergency Procedures checklist I engaged the Auto Pilot and Auto throttles and climbed to 2,000 and stayed in an extended racetrack pattern around ZZZZ. At this point we informed the passenger of the situation and was thinking that the procedure should work and we would land at ZZZZ. We followed gear will not extend checklist, pulling the blow down handle, no change, the pulling the main gear uplock handle, no change the last procedure in the checklist was to try and yaw the airplane. We informed the passengers what to expect, and tried the yaw left then right twice, no change. At this point I made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 again informing the passengers what the plan was, they were fine with that because they had used a local company at ZZZ1 to take them to ZZZZ before. We pickup a clearance to ZZZ1 with ZZZ2 Center, and informed them of our situation. After that hand off to ZZZ2 Approach Control, the controller asked us if we would like a fly by for visual verification of the gear status. We chose to do this option, and he coordinated with the tower. I felt very confident that the gear was down because when the FO pulled the uplock handle he felt very little resistance, from my past experience that is a good indication the gear was not in the uplock. With blow down in the system the gear only has one place to go, so I felt with a very high degree of certainty that the right main was down and locked. The weather at ZZZ1 was VMC 10 miles 5,000 ft. Scattered wind was 110/18 gusting 24. After being vectored for the visual low pass over Runway XXR at ZZZ1 Tower informed us that Airfield Operations was in a position to observe our low pass, we had the aircraft fully configured for landing and made the low pass at 300 AGL and 140kts. Airfield Ops confirmed that he saw three gear. We executed the climb out instructions cleaned up the aircraft except for the gear remaining down, then we were vectored for another visual approach to land Runway XXR at ZZZ1. During our patterned we went ahead and [received priority], to have the trucks just in case. Also the FO radioed Company ZZZ1 if they could have a van meet us to take our passengers to their requested destination on the field, and if they would call the Company1 maintenance facility and let them know we were inbound. We reconfigured the aircraft for landing while on a 3mile final we slowed to final approach speed and with Airfield Ops and the fire trucks standing by we made a normal landing with an extended rollout, confirming the gear was indeed down. We cleared the runway and taxied to the Company1 maintenance facility. We deplaned the passengers and got them on their way immediately. I informed the maintenance staff of the issue and they pulled the aircraft in the hanger and did a visual inspection of the gear. They found that the uplock switch, which is a plunger type, was stuck in the gear up position making the computer think the gear was still in the well.
1809471: I was working arrival and departure for the JAX north area. We were on Runway 26. FHB airport is about 15-mile final for JAX [Runway] 26. We are constantly having to vector air carriers and business jets around 1200 codes traffic over and around that airport. Their altitudes and courses are erratic. The air carriers are audibly uncomfortable with it. Just today I had three 1200 codes from 1,500 feet to 3,500 feet MSL orbiting around my final while I'm trying to get jets into JAX. That sector also has multiple Victor routes that are busy with low level GA overflights. So, we have to get these jets as low as we can to miss the overflight traffic but the 1200 codes are blocking our low altitudes. It takes all our focus because we have to watch the tracks and altitudes of these VFR airplanes and constantly update the jet traffic of where they are. We don't like it. The pilots don't like it. It is a wildly unsafe situation there.Our Class C needs to be extended for the final for [Runway] 26. That is the only solution. No one should be flying around our final at crossing altitudes without talking to us. They just opened a flight school at FHB recently so the problem is only going to get worse. It's almost a daily problem now. One air carrier pilot said this is the only airport he flies into where he is dodging Skyhawks on the final. It is the most unsafe operation I have seen in my career.
1809786: Aircraft X was on Final approach after calling out turning Final Runway 21, Second call Aircraft X on Short final Runway 21. After first call on Final I saw Aircraft Y pull slowly onto the runway and stop, that's when I cancelled Short Final. Just as I was preparing to go-around he started moving and in my judgement I could land if he kept going. He lifted off as I touched down with full brakes and speedbrakes out. I was gaining on him as he climbed to 100 feet and by the time I made the second to last turn off he was 200 feet above and maybe 300 feet in front of my aircraft.Additional realities information. I never heard Aircraft Y announce anything, entering Runway, or even my call to him after I landed close to him. The heavy cross winds were a very big issue for me on the approach to this downhill runway. I know it well and with 160 at 22 knots on a 21 Runway I had 50 degree left crosswind and yaw angle for lineup. I knew I would get a major downdraft at the end of this runway so I elect to land at the 1000 feet marker. My landing speed is normal 100 knots plus 1/2 the wind makes 110 knots approach speed. That is the reason my ground speed and distance is long and fast. I was gaining on him even at his 100 to 200 feet. I also want to point out that as a NON controlled airport no one should pull on the runway and stop for even 10 seconds with an aircraft on final at 110 knots. Since his information indicates he is a commercial pilot I'm sure he realizes that there is no excuse to be on the wrong Frequency XYZ.00 or to stop as in Position and HOLD like you might get at a Towered airport.
1810347: At Cleburne Regional Airport it is hard to see traffic on the other end of field due to center of runway being highest elevation. Traffic was a student who was having trouble with communicating. The plane in pattern in front of traffic had to go around due to the traffic in question joining pattern too close behind them. They announced full stop, however, did not announce taxi back. Prior to taking the runway we announced that we were taking the runway for an east departure and had no response from other traffic. Upon reaching rotation speed we crested the hill and saw traffic, we then rotated and veered to the right side of the runway to avoid over flying traffic. Plenty of separation was maintained. Other flight school instructor was in the pattern as well and they verified they did not hear any intentions of back taxi. The plane in question never made another radio call after short final saying they were landing.
1810355: This was a flight [to] ZZZ for pickup of an item. I monitored the AWOS and listened to UNICOM for traffic. I announced my intention to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX and land at ZZZ with a FULL STOP. It was observing that several aircraft were in the pattern in close spacing on the downwind with an estimated speed of approximately 70 Knots. My pattern entry speed was reduced to 130 KIAS for landing gear deployment and spaced about a 1,000 feet to right, outside of these aircraft. Again, I announced my intention to make a Full Stop landing without interfering with the numerous aircraft doing Touch & Go landings. I reduced the speed 110 Knots on base and 100 Knots on Final Approach. Expecting these aircraft to extend downwind about 30 seconds to give me room, I was surprised when one of them continued on a tight base and turn to final directly in front my plane. At 100 Knots approach speed, I easily overtook the 70-knot aircraft and passed successfully at about 500 feet right of ZZZ Runway XX centerline. I accelerated my plane while retracting the gear and flaps and maintained 180 knots for the climb and turn to crosswind. Again, I observed several aircraft on close spacing downwind and I entered a downwind slightly outside the pattern. For the fourth time, I announced my intention to make a Full Stop landing and turned the normal base for my plane's speed. For a second time, an aircraft made a turn to base and turned to final directly in front of me instead of extending their downwind about 30 second to allow much-faster airplanes to make a Full Stop. On this pattern, I was grateful the other aircraft decided to go-around when the pilot observed the rapid CLOSURE from behind. I said 'Thanks' on the radio and completed a safe Full Stop Landing.After my safe landing, I proceeded to the FBO to pick up the item. Upon reaching the FBO desk, I heard on the FBO radio that Runway XX is now CLOSED for an airplane stopped on the runway. From the FBO windows, it appeared to be an aircraft was sitting on Runway XX without its Landing Gear. The poor soul and retractable aircraft were still out there when I departed. If these aircraft belong to a Flight school, perhaps the instructors should talk to their students about allowing faster, dissimilar airplanes into the traffic pattern for a single full stop landing. There are MANY corporate airplanes that land at ZZZ Airport with approach speed in the 100 - 120 knots range. This would be appreciated by many and certainly may save unwanted distraction during landing. Perhaps the instructor input may save some distracted soul from making a gear-up landing.
1810616: According to my student: While he was doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ, on his second landing, he touched down left of centerline. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position, he turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. When he applied left rudder he said the plane felt as if it would skid, spin or drop the nose onto the ground. Therefore, he applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose wheel and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. There was no damage to plane, runway, or grass area, and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the Alpha taxiway. He continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions.As the instructor, my student called me to inform me he had run off the runway, no damage had occurred, and he had spoken with the tower and FAA. I did not know he was flying by himself that day and had received no notification from him. I asked him to recount what happened to me several times trying to understand what happened. I called the Tower and confirmed that the winds were variable at 3 knots and visibility was very good. Based on his recount, I do not fully understand how he thought going off the runway was his safest option. I have not offered him any training or instruction that would indicate that was good judgment. He has never landed far off centerline with me in the plane and has never demonstrated that he would ever act in such a way. He and I have logged extensive dual hours at ZZZ doing pattern work, and he has never flown in a way that indicated he would act or make a decision in this manner. He had demonstrated consistently with me that he was able to maintain directional control of the airplane both in the air and on the ground. I have informed him that all of his solo endorsements are no longer valid. I was planning to spend an extensive amount of time with him on the ground and in the air addressing what happened yesterday through re-training, but he has decided to discontinue his flight training at this time. As a result of this incident, I have re-clarified to all students that they must inform me of any time they plan to solo and must receive my permission before doing so. I have also implemented a strict rule of no solo touch and goes. Solo pattern work will from now on only be full stop landings. While doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ, on my second landing, I touched down just left of center. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position, I turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. Applying left rudder the plane felt as if it would skid, spin or drop the nose onto the ground and I was too far toward the edge of the runway. I felt it best, to reduce the chances of injury or damage. I applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose movement and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. No damage to plane, runway or grass area and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the taxiway. I continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions. As a result of this occurrence, training has been suspended for evaluation and scheduling with CFI.
1810893: Taxiing out of ZZZZ we called the advisory frequency, we were told there was no inbound traffic and we were cleared to back taxi. It's about a 3,500 foot taxi to the end and roughly 1,000 feet from the end my First Officer points out what seems to be a Citation on a visual left base. We advise the VFR tower that there was an aircraft on final for our runway. Both the tower and ourselves attempted to tell the aircraft to go-around and failed. At this point there is brush and trees lining both sides of the runway and there was no turn off. I pull the aircraft to the right edge of the runway in event that he continued the landing. At an estimated 100 feet, the aircraft was seen adding power and retracting the gear. We advised the tower that we were clear of the conflict and we continued our departure.Suggestions: VFR island flying training or VFR plates to advise of traffic flows to certain airports.
1811005: While being vectored for the visual approach to runway XX at PHL the captain noticed a white drone pass along the left side of the aircraft. Captain observed drone pass the left side of aircraft. Unknown person operating drone near aircraft. Notified ATC. Suggestions: More closely monitor the position of drones in relation to aircraft. On Approach to XX in PHL a drone flew past the aircraft. It was at 5,000 feet, straight and level and heading westbound. I saw it pass off the left side of the aircraft. It didn't cause us to change course or altitude. Suggestions:Be aware of drones by airports. Second trip in a row now.
1811286: While being vectored for the visual approach at ZZZ, approximately while descending through 5,000 feet, the Amber CAS message (ENG CTRL SYS (L-R)) appeared as well as the Master Caution System light, I referenced the Manufacturers Emergency/Abnormal Checklist which dictated the first step is to reset the FADEC to the affected side, which in this case was both sides, the checklist goes on to say if the CAS message clears then no further action is required, or if the CAS message remains, to land as soon as practical. The checklist also goes on to advise of the possible effects that may be encountered, they are:- Degraded or lack of response to throttle movements including possible surging or flameout.- Possible inability to restart.- Possible inability to achieve ground idle.- Loss of automatic Interstage Turbine Temperature (ITT) limiting during ground idle.- Loss of automatic ITT limiting during ground or windmill starts.- Loss of ITT indication.The message did not clear after the reset, and given the possibility of a flameout, I chose to land ASAP, I notified ATC and requested to proceed directly to the final approach course for landing. ATC complied with my request and gave me priority. The landing was uneventful, but on the landing roll out, the L Engine Fail Warning CAS message came up, it distinguished about 15 seconds later, then appeared once again about a minute later during taxi and stayed on for 10 seconds then went away.Once I arrived to the ramp at the FBO I shut the engines down and powered down the aircraft with no further incident.
1811552: We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival into ZZZ inside of the ZZZZZ1 waypoint when ATC instructed us to descend via except cross ZZZZZ2 at 10,000 ft., 2000 ft. higher than published. We informed ATC that if we comply with the assigned crossing restriction that we will have trouble making ZZZZZ at 6,000, [which was] only 8.2 miles from ZZZZZ2. ATC then replied, 'If you will be high on the arrival let me know.' We then decided to slow down the aircraft to prepare for making the crossing restrictions and recalculate our descent inside of ZZZZZ2 to advise ATC if we will be high or if we can comply with the ZZZZZ restriction.Once the Honeywell FMS reached waypoint passage over ZZZZZ2 and cycled to the next fix, we started down to make the next crossing restriction. Within a few seconds of starting our descent, we received a TCAS 'TRAFFIC' alert followed by a TCAS RA. I immediately disconnected the autopilot to comply with the RA and resolve the conflict. After the resolution advisory was resolved, [the Pilot Monitoring] noticed that the FMS had cycled to the next waypoint early and found that we were still a few tenths of a mile from ZZZZZ2 during the event. The assigned altitude at ZZZZZ2 was 10,000 ft., we leveled off during the RA around 9,750 - 9,800 ft. There was no communication from ATC to us regarding the event. The rest of the arrival and approach was flown successfully and we landed safely.The Honeywell FMS cycled waypoints early, leading us to believe that we had reached waypoint passage. [I suggest] finding a solution to prevent the Honeywell FMS from making premature smart turns/waypoint passage cycles. Operating [the] flight as SIC (Second in Command) and PM, we were assigned to descend via the ZZZZZ [arrival] but cross ZZZZZ2 at 10,000. We leveled off at 10,000 prior to the fix and set the next appropriate altitude. At about 2.5 miles prior to the fix, the Honeywell FMS prematurely sequenced to the next waypoint. We began an initial descent and quickly noticed the discrepancy in distance between current position and waypoint. [There was] an RA to 'monitor descent' annunciation. The Pilot Flying immediately climbed back to 10,000 and we waited until the correct DME was displayed. [The cause of the crossing altitude deviation was the] Honeywell FMS [working improperly]. I have noticed this problem in almost all company aircraft containing Honeywell FMS. The airplane will sequence to the next waypoint prior to the actual position. This can, and does lead to, altitude deviations and potential RAs and possibly worse. I would like to either see the problem itself fixed or the company to implement an SOP or training that covers this issue.
1811687: While on approach into ZZZ, we were descending from 6,000 ft to 5,000 ft on the runway localizer tracking inbound to runway, and were cleared for the ILS . While descending through approximately 5,300 ft, on the Localizer, a larger sized, square 'Quad-Copter' drone suddenly went past our right wing, (from aircraft front to back) missing the right wingtip by, in my estimations, about 50 ft. The event happened so quickly that there was no manual reaction to the event (autopilot / auto-throttles stayed engaged, etc). I immediately told my Captain that we just had a near miss with a drone since he did not see it, and we immediately notified Air Traffic Control as to the exact location, altitude, and description of the drone/event. We proceeded on the ILS as normal, for landing. The Captain contacted the Chief Pilot once parked at the gate to report the matter.
1811745: We were on a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. During the approach we received a GPWS Caution 'Terrain' or 'Too Low Terrain' just after the '500 ft stable' call. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring), I failed to call for a go-around. The PF (Pilot Flying), Captain completed the approach and landing uneventfully. Everything about the approach was normal and I have seen it many times in my 3 years here. PF was stable at 100 ft above field elevation as well as at 500 ft above field elevation, the only exception was that the winds that had recently shifted and gusting were causing the airspeed to deviate by plus or minus 10 knots, but not dramatically. The fact that we were visual with the runway, on path and speed and properly configured, made the GPWS caution surprise me. After hearing it, I reverified that we were within all our approach criteria and it appeared safe so I did not call for the go around. However, being that it was not day VMC, I should have called it. In the future I will be sure to comply with the GPWS alert immediately and call for the go-around.
1811750: Original First Officer (FO) called out from the trip. I was assigned a new FO, he informed me that he was low time FO and hasn't flown much during the past few weeks. I took the first leg to ZZZ1, and I let him [have] the leg back from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. He flew really well during the entire flight. We were cleared for the visual approach Runway XXL with great weather. FO did a great job during the approach and he was properly configured and stable at all times. It looked like he was going to have a great landing because he was doing everything by the book. Unfortunately, when it came time to do the flare he barely flared and took the power out a bit too quickly and the main landing gears made contact with the runway firmer than normal. Everything happened too quick, I saw him initially starting to flare but then at the end he let the nose drop a bit and the mains contacted the runway. I didn't get a chance to note the VSI at the time. As soon as we arrived at the gate I called Maintenance and informed them of that I was writing the aircraft for a possible hard landing with minimal flare. We originally had a plane swap, while on the swap I grabbed some dinner. And eventually received a call from the Chief Pilot confirming that there was damage to main landing gear and he wanted to hear from me what had happened. I explained to the Chief Pilot what had happened, and Chief Pilot took notes and said to follow up with an Ops report.A firmer landing than normal due to minimal flare that caused the main landing gears to come into contact with the runway quicker than normal due to minimal flare. FO barely flared during a visual approach at Runway XXL in ZZZ that ended up causing a hard landing situation.[Reporter recommends] possibly rotate brand new FO's and make them fly more often. FO informed me he had not flown in a while and was still low time FO. He did a great job on our leg to ZZZ1 as Pilot Monitoring (PM), and then a great job on his leg from ZZZ1 to ZZZ until his landing flare where everything happened to quick and he ended up barely flaring and making contact with the main landing gear a bit firmer than usual, which prompted me to write up the landing.
1812004: We were cleared the RNAV (RNP) Y 16 L inside of HLDMM (I believe) on the KENNO 2 RNAV. 0.3 was entered into the LEGS Page and 4,500 feet was placed in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) window. Inside of KLOCK, zeros were entered into the MCP. At approximately 1,500 feet AGL, with the aircraft fully configured and a zero vertical NAV deviation, the Vertical NAV suddenly indicated approach 488 feet below the vertical path. The aircraft made a minor attempt with pitch and power to correct the deviation. I then disengaged the autopilot and autothrottles. By the time we sorted this out, we were too high above the glidepath for a normal approach, so I directed / executed a go-around.We subsequently flew a visual approach backed up by (a different RNAV) the RNAV GPS X Runway 16L. We did not engaged the VNAV / LNAV. An ILS is not available to 16L. The weather packet cover page did note GPS interference testing in the PMSR (Pt. Mugu Sea Range) centered on the SXC248/058 and possible impact areas, but RNO was not in the listed area. RAF coverage was 0.3 or better. There was an FDC NOTAM for this approach (to disregard a note for night operations), but was N/A. Company was contacted.
1812040: While enroute to ZZZ we experienced unusually high LP vibrations, still within limitations. No amber indication was observed. However, the vibrations were strong enough to be felt in the aircraft. Descending into ZZZ ATC cleared us to descend to 16,000 and cleared us for the approach. We began to descend when we noticed the vibrations were getting worse. While running the QRH we encountered sudden turbulence, shortly after we received a terrain alert and immediately executed the escape maneuver. We continued to ZZZ without further difficulty and to a safe landing. Crew became task saturated by increasing engine vibrations, sudden unexpected turbulence and QRH checklist.Suggestions - Terrain awareness chart or company jepps. Company awareness video regarding descent and approach into ZZZ. ATC cleared us for the approach into ZZZ and notifies us of no radar coverage under 16,000 feet. The Captain set the initial approach fix and we began a descent on a VNAV path toward the airport. During descent we were handling an engine vibration issue with the QRH along with some unexpected turbulence, when we received a terrain notification. The Captain executed an escape maneuver and we continued to a safe landing on Runway XX at ZZZ. Crew became task saturated with the engine vibrations, QRH, and unexpected turbulence in descent.
1812551: The following narrative is due to a complete lack of threat and error management and operation performance. This was the first leg of a 4 day trip and I would be flying with a First Officer for the first time. We were heavily delayed to start our day and weather was terrible. High winds and windshear were reported throughout the whole Company system with several crews diverting. Yet my release for this flight indicated nothing other than I should evaluate the use of Runway XX for ZZZ departure. When the aircraft arrived I met the arriving Captain and he explained to me the auto pilot master warning EICAS message occurred at 1,000 feet on the coupled ILS approach into ZZZ. The Captain stated maintenance refused to take the write ups as it was going to ZZZ1 and they would casually look at it there. I immediately called maintenance and asked why they wouldn't take write ups and said from what it sounded like a write up was not warranted. The maintenance controller asked if I wished to MEL the autopilot and I stated how can I? At this point I should have immediately refused the plane, but at Company, refusing to fly gets us an immediate phone call from the Chief Pilot office. We Were now operating in the red of the threat and error management philosophy. On the way to ZZZ1 we experienced moderate turbulence as expected and when we turned base for Runway XY the field was surrounded by virga. The FO and I briefed a go around and the windshear escape maneuver once more. On final at about 1,200 feet the Autopilot Fail master warning EICAS message appeared and the Autopilot disconnected. I continued to hand fly the aircraft and remained stable to about 300 feet where I encountered increasing performance and the approach became unstable. A normal go-around was executed and we called positive rate gear up, we received the windshear caution. Immediately after we hit severe turbulence. We diverted to ZZZ without further incident. The remainder of the flight was performed without the autopilot.Company maintenance did not take a write up from a Captain. I wrote up the AP failure and the encounter with severe turbulence. All write-ups must be taken by maintenance.
1812914: The event happened at night on taxi out from gate to Runway XXL. There were significant amounts of thunderstorms surrounding ZZZ requiring the airport to only have Runway XXL for takeoff and XXR for landing. Upon leaving the ramp area, we were given clearance to taxi to XXL via Taxiways '1' then [Taxiway] '23.' We turned north on [Taxiway] '1' and followed a B737. The B737 aircraft stopped holding short of [Taxiway] '23.' After about 30 seconds it proceeded and turned onto [Taxiway] 23 and we followed. It was as we turned onto [Taxiway] 23 that both the Captain and I heard the ATC Ground Controller give excited directions to 'hurry up/go fast.' The key point here is that we never heard our call sign used for any of these calls and assumed he was talking to someone else. As we advanced to a position abeam Runway XXR on our right, the Ground Controller called our call sign and I responded. He then told us, using our call sign, to 'go fast, aircraft on short final to Runway XXR.' We saw the conflict and tried to move faster but it was too late and the aircraft was forced to execute a go-around. The Controller told us the aircraft had to go-around and chastised us for missing several calls. I responded that we 'never heard it.'Ultimately, I believe one of two things happened--either the Controller made several excited transmissions either omitting our call sign or used an incorrect call sign, or both the Captain and I missed several radio calls made to us until a conflict happened. We had been reassigned after a long weather delay and misconnect out of ZZZ. We had to consult with dispatch to confirm our clearance and routing. ZZZ ATC had reconfigured airport and were landing and departing runways XXL/R. At spot X we were instructed to taxi to XXL, [Taxiway] 1, [Taxiway] 23. As we approached [Taxiway] 23 a B737 was stopped ahead of us. That aircraft then turned onto [Taxiway] 23. We followed, no instructions to hold short of the XXR approach was given. The Ground Controller then told the B737 to hurry, then told us to hurry and cross XXR approach, saying that we were expected to hold short of [Taxiway] 23. We were not instructed to hold short of Taxiway 23.
1812952: On approach to landing, engines would not idle. Captain was able to slow and stabilize on profile although it required abnormally low throttle setting. Engines would still not idle on taxi in and throttle settings and thrust were not matched.
1813055: I was Pilot Flying. I triggered a stick shaker/pusher at the Final Approach Fix. I recovered per SOP.[There was] a northbound squall line west of the field. A last minute wind shift caused us to switch runways. Although it was fast, we were able to set up and brief before intercepting course. ATC forgot to turn [us] on the ILS, so we went through the localizer course. This led to reactionary vectors and the aircraft doing S turns until we passed the final approach fix. At this point we were flaps 30 with the power reduced. I called for the go-around, but when I pressed the autopilot disconnect button, I became fixated on the lack of a missed approach course. (I didn't press the TO-GA button.) While troubleshooting, the airspeed continued to decrease leading to a simultaneous stick shaker and pusher. I lowered the nose and recovered per the training, paying special attention to the radar altimeter. I briefly oversped flaps 8 on recovery.Stall recovery training works. I was able to accomplish the recovery quickly without having to think about it. However, it shouldn't have gotten that far. It was my first go-around since OE. I was task saturated and in the moment couldn't remember where the TO-GA button was. We were able to handle weather, ATC error, runway changes and an instrument approach at the same time. However, because our go around was triggered at a relatively untrained aircraft state/position, I missed a critical aspect of the maneuver. I don't believe this is a common problem, but incorporating go-arounds during recurrent in various positions may be beneficial.
1813185: I have departed ZZZ airport to the south to practice landings in ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ I have contacted ZZZ Tower around 7NM to 8 NM south of the field, the Tower has replied standby so I have tuned to easterly heading so I will not enter the airspace, a few minutes after that the Tower has instructed me to join mid left downwind for Runway XX and to report when established on the downwind, after I have established on the downwind I have notified the Tower. To the best of my knowledge and memory the Tower has replied the following instruction: 'you are number 3 for Runway XX continue', I have given the Tower read back and then I looked forward to visually scan for the traffic in front of me, I remember clearly that I saw 2 aircraft in the final for Runway XX, the first one was an airplane in the short final and the second one was a helicopter that was also in the final behind him. I remember that I have pointed the 2 aircraft to my students and explained to them that these are the aircraft that are in front of us and we will follow them as we are number 3 in the sequence. After the helicopter was abeam to my position, I continued to fly on the downwind for an extra 30 seconds to 1 minute so I will allow some extra spacing between myself and the helicopter as I'm flying with students on their first ever fly day. As I was told I'm number 3 in sequence and I visually saw the 2 aircraft that are in front of me I have continued the traffic pattern and turn left to the base leg, and then when I was in the appropriate position I have turned final. Between 30 seconds to 1 minute after I was established on the final for XX the Tower has instructed me to 'immediately turn heading 090 and break the approach', I have immediately took controls from my student and turned to the heading 090 while giving a read back to the Tower. As I have established on the heading 090 I saw that there was a jet aircraft on the final approach behind me, approximately 1,200 feet horizontally and 300 feet vertically in my evaluation. after that I have continued to comply with the Tower instructions and followed a different traffic that was on the downwind to join the final for Runway XX again for a full stop. Before landing when I was on short final I have verified with the Tower that I had clearance to land.I have strong belief in self critic and self evaluation and after this event has occurred I have come up with the following safety measures that can help prevent this situation from reoccurring:1. When you have been instructed to follow traffic while on the downwind, you should always verify with Tower that you can start your turn towards the base leg.2. When you are told that you are number 3 in sequence and you see the 2 aircraft in front of you, that absolutely does not mean that you should stop looking for other traffic in the area, you still need scan for traffic very frequently.3. When flying on the base leg, even in a controlled airport, you should always try to look for more traffic coming on the final, both behind you and in front of you, and make sure that there is no traffic that can jeopardize the approach before actually making the turn to final.4. Do not think that just because you are flying in a controlled airspace under ATC supervision, you are protected. Always actively scan for traffic and verify ATC instructions.I believe that if I had used these safety measures that I have mentioned above this event could have been prevented. I am glad no damage has been done in this event, and I'm committed to learn from this experience and actively seek to improve myself as a pilot and as flight instructor.
1813866: As this report is not timely, it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF, for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified. I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much, the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN, RW 16R, as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But, the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE, but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal, still pissed that I allowed this to happen, I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue, no loss of separation, and no need to file a report.Looking back, how this could have been avoided... first of all, I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night, briefing and installing one arrival and approach then, at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes, and programming, was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist, procedure, or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last, but I know what I will and won't do next time. During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase, we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF, the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival, we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain, as Pilot Monitoring (PM), selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF, I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV, VNAV, opened the speed window for the appropriate speed, requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did), and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint, the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green, engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds, and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn, ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft, a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required, there was no loss of separation, there was no safety issue, and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up, preparing, and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints, altitudes, and sequencing verified in the FMC.
1813993: Approached Runway 28 into GMU and had the Pilot Monitoring turn the pilot controlled lighting up to max (7 clicks). The runway lights for Runway 28 did not appear to turn on. The approach was continued to 500 feet at which point a go around was executed. We joined the traffic pattern and landed on Runway 1. A third check of the NOTAMs showed that there were no NOTAMs identifying the runway as closed or showing the runway lights as out of service. After landing, we learned that several aviation [websites] such as airnav.com and skyvector.com contain this remark: ATC-CTL. WHEN ATCT CLSD ACTVT MALSF RWY 01, REIL RWY 19, HIRL RWY 01/19, PERIMETER LGTS H1, H2 - CTAF. However, the FAA Chart Supplement contains this remark: ACTIVATE perimeter lights H1 and H2--CTAF. Of note, this is listed only as a Heliport Remark, not in the general remarks for the airport. Thus, it appears that the Runway 28 lights cannot be controlled using Pilot Controlled Lighting procedures on the CTAF frequency, however, there is incomplete information is the FAA Chart Supplement. We recommend that the FAA Chart Supplement be updated with the correct information. Also, consider adding the pilot controlled lighting limitations information to the Airfield Sketch and on the Runway 28 Approach Plate, as these products are much more likely to be referenced by a flight crew while in flight.
1813994: During the final segment of the approach phase on short final, we hear gear up at 960 feet RA. Captain told Pilot Monitoring to put the gear down and decided to continue to land. We decided it was safer to land rather to do the balked landing.I believe the cause of the event was fatigue and complacency. I felt a little tired and did not scan and confirm Captain checklist items that were called for. It was night time with turbulence and at a critical phase of flight were several things were happening at the same time.I need to be more aware of confirming actual checklist items at critical phases of flight and scanning everything looks good when the Captain is focused on flying the aircraft into ZZZ.
1814090: Aircraft was in the traffic pattern at ZZZ, downwind leg turning to base, approximate altitude 3;000ft MSL, 90 MPH. Approximately .25 mile from the approach end of RUNWAY. A small impact was heard and felt by the pilot. There was nothing observed by the pilot, no evasive action taken. There were no control issues with the aircraft, initial thoughts were that a bird strike had occurred. After parking in the hangar, the aircraft was inspected. Damage from impact with a solid object was found on the underside of the right wing, outboard wing panel and wing tip. There were scratches on the paint and a slight crease in a wing skin. There was no structural damage and the aircraft is airworthy. The damage was consistent with a hard object with a width of at least 18 inches, and suggested that the impact was with a drone. Within the traffic pattern and at pattern elevation of an airport is not an appropriate area for drone operation.
1814301: We were instructed to line up and wait while the aircraft that just landed rolled out and exited the runway. While we were in position, Tower became busy talking to other aircraft on frequency. The next radio call for us was to exit the runway at C2. While exiting, a cleared to land aircraft was heard asking 'is that an airplane on the runway?' Tower instructed them to not overfly us, that we were exiting the runway. They were never instructed to go-around, instead to offset. We observed them offsetting slightly as to not fly directly over the top of us as they continued to land.Tower becoming busy and possibly forgetting about us on the runway, and the landing aircraft not executing a go-around when they became aware of us in position on the runway, both contributed to the near miss. Query ATC when any delay in position.
1814394: Glide slope alert flying into RST. During approach phase of landing into RST. I was the Pilot Monitoring. We were cleared for the visual to runway 13. I recall we were descending and the Pilot Flying had the FAF altitude of 2,600 set, and the banana bar was indicating that we should level off at that altitude at approximately 0.25-0.75 prior to Ellie (FAF). I believe the approach mode was also activated, and we were fully configured. At the same time we were setting up for the approach there was a GA aircraft taking off, and a [air carrier] taxiing and holding short of Runway 13. I was focused outside and listening to ATC. We were both surprised when we received a glide slope alert. I believe that we were approximately 200 feet below the FAF when we received the alert. Around about this time I believe the 757 was cleared for takeoff. When we received the alert the Pilot Flying kicked off the autopilot, increased power and worked to re-establish a stabilized approach. We were still operating in visual conditions and had the runway in sight. From my perspective it seemed he had re-established a stabilized approach. Around 200-300 feet, or so, we received another glide slope alert. I do not recall us being excessively low to have activated the glide slope aural alert. The aircraft landed normally and safely. The Pilot Flying was frustrated that we had by all indications an unstable approach. In rethinking the events I am confident that we had the aircraft correctly configured and ready to fly the ILS with the aid of the autopilot. While we could not confirm this, our best guess was that the taxiing air carrier had somehow interfered with the glide slope and we began descending prior to the FAF. I felt that he had established a stabilized approach prior to 1,000 AGL, so the second aural alert was also a surprise. I believe it was the PF's first time flying into RST. After the first aural glide slope alert we probably should have called for a go-around. The alert caused a couple moments of confusion. We probably should have just gone around and removed the distraction.
1814627: My student was preforming pattern work at ZZZ. Traffic pattern altitude being used was 1,800 feet. Conditions were VFR. My student made his crosswind, downwind, and final calls every time. At the same time a C182 was operating for a skydive operation out of ZZZ. My students downwinds were always flown to provide clearance for the skydivers designated landing zone. Throughout his 7 landings in the C172, a PT-17 Stearman joined the pattern, not making any radio communication calls so the student paid extra attention to focus on where the Stearman was operating. The Stearman continued to fly low patterns at about 1,300 feet, with tight downwinds right over the skydiving drop zone. The Stearman sometimes would not even take off from the runway. They would add power then come to a complete stop at the end of the runway and taxi back. While the student was downwind midfield, the skydive C182 was holding short of the runway and made a CTAF call they were waiting for the Stearman to to depart.When the student turned base about 1/2 mile from the runway, the C182 announced they were departing. The student then turned to final and made his radio calls. Flaps were extended about 25 to 30 degrees and the student was coming in at about 70 to 75 MPH. At about 500 feet and 1/4 mile final, the Stearman came down in front of the students C172 about 400 feet away in a rapidly descending base to final and cut right in front of the student. The student had no choice but to abort the landing and go-around since they descended to a lower altitude in front of him. The made a CTAF call on 122.8, '<tail number> going around, aircraft on runway'. Adding full throttle and waiting for a positive rate of climb the student retracted the flaps. The student's initial thought was to just fly runway heading and perform a go around but because of the lack of communication his instincts told him they would perform a touch and go. He then made a 30 degree turn to the right of the runway then turned left to fly parallel to the runway and watched below for the Stearman as he gained altitude. To no surprise the Stearman was performing a touch and go.If my student had flown runway heading the Stearman more than likely would have ascended from under him. If he was any lower on my glide slope, and due to lack of communication from the high performance Stearman, his high wing aircraft would not have seen anyone above him, and the Stearman biplanes nature would not have seen him below them and they would have collided on the displaced threshold. The student had plenty of fuel and flew to the west of ZZZ and waited for them to land before returning. The way the pilots of the Stearman were flying a high performance aircraft with no radio, contrary to the flow of traffic, and without observing Part 91 right of way rules while conducting their operations poses a significant safety hazard.
1814658: At 1,900 MSL heard a thump, 20 seconds later, engine lost partial power, adding throttle did not improve power. Began a descent and located a field. Checked ignition and fuel both were on and appeared OK. Engine now making about 30% power so set up for off field landing. Crossing a fence line I struck a wire about 15 feet in the air. The aircraft shook but no other indication of control problem. Engine now at about 1700 RPM and aircraft able to climb about 100 feet per minute. I elected to head for my home base. Engine RPM still wavering but indicating 1800 so I proceeded straight to [home airport] which was now 9 miles away.Engine steady but still not making full power. I was able to complete a normal landing with no further problem. No injuries and aircraft returned to hangar. Upon inspection, found insect body parts stuck in the fuel vent. Damage confined to skin damage on gear legs and cut on right elevator.
1814760: As I applied brakes while rolling out from an otherwise normal three-point landing, the airplane swerved sharply to the right. I do not know whether the swerve was caused by a gust or a brake grabbing. I attempted to regain runway heading by applying left rudder and brake. When I saw I could not remain on the runway and was headed toward collision hazards, I applied full power to go-around. The airplane rolled off the edge of the runway before it became airborne but lifted off soon afterward, at which point I initiated a gentle left turn to runway heading. At some point the aircraft's left lower wing contacted the ground, damaging the paint and fabric on the underside of the aft portion of the wingtip and the outer section of aileron. I complied with the Tower's instruction to make right traffic and followed other aircraft as instructed for a second landing. I landed long with the tower's permission because a departing aircraft had reported debris on the runway, then uneventfully taxied onto a taxiway and to the airplane's hangar. During a phone call to the Tower I was told the debris was grass and gravel. I was well rested and not tired from the approximately one-hour flight.
1814794: I set up for a visual approach with an ILS back-up to Runway 13L at DAL. We were in good shape from a speed and altitude standpoint at NNATE. I was hand flying. I was distracted by the localizer guidance which showed me well right of course when I was actually slightly left. I mentioned that to the Pilot Monitoring. While troubleshooting the lateral guidance, I got behind the jet for getting flaps 15 and gear down and we ended up high. As I regained my crosscheck, I subconsciously followed vertical guidance, which now was taking me erroneously higher. I called for flaps 30, and realized we were now 800 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called out the PAPIs (Precision Approach Indicators), which showed all white, but the glideslope guidance was taking me higher. I called for a go-around. My go-around was sloppy, but the Pilot Monitoring brought his A game, so it was manageable. On the second approach, a visual approach backed up by the ILS 13L, both lateral and vertical guidance were erroneous. I had to fight the tendency to cue on the vertical guidance, which again was taking me high. The Pilot Monitoring turned off both flight directors. On short final, we got an audio glideslope alert. The glideslope raw data showed me way low. The PAPIs were three white and one red. We should have also turned away from the ILS on the NAV tuning panel. On both approaches, an Aircraft Y was parked right at the hold short line in front of the glideslope antenna. I suspect we will see more aircraft stopped at the hold short line with the runway closure at DAL, and so we will see more ILS interference. I have seen similar ILS behavior at other airports with an aircraft stopped at the hold short line. We did not write up the aircraft. An ILS test was completed and passed prior to the flight. NOTAM (or other reminder) that the 13L ILS may be unreliable with aircraft in the ILS critical area. More training on go-arounds.
