1815173: I was performing touch-and-go's during a supervised solo flight. On my final approach (GMU Runway 19), the other aircraft, who was told by ATC to continue flying through the final, took a northbound turn straight in front of me, flying directly towards me. I took evasive maneuvers by dropping down to the right. The other plane, only after being told by ATC that he had cut someone's final off, also took evasive maneuvers and started flying to his right and upwards. Following the evasive maneuver, landing on Runway 19 was uneventful.
1815459: We were attempting to land at the FOK airport. We attempted to use the pilot controlled lighting system, and made several attempts to key the microphone to turn on the lighting for landing. However, the runway lighting did not illuminate.We contacted a person on the ground attempted to activate the lights for us using a radio, and reported that they were unable to activate the lights. Air traffic control vectored us directly overhead the airport. We attempted to activate the lights again while we were overhead the airport, and we were able to successfully activate the lighting.We made a normal approach and landing. We unloaded our passengers, and prepared to takeoff. While on the ramp and during the taxi for departure, I tried to adjust the runway lights intensity, and we were unable to do so. We took off before the runway lights turned off, and reported this issue to ATC. I checked later that day, and a NOTAM had not been issued regarding the issue that we experienced.
1815680: Short Final to S95's Runway (RWY) 23 - a motorhome and trailer crossed the runway. Executed a Go-around as I was just crossing the threshold. I thought I was making calls on the CTAF of 122.8, but I had failed to select the proper radio, and was actually making calls on the [wrong frequency].
1816397: Flying Pilot thought he was cleared for visual approach.ATC then gave us a low altitude warning and instructed us to climb back up to 3,000 feet.During descent the Flying Pilot asked the Monitoring Pilot to ask the ATC Controller how to cancel our IFR flight plan. The Controller then gave the Pilot Monitoring instructions on how to cancel our IFR flight plan. Upon hearing this, the Flying Pilot mistook it for cleared for a visual approach. The altitude alerter was then changed and no communication was exchanged to the other Pilot about the change.We complied with instructions.Suggestions - Verify you heard what you thought you heard. Always keep other Pilot informed of altitude change in altitude alerter if self changed or have the other Pilot change it. During descent, Controller went over canceling procedures. Pilot thought we were cleared for approach. Altitude was changed without confirmation and was told to climb back up. Lesson learned.In approach mode, confusing instructions, did not verify altitude. Lesson learned.
1816661: I was flying Aircraft X. I was incoming to SQL from the north for [a] full stop landing, exiting the SFO Bravo, heading south towards the airport. SQL Tower initially asked me to enter a left downwind for Runway 30, keeping 101 freeway to my left, and they would call my left base for Runway 30. A couple of minutes later they asked me to turn left, overfly the runway and enter a right base for Runway 30. I crossed the runway at 1200 feet and began to descend to pattern altitude. SQL Tower told me to follow Aircraft Y that was on an extended right base for 30. As I was searching for Aircraft Y, I began to turn right downwind for 30 right as I noticed Aircraft Z cross in front of me....both of us executing an evasive maneuver. I told Tower that I had a near miss with Aircraft Z....and Tower responded that this aircraft was not on frequency. I was able to land safely. Upon reviewing ADS-B data and ATC recording of the event, it appears that Aircraft Z took off from Runway 30 and was asked to follow Aircraft A, Aircraft A was told to proceed to KNBR [radio station] antenna and then proceed on course, which they did. Aircraft Z however did not follow Aircraft A and turned too early into downwind. The tower also gave Aircraft Z a very early frequency change so they were not on frequency at the time of [the] near miss. It seems to me that the failure of the Tower to verify that Aircraft Z had Aircraft A in sight was a factor in this near miss, as well as the Tower's early frequency change for Aircraft Z.
1817312: I was seated at XX on approach to EWR. We were going in and out of large clouds. I saw what at first appeared to be a balloon just to the left, under wing level. I watched as it climbed. I could see that it was not a balloon, but a large drone. We were under 10,000 feet, as the captain had signaled such. The drone was yellow and black, black rotors. I estimate that it was 50-75 yards away. I took a time stamp on my phone about 10 seconds later. It was XX37Hrs Eastern Time. The pilots had left the aircraft before I could make my way to the front of the plane.
1818646: While piloting my aircraft at Northern Colorado Regional Airport (FNL), I was holding short of Runway 33 at Taxiway A1, and I contacted the Tower and requested to takeoff Runway 33 and remain in the pattern for landing Runway 33. Tower cleared me for takeoff, advising me of an aircraft just departing ahead on Runway 33. I was instructed by the Tower to remain in left closed traffic for Runway 33.After climbing to pattern altitude, I turned crosswind, and then downwind for Runway 33. While mid-field downwind for Runway 33, I noticed several aircraft targets ahead of me to the south were all converging toward runway 33 on my ADS-B display, one from the east and one from the west, both apparently on base for Runway 33 from opposite directions, and a third target (Aircraft Y) approaching from the southeast. Spacing among all 3 appeared inadequate. The Controller told Aircraft Y from the southeast to report 3 mile final. I was scanning the sky and acquired visual contact on all three aircraft. Aircraft Y was unable to turn final due to inadequate spacing with the other two aircraft. I was unable to continue in the standard traffic pattern, as I needed to maneuver east to avoid Aircraft Y as it crossed through final from the southeast and across the downwind to the west, which I estimated to be 500 feet in front of me and 300 feet overhead. Turning east was the safest alternative to remain clear of Aircraft Y and the other two aircraft, as I had them all in sight. The Controller began shouting to all of the pilots 'I don't have radar! I see two targets converging to the south!' The Controller sounded very anxious. I immediately informed the Tower that I was maneuvering to avoid Aircraft Y now in front and above me. I recall that the Controller then called one of the other aircraft and said loudly to 'leave the pattern!', but his instructions were not clear. He then asked where everyone was located. I clearly and calmly replied 'Aircraft X, turned left base to avoid the traffic conflict' with Aircraft Y. The Controller then asked seconds later, 'Who is that on left base?', and I again replied calmly 'this is Aircraft X on mid-left base.' He then cleared me to land Runway 33, told the traffic ahead on final to turn east, and then instructed Aircraft Y (now west of the field) to return to land on Runway 33. There was inadequate traffic spacing for incoming traffic entering the pattern, and incomplete awareness by the Controller of the four aircraft positions relative to one another, followed by his distraught demeanor and very exasperated tone as he complained of having no radar feed. It is also possible that the Controller forgot about my aircraft position in the pattern and that he had instructed me to maintain closed left traffic for Runway 33. I did my best to remain clear of any traffic conflict, communicate calmly and clearly, and defuse the Controller's anxious situation, while maintaining safe spacing from all traffic in the pattern. I was cleared to land Runway 33 and did so safely, and taxied to parking as directed by the controller. No other communication took place between me and the controller.As a recommended solution, the temporary Tower at FNL needs a radar feed installed as soon as possible for better situational awareness for the Controllers. The Controller's shouting and anxious tone heightened the tension of the situation for the other pilots, which was not helpful in this scenario. A professional demeanor by the Controller with clear, yet rapid instructions would have been more effective at resolving the traffic conflicts.
1819509: My student pilot and I had just entered the pattern from a 45 degree leg to left downwind when a call on CTAF addressed us by call sign, asked our intentions, and said we were 'all over the place'. I looked to my right and saw another airplane about 500 feet from us, also on left downwind. The pilot said on CTAF that he had just turned from crosswind to downwind and was aware of our entry from the 45 based on our position reports. He said he would extend downwind to allow us to land ahead of him. I can think of three factors that contributed to my failure to see the traffic until so late.First, the CTAF frequency for ZZZ is shared by numerous airports in the area. While I was talking my student through the pattern entry, we were hearing calls for at least four different airports without any silence, so we had to talk to each other over these calls. In such a situation it was easy to miss the one call we needed to hear.Second, the frequency was congested shortly before the traffic conflict by a lengthy and non-standard position report ending with, 'could any traffic in the area please advise'. This may have been the pilot of the aircraft that conflicted with me, or it may have been an unrelated call at another airport that blocked the frequency. A colleague who had just landed at the same airport later told me that the same pilot had also called him on CTAF while he was on final, asking his 'intentions after landing'. Third, my student had become disoriented while making a teardrop turn to the 45 degree entry, and I was distracted by helping her get reoriented to the airport and make a correct pattern entry.
1819754: While supporting a Metro pilot as a non-acting crew member on the ZZZ-ZZZZ run who was unfamiliar with the specifics, we were returning to ZZZ and found the airplane in a near-miss with VFR Traffic. The pilot, was instructed to fly direct to the IAF. The controller alerted us about VFR traffic, later instructing to expedite descent to 4,300 feet. I continued to watch for traffic as it was on my side of the aircraft. I found the traffic and alerted the Captain that it was at the same altitude, heading in our direction of flight. Being unfamiliar with the aircraft I'm not sure if there is proper TCAS, but we received an alert and immediately descended to avoid the near-miss with VFR traffic. The pilot flying then told the Approach Controller his action and intent, and the controller repeated twice 'below MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) climb to 4,300 feet but we were unable due to the VFR traffic we were avoiding. After successfully avoiding the traffic the Captain climbed to 4,300 feet and continued the approach. I saw the VFR/colliding traffic at the airplane's 3 o'clock, the side of the airplane I could visually see from my observation seat. Lack of vectoring instruction from ATC for two airplanes on a collision course. Captain immediately descended to avoid collision with VFR traffic. IFR traffic and VFR traffic needs better observation from ATC. Though I was a non-acting crew member on this flight the Captain and I worked as a team and executed proper CRM to avoided a mid-air collision. I was operating Aircraft X to ZZZ, as the Captain and Pilot Flying. Onboard I had a Brasilia First Officer, who flew down to ZZZZ with me to assist with customs and all the paperwork associated with the run. ZZZ-ZZZZ was his regular run, and I was covering it for the day. The additional crew member was not an active crew member during the leg, but he was on headset with me helping to monitor the flight. It was towards the end of the flight, and we were being vectored by Approach. We were flying towards the Initial Approach Fix for the ILS Approach and descending to 4,300 feet. During the descent, ATC called out VFR traffic to our 3 o'clock position several miles away, at an altitude of 4,500 feet. During the descent, ATC has also told us to expedite our descent. Initially, we saw traffic in that direction and called 'in sight' to ATC, but I quickly realized we had identified a 737 climbing, not the VFR traffic we were looking for. I decided to use the First Officer and asked him to continue to look for the VFR traffic. He told me he had it in sight, and he helped me locate it. At about that same time, the transponder gave an aural alert 'traffic, 1 mile, same altitude'. When I saw the traffic, we were very close and a couple of hundred feet below it. The other aircraft had little relative motion on the windscreen, so I knew our flight paths would cross very closely. At that moment, I made a split-second decision to exercise Pilot in Command authority, and I deviated from our altitude by initiating a descent. I immediately advised ATC that I was deviating due to traffic, and I was descending to 3,500 feet. The weather was VFR, so I felt like descending was the safest option for the flight. The controller responded that I was below his Minimum Vectoring Altitude and needed to return to 4,300 feet. I told him that we would go back to 4,300 feet when able. I stayed around 3,500 feet until I felt like we were clear of the traffic. The controller asked if I was responding to an RA. I told him, no. I'm not sure if was explained that the aircraft was not equipped with a TCAS. Eventually, we returned to 4,300 feet, got a visual on ZZZ, flew a Visual Approach to the field, and continued the flight without further abnormalities. We were aware of the event the moment it occurred through active monitoring. I think the instructions we received from ATC were the primary factor in this event. I deviated from our assigned altitude to create a safe amount of separation between our aircraft. I should have queried the controller more about the traffic at 4,500 feet as he was having us expedite our descent. That could have given him an opportunity to change his instruction for us. I thought his plan was to get us further below the traffic.
1820170: It was my second day on the line. This was a repositioning flight with two other crew members in the back who I was taking to ZZZ to fly their lines. I was on standby for the first half of the day and I had just flown ZZZ to ZZZ1 then to ZZZ2 and was in IMC from take off to landing on each flight. I was unaware upon leaving ZZZ1 that they had scheduled me to fly these other pilots to ZZZ after reaching ZZZ2. So I operated the flight and all went according to plan except I had an unstable approach into ZZZ. Using the auto pilot for the approach I ended up descending below minimum altitude for the final approach fix and continued well below glide slope until I was approximately 1200 AGL at which point I disconnected autopilot, increased power to help arrest the descent rate, caught up to the glide slope and hand flew the rest of the approach. I relied too heavily on the autopilot and lost situational awareness. I also could have asked one of the other pilots to act as copilot.I think it would be safer to not have new hire Captains fly without an FO (First Officer) in hard IMC for multiple legs even if it is just a reposition flight. And if there is a crew member on board they should sit right seat.
1820885: Coming from the DYMND Arrival for visual/ILS backup to [Runway] 28L. ATC cleared traffic onto 28L for departure. We were around 800 feet on the approach as they began their takeoff roll. Separation looked tight and we mentioned the possible go around. As they rotated and began their climb, we incurred wake turbulence which pushed our limits on a stable approach and would have led to a landing outside of the touchdown zone, a go around was commenced. Returned and landed uneventfully on 28L.
1821139: I was flying with a private pilot student to practice landings at ZZZ1. We departed ZZZ, and arrived midfield at ZZZ1 at XA:40 local time according to my ADSB track log. Other traffic in the pattern was using Runway XX, so we made right traffic for XX. The student and I completed two laps in the traffic pattern for XX. On our third lap in the pattern, we were flying in front of another Skyhawk in the pattern, Aircraft Y. At XA:57 we turned base to final for runway 26 and made a radio call on CTAF. We heard Aircraft Y call base behind us. At XA:58, just past the numbers of Runway XX, I saw Aircraft Z low and climbing towards us. I could see his tail number. I called my controls and executed a go around and a turn to the right. I attempted to raise Aircraft Z on the radio, but had no answer. Aircraft Y responded to my calls and advised me that the aircraft appeared to be making a left crosswind turn and exiting the pattern to the north. I attempted to raise the pilot on 1XX.X, in case he maybe just had the frequency wrong, but this did not work to raise a response. My student and I exited the traffic pattern to the north to gain altitude. Then, re entered right traffic for [Runway] XX with a 45 degree entry to the downwind. We continued to make our radio calls for the traffic pattern. As we turned base for XX, I observed on my ADSB that Aircraft Z had made a 180 degree turn from his heading and was now headed directly for us, 300 feet high and descending. I took the controls and called a go around, extending the base. The aircraft was now at my altitude, close and lining up for the base to final for Runway XX. I had not heard any radio calls from the aircraft. We exited the ZZZ1 area and departed to another area until we could contact approach to get clearance back in to ZZZ for a landing. After the incident, I called the pilot of Aircraft Y to confirm what had happened. The pilot mentioned that they had landed at ZZZ1 and talked to a mechanic who witnessed the incident and talked to Aircraft Z after he had landed. According to the mechanic, the pilot of Aircraft Z said that they had a radio failure. It is unknown to me what transpired with the aircraft after that.
1821169: Planned flight for the day was to ZZZ1 (for fuel) then to ZZZ. Preflight planning conducted with assistance from ForeFlight mobile application. Departed Runway XX. Climb to 1500 MSL, 14 min cruise to ZZZ1 with landing. Landed at ZZZ1. The flight was conducted satisfactorily. The aircraft was then fueled as necessary.Secondary preflight planning was completed. Satisfactory takeoff and climb out to 7,500 MSL. Approximately 29 minutes, started to notice engine roughness with a significant drop in tachometer RPM. The Pilot in command (PIC) took over as sole manipulator of control and emergency checklist for engine failure in flight initiated. Looked for suitable landing area. Increased in engine RPM occurred and became within glide distance of ZZZ. Engine roughness and drop in RPM began again and ZZZ Tower contacted, advising of need for precautionary landing due to engine roughness. Decision was made to not [get priority handling]. Smooth and satisfactory landing made at ZZZ. After slowing and attempting to turn off Runway, the aircraft did not have any right turning authority. Airplane would only turn left in circle when power applied. Suspected right tire or brake malfunction. Contacted the Tower and asked for permission to shut down aircraft on runway to inspect aircraft.Aircraft was satisfactorily shut down on Runway XY with airport crew arriving for assistance. On post flight walk around, it was found that the right tire became flat, no other external damage grossly observed. Also found to have fluid leak within right pilot side inside firewall. Aircraft was towed to FBO for diagnostics of engine and repair of right tire. When asked if needed to report anything to Tower or FAA, the ZZZ airport crew stated nothing was needed. Furthermore, the Tower did not mention of any need to provide any post flight report during communications. No accident or serious incident occurred.There were a few factors found on post-flight that may have caused the problems:1. Engine Roughness: The engine was new with approximately 28 hours on the engine. Engine during break in period was using Aeroshell 100W. Furthermore, this flight was conducted with cruise altitude at 7,500 MSL. Miscommunication and ill-information about any special procedures regarding aircraft break in were not discussed between aircraft owner and PIC. PIC was told to use 100W oil from previous aircraft owner (box in back of aircraft). Furthermore, the aircraft owner did not provide engine overhaul information or procedures needed for aircraft. On mechanic review, it was found that the left magneto was rotated 17 degrees causing the engine to overheat, an oil line by the firewall was damaged causing a leak, cylinders were glazed, induction air leak, and some crankcase oil leak. Overall a combination of these factors is what probably lead to engine roughness. Post flight testing, the engine performed within specifications 2250 static RPM, 600FPM climb, 2350 dynamic RPM. Engine oil consumption has increased, likely due to glazed cylinders, and is being sent to Company1 for re-honing. Furthermore, the magnetos are being sent in to [Company] Magneto to be re-checked.2. Right Flat Tire: No noted gross evident issues on pre-flight inspection for tires, struts, fairing, or braking systems. Landings was smooth and satisfactory. Theory for tire damage could be due to stuck break after landing and prior to right turn out to taxiway, in conjunction with weak spot on tire and/or a foreign object on runway and/or other. Tire was satisfactorily repaired at ZZZ. Reviewing this scenario there are a few factors to consider. There needs to be improved communication between aircraft owner and operator (PIC), especially during critical times where specific procedures are needed (such as a new engine break in). The right tire flat is a chance occurrence, and I do not think that the flight could have been handled different to prevent. The pilot did all in power to safely shut down the aircraft and immediately check out airplane to prevent any further damage.I have had a clean pilot record, commercial license and CFI. I will use the lessons from this flight for myself and all future students for the purpose of discussing complete airplane maintenance with airplane owners (especially new airplanes), what to do when engine becomes rough, and procedures to follow with a flat tire.
1821532: On the RNAV Stadium Visual to runway 29 we were vectored behind an Airbus 321 on the ILS to 22R. We joined the visual at GIMEE with the airport and the [A321] in sight. We had been cleared to land prior to crossing GIMEE. Tower reported winds calm, ATIS had winds 200/6. Prior to SLIMR we were configured and slowing to approach speed. At approximately 1,500 ft AGL I called for the landing check and called to the FO that [the A321] appeared to be crossing the numbers and spacing looked good. Continued in LVAV/VNAV till the autopilot rolled us out on final at about 1,000 ft AGL. At this point PAPI showed slightly high and corrected to visual glide path. A rapid right roll was encountered just prior to touchdown causing contact of the right main. This slowed the roll but aircraft was still rolling right. Immediate left aileron was applied along with deployment of the auto speed brakes quickly caused the left main to touch down. Roll out was normal from this point. Wing drop was so rapid that I thought the right gear leg had collapsed. The event occurred so quickly that there was not even time to consider a go-around. The application of power and lifting off again would likely only have exacerbated this situation placing us at a bank angle at low speed with an at the time unknown problem. During debrief we determined that the event occurred just prior to the intersection with Runway 22R and was likely a wake turbulence event. An ACARS generated report showed a max bank angle of 6.9 degrees with a predicted wing tip strike at a bank angle of 7.5 degrees. The FO inspected the aircraft for possible damage, none was found. The event was reported to Tower, but they did not seem concerned. I contacted Clearance Delivery to get more information on the preceding aircraft. CD took more interest and sounded like it would be reported.
1821612: En route from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 we were directed by the physician on call to divert to ZZZ which we had just passed at FL350. The Captain gave me controls of the aircraft and radios and began the fix strategy. We were given a heading direct to ZZZ and began a descent to the airport. We began the approach on a visual right downwind as there was a cell to the north and west of the airport we wanted to avoid. Selected speed was chosen as we slowed down, however, when managed speed was selected the aircraft accelerated because I had not activated the approach. We captured the error, however, these few seconds caused us to be high and fast. Given the already high-altitude airport and compressed diversion time for the medical issue, we elected to do a visual left 360 and rejoin final. We had selected the final approach fix altitude, however, when we did our left 360 turn it took us away from the airport. The Tower Controller alerted us that he had an altitude alert and we climbed back to the 7,200 feet altitude for the fix we were now joining the ILS. We continued the approach without further issue.Cause - 1. Compressed, high pressure with the medical emergency of passenger with 60/40 blood pressure.2. Out of sequence normal approach and landing with the diversion that greatly compressed our time from top of descent to landing. 3. Choosing ZZZ - high altitude/high terrain as a divert airport.4. Loss of situational awareness as we made the turn away from the airport.Suggestions -1. Take vectors out for a longer final approach.2. If possible, choose diversion airports that have less threats. 3. If a turn for an airport is needed to descend or slow - make them towards the airport not away as altitude is less likely going to be an issue with regards to terrain avoidance. During a medical divert we were high and fast. On approach we accomplished a left 360 to descend. We initially had 7,300 feet set and when we turned inbound and had the field insight we began a descent to 6,300 feet the final approach fix altitude. Approach received a low altitude alert and informed us. We climbed and continued the approach visually. We never descended below 6,300 feet before the FAF.Visual approach, high and fast resulted in loss of situational awareness. Avoid visual approaches when in unplanned situations, get vectors for an instrument approach.
1821685: The FO was flying a visual approach to Runway 33 in BGR. He was descending to 2,300 feet between ELSUH and CUVOT intersections and got terrain warning. There are towers on top of these small hills near the course. He turned the autopilot off and climbed a little with some extra power and the warning went away.
1823418: Aircraft X had landed [Runway] XXR and stopped on the runway to question the exiting instructions. This delay in exiting caused the next [Runway] XXR arrival to go around. Then, an airport vehicle requested permission to inspect the runway because there's some local airport procedure to sweep the runway behind a [type aircraft]. There was a full sequence of arrivals to [Runway] XXR and [Runway] XY. Then, while the Local Controller was sorting out the Aircraft X arrival, the succeeding go-around, and the airport vehicle, Aircraft Y ([Runway] XXR) and the Aircraft Z ([Runway] XY) tied at the intersection. ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed, Local Controller issued a late go-around.Actual time on position may not have been a factor, rather the lack of staffing to open other positions and reduce the Local Controller's workload. There were only two of us in the tower at the time, simply because no one else was available. We had asked, and been told that we would be getting more people at XA:30z. Positions in the TRACON were also combined, and despite the fact that management had kept 3 tower-certified controllers down [in the TRACON] to 'get time', one controller was working both the runways Arrival position, and vectoring the final to Runway [Runway] XY having to sequence in with the intersecting [Runway] XXR arrivals. The search for more controllers is on-going. What else can one do, when asking for more staffing, and being told to just wait? I was working Local Controls combined. I had Aircraft X land Runway XXR. I told the aircraft to exit the runway at taxiway. An airport vehicle asked to check the runway behind the Aircraft X as per our SOP (Standard Operating Procedure). Aircraft X then stopped at taxiway on the runway an asked if I was sure I wanted him to clear there as he is a [type aircraft]. I said affirmative. It was then too close for the next arrival to land safely so I sent him around. I then got the airport vehicle on to the runway but had to have him exit early as more arrivals were too close. It was then that the ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed informing me that the next [Runway] XXR arrival and [Runway] XY arrival were in conflict. I sent the [Runway] XXR arrival, Aircraft Y, around. Aircraft Y was about to touch down when he executed the go around. I had become distracted by the situation with Aircraft X and vehicle. By the time I was made aware of the tie between the [Runway] XY arrival and [Runway] XXR arrival the ASDE-X had alarmed. I would give more space behind Aircraft X to do the runway sweep and maybe have local controls split during the push.
1823851: Early descent and low speed condition resulting in go-around. I was the Pilot Flying. Very short flight. Visual approach to RWY 15 at CHS. I was expecting the ILS approach. I missed that the GS for RWY 15 was out of service. We had briefed the OSPRI7 STAR. ATC recleared us direct to the airport and eventually direct MAMAE intersection to join the localizer for [Runway] 15 at 3,000 [feet] ft. Airport was in sight and we were cleared for a visual approach. I armed the approach and when we went into altitude capture at 3,000 [feet] I incorrectly set an altitude below 3,000 [feet] to allow the descent to continue in order to join the glide slope. I then realized we were not receiving the glide slope and were below the FAF crossing altitude at 1000ft. I disconnected the autopilot and stopped the descent. Unfortunately I did not also call for the flight directors off initially. I am relatively new to the equipment. Since we were in landing configuration of course the speed dropped rapidly. We were in landing configuration with the airport and PAPI's in sight but since the approach was unstable I decided to go around. We then flew the RWY 15 RNAV (GPS)Y to a normal landing. It was the third leg of a busy day with thunderstorm avoidance on the first two flights. It is my practice to carefully review the NOTAMs but somehow I missed the GS OTS. I haven't been into CHS as yet and the flight is very short and our ATC clearance had us high from the top of descent.Direct to a new airport on a time compressed flight for a visual at night is never in my opinion a pleasant way to conclude a long day of flying. Upon honest reflection I fully acknowledge I had a strong expectation bias for the ILS to 15. The lack of the GS and the unexpected consequences placed us in a reactionary position which is unacceptable.Our training is clear on how to capture and correct erroneous situations should they occur and we did our best to stop and correct an inadvertently entered unstable position. This was a clear example of the value and necessity of our human factors training. I know these things have happened before and I consider it my professional responsibility to not allow it to happen to me. And yet it did. Recognizing, and fully appreciating how higher than expected workload situations can present themselves is an essential aspect to our work. An increased diligence regarding the review of NOTAMs is a resounding suggestion I'm making to myself for one. Also, the need for particularly increased vigilance when in situations such as this is something I'll never forget.
1823883: Low altitude alert from AFW Tower during night visual approach to [Runway] 16L from the south. We entered a left downwind to [Runway] 16L, turned base early due to traffic ahead, and descended initially to 1,000 feet AGL. At the alert from ATC, we cross-checked our altitude, intercepted the glide path from below but inside the instrument FAF, and landed uneventfully. Turning earlier than what would have set us up at the instrument FAF and attempting to interpolate a visual descent path, cross cockpit, at night. Set up for a left base at AFW at 1,500 feet AGL rolled off for the turn to final and slowly descended to 1,000 feet AGL to join up on the ILS glide slope for [Runway] 16L. During the rollout received a call from ATC saying they were getting an altitude alert and heck our altitude. At no point during the rollout did we go lower than 1,000 feet AGL and rolled out on final on glide path. Landing was uneventful. We were on a visual and turned inside the FAF for traffic. As a result we were lower than normal during the final turn.
1823988: Captain [was] Pilot Flying. He briefed the OSPRI arrival and ILS to [Runway] 15. ATC kept us high, then Cleared for the straight in visual. Gear, flaps and speed brakes out to get down. We both missed that the glideslope was out of service on the ATIS. We realized we were too low and leveled off around 1,000 feet. At some point we got the low energy speed warning. We had left the speed brakes out. Retracted them. Disconnected the FD's. Captain called for a go around. Preformed the GA and returned for the RNAV 15. Busy day flying around storms. Last flight at night. Short flight. ATC keeping us high. Expectation bias to the ILS. I had recently been to CHS at night and the ILS was working. New Captain to [aircraft], all his other time was in Boeing aircraft. My failure to trap our errors earlier. I will create more effective barriers going forward. For example: Request ILS/RNAV approaches vs visual at night. Get delay vectors when ATC keeps us high.
1824682: I was making a normal approach to Runway XXR on a solo flight. Winds were about 220 @ 6 mph at the time. After I had turned to base, ATC inquired if I had turned to base. I informed ATC that I had turned to base and at that point immediately needed to turn to final. ATC asked the plane at taxiway to hold position. Glide slope was normal. I was on centerline and airspeed was 85 mph. Final approach continued normally and as I crossed threshold, I reduced throttle to idle. The airplane landed firmly but did not bounce. When the nose wheel came down, I perceived a violent shaking of the nose wheel. The airplane began heading to the right side of the runway and I attempted to correct as normal. However, my corrections started a series of oscillations that grew in amplitude. The airplane was now headed in to the grass safety area after taxiway and I let the plane continue on its track for fear of flipping the plane. The airplane went into and out of the drainage ditch and came to a stop about 2-3 yards from taxiway X. I believe that one of the contributing factors to the event was task overload. This was my second solo flight and the additional load of ATC's inquiry, the follow on instructions to the other plane near my intended runway, and my focus toward the other aircraft may have used more attention than intended. I believe also that a greater emphasis overall on safe after landing roll would be good. In the FAA 'Airplane Flying Handbook', after landing roll safety is addressed but does not receive the emphasis it deserves.
1825554: Inbound on the ILS [Runway] 03 practice approach into OGD. Tower had departing traffic off of [runway]17. Departing traffic told to fly runway heading and get us (ILS traffic) in sight. Departure aircraft reported us in sight. Tower then requested the traffic pass behind us to continue on their course to the northwest. Departing traffic then turned in front of us on the ILS with myself as the instructor having to take control from my student who was under the foggles and break off the approach to the south in order to avoid a closer occurrence.
1825576: On a visual approach to runway 19 at MKC, we were flying on a extended (wide) right base for runway 19 in a descent and were about to start leveling out when ATC (MKC Tower) gave us a minimum safe altitude warning (MSAW). Tower advised us to level out or climb and to check our altimeter setting to the local. I leveled the airplane and began a shallow climb while checking my altitude and surroundings. The altitude we were at wasn't too low for the local terrain. Nor was our altimeter setting off. The aircraft that was being flown is equipped with a terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS) that wasn't triggered at any point in the flight. We continued our approach, joined the visual glide path, and landed without incident. Later, after some research, I learned that MSAWs can be triggered based on descent rate. Our descent rate may have been high during the visual approach. In the future, I will do better to monitor and control my descent rate, especially in wide patterns to urban runways.
1825928: Landing Runway 28 GDL, night VMC with bright moonlight. Set up to land Runway 28 using the ILS DME 2 with the ILS DME 2 transition from IKBAN. At the last minute, Control told us to descend via the LIVRI 1D Arrival. We quickly put this arrival into the FMC, but did not change the approach. Shortly after starting the arrival, we were given direct to PLADE with continued descent to the mandatory altitude of 9,000 ft at PLADE which is the point leading into the ILS Approach to Runway 28. There was a discontinuity between PLADE and CI28, which I closed up. Once we reached PLADE, I asked my FO (First Officer) to set 7,100 ft. in the mode control panel which is the minimum altitude at CI28 and started a VNAV descent with the intention to arm the ILS just prior to CI28. At approximately 7,600 ft. we received a warning 'too low terrain'. We could visually see the terrain and started to level off, then, very quickly received 'terrain, pull up' with amber showing on the terrain display. I immediately complied by going into the CFIT recovery procedure. We climbed to approximately 8,000 ft. and leveled off seeing that we were well clear of all terrain (no more warning and terrain indicator showed us to be clear). We then reassessed. At that time, we were very close to CI28 and had plenty of light from the city and a very bright moon. We were also in a good position to continue to the airport, so I continued to an uneventful landing. We were landing Runway 28 in Guadalajara. Night VMC conditions with moonlight provided adequate visual references. We were set up to land Runway 28 using the ILS DME2 or localizer Runway 28 with the transition for the ILS DME 2 with the IKBAN transition. At the last minute, Control told us to descend via the LIVRI 1D arrival. After changing to this arrival in the FMS, we realized that we needed to descend quickly. To complicate matters, Control give us directions to go direct to PLADE. I estimate Control shortened our arrival by 40 to 50 miles in giving us the arrival change and direct PLADE which greatly compounded our decent plan. This caused us to have to execute an expedited decent while having to re-program the FMS and plan for this new routing. I verbalized terrain that was to our right as we were turning direct PLADE and both the CA (Captain) and I correlated this to what we were seeing on our terrain displays. Prior to reaching PLADE, Control cleared us for the ILS Zulu Runway 28. However, we heard cleared for the ILS Two. I attribute this miscommunication to language barriers. CA asked me to set 7,100 ft., which would've been correct for ILS 2 but 7,700 ft would've been correct for ILS Z. We got the 'too low, terrain' oral warning followed by the 'terrain, pull up'. CA commanded auto pilot off, stow speed brake (Even though they weren't in use), pitched up and added full thrust. We had the terrain in sight the whole time, as well as the Runway environment. We climbed approximately 500 ft before determining that we could safely continue the approach without incident. We landed on Runway 28 without incident.
1826206: I was approach the ZZZ from the north, preparing to perform a touch and go at the airport before flying northbound back towards ZZZ1. Before beginning my VFR descent, I obtained the current weather at the airport, and I found that the wind would be favoring Runway XX at the airport. From there I determined that in order to conduct a standard pattern entry, I should overfly the airport at 1,700 ft. MSL or 500 ft. above pattern altitude, and then perform a 225 degree turn to enter the left downwind from a 45 degree angle to Runway XX. At 10 miles, I began to announce my intentions regularly at intervals of approximately 2.5 miles.At a distance of around 5 miles from the airport, a Piper Pawnee preparing to tow a glider announced that they would be making a right downwind departure from Runway XX, towards the east. This would be the only transmission I noted from this aircraft until I would be touching down on Runway XX. I continued approaching the airfield and I had the two aircraft in sight. As the Pawnee turned downwind, I noted that my flight path would create a collision hazard, should I have continued my descent. As such, I immediately applied full power and climbed to 2,800 ft. MSL. I continued to watch as the Pawnee, with its glider in tow passed underneath me by approximately 500 ft. Climbing was likely the best evasive action in this case because I was in a high wing Cessna, while he was in a low-wing Pawnee. Had I descended, we both would have lost visual contact with each other and no additional action could have been taken should it have been necessary. The factors which appear to have contributed to this event appear to be the Pawnee pilot's lack of communication when departing, thus preventing me from restructuring my arrival plan so that I may safely avoid him. Additionally, he utilized a non-standard right downwind departure that was not charted at the airport for Runway XX. I believe that the Pawnee pilot could have extended their crosswind leg so as to remain well clear of me. On my own part, I should have taken earlier action to increase separation such as maintaining 3,000 ft. over the airport, as I was indeed aware that he would be making right traffic and climbing out of the airport. I had misjudged the climb rate of the Pawnee, and as such suspected that I could pass in front and above them before there would have been a collision hazard.
1826213: In an extremely busy pattern on both sides of ZZZ's Runway XX, 2 planes (Aircraft Y and another- Aircraft Y might have been the lead flight in a flight of two, which I thought were normally not allowed at ZZZ) are given instructions by ATC to extend their right downwind and not turn base due to incoming straight in traffic (my airplane, Aircraft X). Aircraft Y seemingly acknowledges instruction, reports myself in sight, then turns base contrary to instructions. Aircraft Y is at this point 100-200 ft. above Aircraft X, and enters Aircraft X's field of view high and crossing to the left.ATC spots the deviation right as I did, and issues instructions to Aircraft Y to proceed and enter a left downwind.Aircraft Y then turns right- and begins entering final when ATC again contacts Aircraft Y to issue corrective action.During this time I have expedited my descent by going engine idle and adopting a slightly nose down attitude. Due to low AGL, nearby towers and already having 20 degrees of flaps in, I am hesitant to enter a forward slip and descend faster (aircraft type placards state to avoid forward slips with flaps). It's possible that I'm also reaching the end of my endurance- coming back from an hour of pattern practice at ZZZ1 where conditions were gusty. My flight time at this point was around 1.6 hours, and my flights up to that point at typically max of 1.8.I have debated if I should have immediately turned right or even left. While I had the right of way (a lower craft engaged in landing), the right of way isn't going to help me if I end up in a midair. In the end I think it was correct not to turn- the pattern was extremely busy, there were higher towers to the right and planes on extended down wind to both sides. I could have caused another NMAC by turning suddenly. ATC was aware of the situation, issuing instructions to Aircraft Y and I was going to pass safely- although close- below.While I pass under (300-400 ft. estimated?) Aircraft Y either completes a right 360 or an S-turn, and ends up in an extended left downwind.Because I am below the ideal approach path to Runway XX, I put power in and arrest my descent. I actually end up too high for the runway and decide to do a go around. The go around is uneventful and I land safely. I believe Aircraft Y actually landed in between my go around and actual landing. Moderately heavy traffic relative to ZZZ, training in progress, everything under control of the Trainee until I noticed an aircraft turning base without any sequence or landing clearance yet. This aircraft was initially part of a flight of two who had just separated in the downwind, because we have to issue separate landing clearances at ZZZ, the AID (Aircraft IDentification) is Aircraft Y. Multiple inbound aircraft on either downwind and on straight in.I key up and say 'Aircraft Y and flight, both of you guys, Don't come in on base, there is traffic at the [VFR reporting point], so don't come in on base right now, you are going to follow the guy on a 3 mile final' The [VFR reporting point] is 3 mile final, Aircraft Y is starting a 1 mile right base so this is plenty of time to catch and correct this pilot. The second aircraft from the original flight of two responds traffic in sight and immediately corrects back to the downwind. I respond to 2 other calls then scan back to ensure Aircraft Y was correcting, he wasn't, I say 'Aircraft Y it looks like you are doing exactly what I said not to do, unless the radar is deceiving me here.' Pilot responds 'Aircraft Y was already on base', I respond 'OK, well I just said don't go on base, you missed that part, so let's go right turn back to the north downwind for both you and the other guy (his flight wing man, who was following instructions)' Pilot responds 'Affirm, right turn, north downwind, Aircraft Y'. I tell the original wing man to now turn base, he correctly responds, I then scan back and see Aircraft Y not following instructions, again the pilot does the opposite and starts a left turn towards final before correcting right and continuing for the north downwind. I then say 'Aircraft Y are you literally on final right now cutting someone off?' Pilot responds 'No, I'm trying to get out of here, we're turning, Aircraft Y'I advise the traffic on final 'Aircraft X, the guy in front of you is moving out of your way, Runway XX cleared to land' His response seemed to be partially blocked but I heard 'Aircraft X'.All aircraft eventually land, brasher warning was not issued. The pilot of Aircraft X called the tower a couple hours later and said he wanted to file a NMAC. He said he was aware of the situation developing and heard the controller (me) several times tell the other aircraft not to turn base and issue instructions which the pilot of Aircraft Y repeatedly disobeyed. I should have issued a traffic alert to both aircraft, but at the minimum to Aircraft X.
1826565: Upon arrival at ZZZ, A normal landing was set up. Engine and flaps were in landing configuration. Landing gear was extended and confirmed down by green indicator light and by visual (pilot side main gear by viewing out pilot window, co-pilot side main and nose gear by wing located mirror). I landed on both main gear as normal. As the nose settled during deceleration, the nose fell to the runway. The plane slide to a stop on the center line of the runway. I turned off electronics, master switch and fuel. I exited the plane. I did not notice any fluids leaking from the engine compartment or any other location. I contacted the Manager of the airport and the Manager of the FBO. I also spoke briefly with the FAA. The FAA authorized removal of the aircraft from the runway. Upon lifting the nose of the plane by a front end loader, the nose gear limply extended. Upon kicking the nose gear a few times, the gear appeared to lock down. The plane was towed from the runway.
1826885: During a normal flight lesson in the traffic pattern with my student, my student landed the plane with full brakes and the brakes locked up. The plane took a hard right toward the edge of the runway and I took the flight controls. With barely any directional control left I was able to keep the plane on the runway long enough to to make a taxi way. We took the taxiway at a fairly high speed and then I was able to regain directional control and bring us to a full stop. No damage was caused to the plane, runway or taxiway, or any signs or lights on the airport. Tower asked if we needed any assistance and I said negative just to taxi back to the ramp.
1827217: I was vectoring Aircraft X into ZZZ for an ILS Approach. He was vectored through final and left high for VFR traffic on the localizer. He called the field in sight over the Final Approach Fix, was cleared for a Visual and switched to ZZZ Tower. He turned towards ZZZ1. VFR aircraft above 1500 feet near the localizer are a conflict because 2400 feet is the crossing altitude for the Initial Approach Fix ZZZZZ. VFR aircraft departing ZZZ or ZZZ2 Class D southbound are in a head on conflict with any aircraft on the localizer into ZZZ. IFR aircraft often end up being too high for a localizer approach because they can't descend because of VFR traffic on the localizer and they get a Visual Approach instead. It's also not uncommon for aircraft to be vectored through the final approach course to avoid traffic or descend. Both of these courses of action can disorient pilots, but there is nowhere to break them out without creating another conflict somewhere else. A few miles east of the localizer is higher terrain. An aircraft at 3000 feet within 10 miles of the airport will not be able to climb to the Minimum Vectoring Altitude in time. If the aircraft continues on a vector north to parallel ZZZ1, they could conflict with a departure off of ZZZ1, likely a prop on a 020 heading climbing to 3000 feet. ZZZ1, ZZZ, and ZZZ2 are so close to each other that it can be confusing which airport they see when they aren't able to fly a straight path inbound because of VFR conflicts.ZZZ localizer approach course need to be controlled airspace. VFR aircraft should not be able to fly on or through the localizer without talking to ATC. It's impossible to predict the actions of a VFR aircraft not on frequency. They climb, descend and maneuver around traffic they do see, sometimes making 360's. About XA:25 PST I observed Aircraft X, who was on an ZZZ ILS Runway XXL approach, heading westbound about 2 miles east of ZZZ1. They had gone through the ZZZ final and appeared to be flying towards ZZZ1 and not ZZZ. I told the Local controller and the Cab Supervisor then called ZZZ1 Tower on the shout line advising them of the traffic and that ZZZ Tower was attempting to turn Aircraft to the north towards ZZZ. Aircraft X's data tag was then changed to Visual Approach, ZZZ VA XXL. Aircraft X landed ZZZ Runway XXL without incident.
1828483: Aircraft was on final approach segment of GPS36 at M41. Conditions were hazy with scattered clouds at 3000 ft MSL (2500 ft AGL). Subject aircraft was VMC prior to FAF and had cancelled IFR and switched to CTAF. At two miles from touchdown end of Runway 36, with aircraft at approx 1000 ft AGL, pilot not flying (PNF) called traffic off right wing. PF noted rapidly approaching target and banked left. Both PF and PNF noted a large UAV (drone) pass within 1/4 mile of right wing. PF switched to Memphis approach frequency and reported near miss. A missed approach was not required and PF was able to recover to stabilized approach and land without further incident. Subject aircraft had ADS-B in/out capability (L-3 Lynx NGT-9000 transponder). The UAV did not show on display (Traffic Information Services).Operating a drone on final approach course to airport, in MVFR conditions is extremely careless and reckless. Due to haze conditions, the unlighted drone was difficult to spot and subject aircraft was fortunate to have rated pilot in right seat watching for traffic. Due to conditions, PF was focused on maintaining stabilized approach in marginal VFR conditions.
1828753: Pattern work at ZZZ. Normal landing, normal circumstances, no side loading or hard landings. Airplane veered right on landing, felt like a flat tire. Student, who was pilot flying applied full left rudder to correct but with little effect. Airplane exited the right side of the runway and the right main gear separated from the aircraft. I was able to shut the engine down and prevent engine damage or prop strikes.
1828935: [We] encountered two wake turbulence events while on the downwind at 8,000 feet with Atlanta approach control. First Officer maintained control of the aircraft on both occurrences. After the second sudden right roll we observed the large aircraft we were in trail of and now was below our altitude. We realized the roll was likely not associated with a shear event from the cell nearby. We notified ATC. I would not classify either event as a severe wake turbulence event. There was no 'bank angle' aural. Perhaps ATC separation issue.
1829288: I was performing touch and goes at the local airport ZZZ, I was in the landing phase of flight and flaring. A gust of wind came up as my left main hit the runway and bounced. This made the aircraft swerve right and into the grass. The aircraft was not in control when it suddenly turned right. I applied brakes and the aircraft came to a stop and then I turned left back onto the runway. I made my way to the hanger area and inspected the aircraft from front to back and top to bottom. No damage just some grass blades. Prop was not struck and was clean and free of any indication of prop strike.Looking back after a couple of days leads me to believe that I became too slow at touch down which caused the bounce and temporary loss of control. My perception of my speed was incorrect, it was too slow. My personal minimums were considered prior to flight as I always do, and they were in check and I was mentally and physically ready to fly.I am currently scheduled for some recurrent cross wind training with an instructor as of date.
1830046: ILS XXR with circling to Runway XY with tailwind of 10 knots. Briefed the approach for the ILS with the special ops note for the circling approach to Runway XY. Fly the ILS and turn left at 2 miles from Runway XXR threshold to parallel Rwy XY with flap 3 and initially 160 knots till we have the threshold XY at about 45 degrees of shoulder before turning in and going flaps full when somewhat aligned with the landing Runway. We discussed the wind issue. It didn't work out as planned. ATC late speed reduction and clearance, Captain's confusion of 'cleared for the approach' with the 2,500 foot altitude constraints and the resulting delay in descending and speed reduction despite gear down before the FAF kept us higher and faster then ideal. Autopilot was deselected once below the cloud layer while descending to 1,000 feet MSL. I did hand fly the turn to 110 degree before reversing to align myself with the landing Runway. Just before turning in we got the altitude alert. Crew communications could have been better while the Captain wanted full flaps before the turn to align myself with Runway XY. This could have been avoided by a more thorough briefing to the to refresh the procedure. Final Approach to XY was continued safely to an uneventful landing.ATC Issued Low Altitude Warning
1831529: I set up for the visual to Runway XX backed up with the ILS into ZZZ. The approach met stable approach criteria and landed at approximately 85 knots. Upon landing with all three gear down, the left gear began shaking. I assumed I had a flat tire as we started to drift left slightly. I applied brakes and right rudder, neither of which rectified the situation. The aircraft then continued to roll off to the left of the runway. We hit the grass and the gear caught and we spun around 180 degrees. I notified ATC and shut down the engines. I then called company to inform them that I was off the runway and needed the FBO to bring their passenger van. I asked the passengers if they were okay and explained I thought we had a flat tire. A passenger then informed me my left tire was on the runway about 500 feet further down. I helped the passengers get off the aircraft and told them to stay behind the wing. They all said they were uninjured and were brought to the Gate XX where our agents met them. I stayed with the aircraft and got in contact with Maintenance. When I returned to the terminal I wrote up the aircraft for the tire coming off and the aircraft departing paved surface. I was asked to go back and take more photos of the tire. FBO mechanics came awhile later and were able to get a spare tire on. They said half of the rim was missing so operations and fire went back to the landing spot where they found part of the rim and a handful of pieces of the landing gear all over the runway. The aircraft was towed to the hangar and I left the pieces with the log book with operations in ZZZ.
1832749: While flying the Stadium Visual Approach to Runway 29 at Newark Liberty Airport as Pilot Flying, I saw a white squarish object pass off the lower right side of the aircraft in my peripheral vision. I asked the co-pilot what that had been and he replied it had been a drone. We were at approximately 1000 feet in a descending right turn between the fixes SLIMR and CHUMR. I would estimate the drone had passed underneath the right wing at less than 100 feet separation but far enough away to feel reasonably confident that it had not struck the airplane. The co-pilot agreed and then alerted Newark Tower of the presence of the drone on final approach so that they could pass this information on to the succeeding aircraft on approach. They requested that after landing we provide them with any additional description we could, which we did with Ground Control after clearing the runway and beginning our initial taxi to the gate.
1833101: On visual approach to Runway 01L Tower Controller called an 'altitude alert'. We were cleared for the visual to Runway 01L to Tampa. The glideslope to the ILS 01L was NOTAM'd Out of Service. Tower instructed us to maintain 2,600 feet until north of Macdill AFB. I had briefed that this would cause us to be high and that I would configure the aircraft for landing at 2,600 feet and prior to Macdill. I had also briefed that we would need a high rate of descent to get us on glide path. Once north of Macdill, and runway in sight, I disconnected the autopilot, and started to hand fly the visual approach. At approximately 1,000 feet the First Officer stated we were approaching the (visual 3:1) glidepath. At that time, I had started to reduce the rate of descent. At about the same time the Tower called an altitude alert for Aircraft X. I started to pick up the PAPI and saw we were below glidepath. I continued reducing descent rate to intercept the PAPI glidepath. Aircraft was on glidepath and stable at 500 feet. Landed normally. [Suggest] Brief the visual in more detail on 3:1 glidepath and required rate of descent to intercept from above.
1834238: After we landed in INL we had a runway excursion with a GA aircraft. While on approach we heard the GA traffic make radio calls about being inbound about 3-5 miles north of the field. We notified them of our location of about a 10-mile final for Runway 32 and they said they would wait for us to land before landing themselves. They also called us, 'In sight'. After we landed we advised on the radio we were back-taxiing, and as we were turning around we saw the GA traffic landing while we were still on the runway. They stayed well clear of us and were able to exit the runway so we could back-taxi with no issues, and no evasive maneuvering was required at any point.GA traffic apparently not being aware of the risk of landing on a runway we were still on. While he had us in sight I did not have him in sight or on TCAS, and therefore did not know exactly how close behind us he was. Construction in INL requiring back-taxiing and therefore a longer landing time than usual that the GA traffic was probably used to. Try to advise GA traffic earlier if a need to back-taxi is required. We were flying into an uncontrolled airport and made two-way radio contact with another aircraft north of the field coming into land on the same runway we were. He told us that he would let us go first since we were much faster than him and that he would follow us and be #2 to land. Normal radio calls occurred after that and we landed without incident. Because of construction there are no taxiway turn offs available on the runway and a180 degree turn and back taxi is required. After coming to almost a stop and just about to turn around I made a radio call stating that we would be back taxiing on the runway. Once we just about completed our 180 degree turn we saw the other aircraft about 50 feet off the ground at the other end of the runway in his landing flare. So we pulled as far to the side of the runway as we could just in case he made it down to us. We stayed still until he landed and pulled off on the taxiway about 2,000 feet down the runway where we needed to exit. Once the other aircraft was clear we continued our back taxi to the exit point without incident.The other aircraft stated he saw us on about a one mile final and would be number 2 to land. A contributing factor could be that he never actually saw us or he just disregarded us. Being that he was in aircraft type he might have just assumed he had plenty of runway to land and turn in before us without it being an issue on his end. Poor communication on his end as well, very few radio calls almost all of them were non standard, no tail number, no position reports at all outside of being north of the field, and simply stating 'I'll follow the jet'. A pilot with little regards to aviation safety more or less.The only thing I could think of is maybe more communication. We could have tried getting back on the radio real quick and attempting to have the other aircraft go around. By the time we saw it however, he was basically on the ground
1834739: While crossing the threshold at Vref, a loss of speed and slight roll was encountered, similar to that of mild wake turbulence. Power was added in a timely fashion to arrest descent and neither horizontal, vertical, or speed stability was lost. The GPWS called 'don't sink, don't sink.' The approach remained stable so the landing was continued. We uneventfully touched down safely in the touchdown zone and exited on a high-speed taxiway short of B intersection.
1834845: Landing XXR ZZZ during gusty conditions, received too low terrain while on short final. Low-level windshear reported on east side of field. Wind gust took airspeed up to 175. Neither pilot flying or pilot not flying saw airspeed go above flaps 30 speed of 175, or any movement in flap retraction due to airspeed. Original flap 30 speed was 147. Added 15 for gust. Reported stable at 500 ft. AGL with 1,000 FPM descent. Gusty conditions from above FAF to 100 ft. AGL, but under control. Largest gust after 500 ft. AGL stable call, approximately 150 ft. AGL. On short final, I thought 'too low terrain' was an erroneous warning. Visual conditions from FAF inbound. Touchdown uneventful. Wrote up maintenance discrepancy for possible overspeed due to unusual GPWS warning.
1835135: Landing XXL at ZZZ. Wind reported variable at 5 kts. Wind estimated to be 090 at 10 kts. gusting 20. Held crab and transitioned to slip for landing. Landed center line, but sudden gust lifted right wing and the aircraft veered left. I applied full right aileron, but aircraft departed the left side of the runway. The left main wheel fairing struck a runway light before I could reenter the runway. The nose wheel and right main remained on the runway. The aircraft suffered minor damage to the wheel fairing, and the runway edge light was damaged. Reported damage to Tower, Airport & FAA.
1835695: Landed at ZZZ, Runway XXL, full flap landing. Touched down on centerline, short of the 1,000 feet marker. As plane rolled-out, plane deviated to right. Applied left rudder pedal to turn nose wheel back to center, but airplane continued to the right, in almost a skid motion. Released left rudder due to perceived unsafe condition. Checked to confirm feet not uneven braking. Began to apply even braking, but plane continued to [go] right. Released brakes, and confirmed feet off brakes. At [the] same time, confirmed throttle idle.Assessed situation for potential go-around, but speed was reduced and quickly approaching runway edge without noticeable correction to centerline. Determined go-around not feasible or safe. Once I assessed the plane was going to exit the centerline and enter the grass, I then confirmed throttle idle and attempted to once again straighten nose wheel and traversed through the grass between Taxiway XX and XY off XXL. Plane then exited grass onto Taxiway XZ and I was then able to stop safely, having been slowed by the grass. Fire services were dispatched to inspect the plane and Operations to inspect area and runway. Aircraft had no noticeable damage and no leaks. Operations did not note any parts on runway. Aircraft was able to taxi safely back to parking and nose wheel directional control was adequate.Unknown cause to incident. Maintenance was called to inspect plane. Inspection not complete. Consideration is being given to right main wheel pants catching the tire and creating a speed differential that induced the uncontrolled turn to the right that could not be corrected prior to exiting into the grass.
1836140: On landing roll out on Runway XX an opposing Cessna was trying to land Runway YY. We angled to the side of the Runway. The Cessna finally did a very low altitude go around. Very close call.
1836149: We were approaching the airport from the west on an IFR flight plan. We called the airport in sight roughly 13nm from the field and Approach Control handed us off to Tower. Our company aircraft was ahead of us and already talking to Tower. They were told to enter a left base for Runway 2. We then checked in and gave our position and informed Tower we were on a visual approach for Runway 2. We were told to enter a left base for [Runway] 2. We then saw that our company was just ahead of us by maybe 2 miles and I turned right (to the south) and pulled the power, lowered the landing gear and configured to slow to our final approach speed to ensure separation between us and our company aircraft. Shortly after we were cleared to land on Runway 2. On about a 3-4 mile final and fully configured, we heard tower tell a small aircraft to enter left base, Runway 2. To our surprise, there was a small aircraft just ahead of us and to our left on the base leg. I told the PNF (Pilot not Flying) with me that the small aircraft was very close and was going to hit us. I had to push the nose down and turn to the right while the PNF simultaneously told the Tower Controller about that other airplane. At the same time, the small aircraft began turning final, right into our path. Within a matter of seconds the Tower controller told the small aircraft to go around and he started climbing above us. Since we were faster and below him, I turned back onto the extended centerline and stabilized the approach. This happened on about a 2 mile final. The PNF and I were both in shock that this had happened, especially since the tower was supposedly going to alleviate close calls in the pattern. Upon landing, I called the Tower to speak with a supervisor to discuss what had happened. The supervisor had gone home for the day but the person who answered the phone was the controller who was working tower position at the time of the incident. I told him that we were upset that another plane had come so close to us. I told him that in my XX years of flying, I had never come so close to another airplane in the air and that it shook me up. He said that the small aircraft had reported both us and the company small transport in sight, but I don't remember hearing the small aircraft call us in sight until he pointed us out and told us to go around.I think a major factor in this incident was the fact that the new tower had just begun operations that morning. I also think the controller, not being familiar with the local terrain and area contributed as well. Lastly and what I think is a major factor and was a total surprise to me, was the fact that the tower does not have a radar feed from BNA. In other words, it's a matter of the controllers asking for position reports and trusting that airplanes are where they say they are. From a safety standpoint, this should be added very soon.
1836518: Initially set for ZZZZZ ONE arrival to ZZZ. Runway XX active so they had to re-clear us on the ZZZZZ1 TWO. Center asked us to go direct to ZZZZZ2 and keep 290 or greater as we were out front of other traffic. Approach told us to go direct ZZZZZ2, cross ZZZZZ2 at 11,000 feet and cleared for RNAV GPS X XXR. The clearance of DIRECT ZZZZZ2 put us 90 degrees off the outbound course from ZZZZZ2. ZZZZZ2 is a fly-over fix. We arm the approach and cross over the top of ZZZZZ2 at 11,000 feet and the plane turns north and begins decent to next altitude. Approach calls us and says they have a low altitude alert on use as we were now below the minimum vector altitude for that area. She asks if we missed the turn and I said 'No', that the aircraft has a turn radius as we are turning to the north. She said minimum vector altitude was 10,900 feet and we were at 10,300 feet. We stopped our descent and the aircraft dropped out of the approach mode. Approach asked if we had the terrain insight, luckily for us it was clear with 10 mile visibility and we could see cultural lighting on the hills and knew terrain was not an immediate factor. None of the Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System annunciated and we were always in either the black or hashed green on the ND. Back on the inbound course, we selected a lower altitude and armed the approach. Nothing further.Center gave us a speed and we didn't get relief until we asked Approach. This higher speed resulted in a larger turn radius than had we been at the mandatory 210 knots restriction at ZZZZZ2. They also gave us direct to a Fly-Over fix with a 90 degree intercept, which set us up to fly through our final approach course, and asked us to cross ZZZZZ2 at 11,000 feet instead of the mandatory +13,000 feet restriction. This was all done to keep the other aircraft from getting a vector or slowing down. Don't give direct to a fly-over fix with 90 degrees of turn required at the fix, especially at night, at lower than published altitude, and in mountainous terrain.
1836564: First Officer's Qualification Line Check which concluded First Officer's IOE (Initial Operating Experience). First Officer was Pilot Flying. Check Airman was Pilot Monitoring. Normal arrival via SILCN5.KLIDE for ILS 30L at SJC. Shortly after KLIDE, both pilots became aware of flashes of intense blue laser light illuminating the windscreens for 1 to 2 seconds. Pilot Flying continued the approach referencing the instruments rather than scanning outside. Pilot Monitoring reported the threat to NORCAL Approach. After the handoff to SJC Tower, another burst of the same blue laser light appeared, this time from the right side of the aircraft. The flight leveled off at 3,300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring reported the latest burst to the Tower Controller.The distraction of both the laser events themselves and the reporting of the events to NCT (NorCal TRACON) and SJC Tower caused the Pilot Flying to lose track of the briefed stabilized approach plan. The delay in configuration caused the aircraft to be well above the glide path past the final approach fix. There was no way to continue the approach and remain within stabilized approach criteria, so the crew executed a missed approach. SJC Tower Controller instructed crew to climb to 3,000 feet and to contact NCT. NCT issued vectors for an ILS 30L. The second approach was unremarkable, as no further laser activity was noted. The Pilot Flying drew the sunshades on the right side of the aircraft to mitigate the threat of subsequent laser bursts. The remainder of the flight was normal. Following the termination of the flight, the crew [was] informed that the source of the laser activity was some sort of club establishment. They determined that the lasing appeared to be random and not intentionally targeted at aircraft. Flight was final leg of First Officer's (Initial Operating Experience) with the Captain as Line Captain. Line Captain was Pilot Monitoring while First Officer was Pilot Flying. This was the First Officer's Qualification Line Check. Flight was descending normally via the SILCN 5 arrival for transition via KLIDE for the ILS 30L approach to SJC. Past KLIDE, the Pilot Monitoring noted a brief (2-3 second) series of flashes of bright blue light. The Pilot Monitoring continued to scan for additional evidence of directed laser illumination and landmarks for reference, but did not mention the initial burst to the Pilot Flying. Several seconds later, a subsequent burst of flashes of light appeared to illuminate the windscreens, at which time the Pilot Flying also saw the light.Pilot Flying reported the incident to the NCT Approach Controller, and passed along generalized street locations of the position of the light. Within a minute, at the time of handover to SJC Tower, the flight was subjected to a third illumination burst viewed peripherally by the Pilot Flying, with the Pilot Monitoring noting the dazzle effect of the light on the flight deck windows. At this point, the flight leveled off at approximately 3,300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring contacted the Tower Controller, reporting the continued laser illumination from the same vicinity.At this time, the Pilot Flying noted that the flight was well above the vertical path and was not yet configured according to the briefed Stabilized Approach Plan. The crew immediately began speed reductions and configuration for approach, but soon determined that the flight was 'well above' the glide path and well past the final approach fix. The crew discontinued the approach at approximately 2,700 feet and climbed to maintain 3,000 feet per Tower instruction, and soon switched back to NORCAL for vectors back to final.Subsequent vectors to final and final approach and landing via the ILS to 30L were uneventful. The Pilot Flying drew the flight deck sun shades as a precaution from possible further laser illumination. There were no further illuminations observed during this second approach.It appeared that the source was from a club establishment that was using a laser light source with some reflective device that was reflecting the light upwards. The illumination appeared to be random and unintentional. The atmospheric conditions were clear with very little particulate in the air, which did not refract the laser light when it was directed away from our aircraft, neither crew noted any laser light being directed anywhere other than at our aircraft.
1836832: During flight on a practice VFR/VMC approach, the engine began sputtering. I swapped fuel tanks and it fixed the issue but I immediately began making my way to the nearest airport (ZZZ about 10NM from our location). Roughly 5-10 seconds later, the engine began sputtering again. I swapped the tanks again, and identified a location to set it down. A few seconds after swapping fuel tanks for the second time the engine quit. The auxiliary pump was on before the first instance of engine sputter and remained for the remainder of the flight. Once the engine quit and I realized I was not going to make ZZZ, so I [advised ATC] on XXX.YYY (ZZZ Approach). I advised Approach I was over the town of X and was going to set it down on a road in town. It was the only road that had enough lamp posts to where I could actually see the road. I executed the landing with no power. There was no damage done to any property or the aircraft, and there were no injuries or deaths.The conditions the night of the off field landing were night time (approximately 3 hours after sunset), winds from the south around 5 kts, 0% illumination with the moon still below the horizon at the time of the landing, and clear skies.The POH of the aircraft flown states at 75% power at the altitudes I was flying the aircraft should have been burning 10.5 gallons per hour. The 48 gallons total usable fuel capacity of the aircraft allows for appximately 4.5 hours of flight time before empty. We took off with full fuel. We ran out of fuel at 3.5 hours of Hobbs times. At the time of the engine stoppage, we should have had approximately 10 gallons/1 hour of fuel remaining.A new engine had just been installed on the aircraft. It had already flown on the new engine for approximately 2-3 hours when I was dispatched the aircraft for my flight. There was no fuel leak identified during the pre-flight. Or reported from the prior users of the aircraft.
1836876: I made a visual approach to Runway XX after completing a before landing checklist.An anti-skid check was performed as part of this checklist.I then landed on Runway XX which was dry and the wind was a light and variable. The approach was made at Vref +10 and touchdown was at vref within the touchdown zone. Air-brake was deployed as well as the thrust reverser. As I applied my initial brakes the airplane slowed, but seemed to drift left. I released brakes applied right rudder and continued the roll out and the aircraft straightened output still left of center. The aircraft continued to decelerate using reverse and nose wheel steering. Slowing below 80 knots additional braking was used slow to a taxi speed. The airplane pulled left with additional braking and steering applied and the nose gear and left main tires went into the grass just to the left side of the runway at the speed of a fast walk and then came to a stop with approximately 1,500 feet of runway remaining just prior to the taxiway. The right main gear remained well on the runway. There was no damage to the aircraft, airport surfaces, or airport signage. The aircraft was shutdown and passengers were deplaned and the runway was closed until the aircraft was towed back to the hangar. The crew had normal brake pressures and quantity indications and no reason to suspect a loss of fluid or braking ability.
